drafts.canonical_statement: Let G be a finite group whose order is nonzero in the field k. Every k[G]-submodule p of a k[G]-module V has a complementary k[G]-submodule q.

drafts.proof_strategy: Average a k-linear projection onto p over the group to obtain an equivariant projection, then take its kernel.
sketch_steps: setup: Choose a k-linear projection π from V onto p.
construct: Define π̃(v) = |G|⁻¹ Σ_g g⁻¹ π(g v), which makes sense because |G| is invertible in k.
derive: Check that π̃ is k[G]-linear, has image in p, and restricts to the identity on p.
conclude: The kernel of π̃ is a k[G]-submodule complementary to p.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply irreducibility to the kernel in the source and the image in the target.
sketch_steps: setup: Note that ker f and im f are subrepresentations of ρ and σ.
case_split: By irreducibility of ρ, ker f is either the whole space or zero.
derive: If ker f is everything then f = 0.
conclude: Otherwise f is injective with nonzero image, so irreducibility of σ makes f surjective.

drafts.proof_strategy: Take an eigenvalue of f and apply irreducibility to the kernel of f minus that scalar.
sketch_steps: setup: The space V is nonzero and finite dimensional over an algebraically closed field.
apply_theorem: Choose an eigenvalue c of f.
derive: The map f - c is an intertwiner with nonzero kernel.
conclude: Irreducibility forces that kernel to be all of V, so f = c.

drafts.canonical_statement: The character of a finite-dimensional representation is a class function, that is, χ(h g h⁻¹) = χ(g) for all group elements g and h.

drafts.proof_strategy: Expand the conjugate with the homomorphism property and use cyclicity of the trace.
sketch_steps: translate: Write ρ(h g h⁻¹) as ρ(h) ρ(g) ρ(h)⁻¹.
derive: Cyclicity of the trace removes the conjugation.
conclude: Hence the character takes the same value on g and h g h⁻¹.

drafts.proof_strategy: Identify the sum with the dimension of the space of intertwiners through the trace of the averaging projection, then apply Schur's lemma.
sketch_steps: translate: The function g ↦ χ_ρ(g) χ_σ(g⁻¹) is the character of the Hom representation.
derive: The averaging operator is a projection onto invariants, so its trace is the dimension of the invariants.
translate: The invariants of the Hom representation are exactly the intertwining maps.
apply_theorem: Schur's lemma gives dimension 1 for isomorphic representations and 0 otherwise.
conclude: The normalized sum equals that dimension viewed in k.

drafts.canonical_statement: In a Lie ring L, the bracket is anticommutative, that is, [x,y] = -[y,x] for all x and y.

drafts.proof_strategy: Expand the alternating identity for x + y using biadditivity.
sketch_steps: setup: Start from [x+y, x+y] = 0.
derive: Biadditivity expands this into four terms, two of which vanish.
conclude: The remaining relation is [x,y] + [y,x] = 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: In a Lie ring L, [x,[y,z]] + [y,[z,x]] + [z,[x,y]] = 0 for all x, y, z (the Jacobi identity).
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_bracket"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_bracket"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_bracket"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_bracket"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_bracket"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_bracket"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Rewrite the Leibniz rule with anticommutativity and move all terms to one side.
sketch_steps: setup: Write the Leibniz rule for x acting on [y,z].
derive: Replace [[x,y],z] by -[z,[x,y]] and [x,z] by -[z,x] using anticommutativity.
conclude: Collecting terms gives the cyclic sum equal to zero.

drafts.canonical_statement: For Lie ideals I and J of a Lie algebra, the ideal [I,J] is contained in the intersection of I and J.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="commutative_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="subset"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_ideal_bracket"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="intersect"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Check the generators [x,y] lie in both ideals using the ideal property and anticommutativity.
sketch_steps: setup: Take generators [x,y] with x in I and y in J.
derive: The ideal property of J gives [x,y] in J.
derive: Anticommutativity and the ideal property of I give [x,y] in I.
conclude: Since I ∩ J is an ideal, it contains the ideal generated by these brackets.

drafts.canonical_statement: The derived series of a Lie algebra is decreasing, so L^(k) is contained in L^(l) whenever l ≤ k.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="commutative_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="leq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="subset"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_derived_series"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_derived_series"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Show each term contains the next and iterate between l and k.
sketch_steps: derive: Each L^(n) is an ideal, so its bracket with itself stays inside it.
induction: Iterate the one-step inclusion from l up to k.
conclude: Therefore L^(k) lies in L^(l).

drafts.canonical_statement: If there is a surjective Lie algebra homomorphism from a solvable Lie algebra L to M, then M is solvable.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="commutative_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_algebra_hom"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="surjective"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="solvable_lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="solvable_lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Transport the derived series along the surjection and use the vanishing term of L.
sketch_steps: induction: Show f maps L^(k) onto M^(k) for every k using surjectivity.
apply_theorem: Solvability of L gives a k with L^(k) = 0.
conclude: Then M^(k) = 0, so M is solvable.

drafts.canonical_statement: Engel's theorem. A Lie algebra that is Noetherian as a module over a commutative ring is nilpotent if and only if ad x is a nilpotent endomorphism for every element x.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="commutative_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="noetherian_module"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="nilpotent_lie_algebra"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="nilpotent_op"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="adjoint_map"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: The forward direction reads off the lower central series; the converse takes a maximal subalgebra with the Engel property and grows it inside its normalizer.
sketch_steps: derive: If L is nilpotent, iterated ad x maps L into the lower central series, which vanishes.
setup: For the converse, consider subalgebras on which the conclusion holds.
apply_theorem: Noetherianity gives a maximal such subalgebra K.
contradiction: If K is proper, its normalizer yields a strictly larger subalgebra with the same property.
conclude: Therefore K = L and L is nilpotent.

drafts.canonical_statement: The ring of integers of a number field is a Dedekind domain.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="number_field"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="dedekind_domain"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ring_of_integers"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Verify the three defining properties, Noetherian, integrally closed, and dimension at most one.
sketch_steps: derive: An integral basis makes the ring a finitely generated Z-module, hence Noetherian.
translate: The ring is integrally closed in K by definition.
derive: A nonzero prime contains a nonzero integer, so the quotient is a finite domain.
conclude: Finite domains are fields, so nonzero primes are maximal.

drafts.canonical_statement: The ideal class group of the ring of integers of a number field is finite.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="number_field"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="class_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ring_of_integers"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Use a norm approximation bound from an integral basis to represent each class by an ideal containing a fixed integer.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix an integral basis and derive a constant M for approximation in the norm.
derive: For a nonzero ideal I, take a nonzero element β of minimal absolute norm.
derive: The approximation bound and minimality give M! I contained in (β).
translate: Thus the class of I is represented by an ideal containing M!.
conclude: Only finitely many ideals contain M!, so the class group is finite.

drafts.canonical_statement: A number field has class number one if and only if its ring of integers is a principal ideal domain.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="number_field"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="class_number"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="principal_ideal_domain"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ring_of_integers"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Read triviality of the class group as principality of all fractional ideals and pass between integral and fractional ideals.
sketch_steps: translate: Class number one means every nonzero fractional ideal is principal.
derive: Integral ideals are fractional ideals, so they are principal.
derive: A fractional ideal is an integral ideal divided by a nonzero element, which gives the converse.
conclude: The two conditions are equivalent.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a finite field extension L/K and x in K, the norm of x from L to K equals x raised to the degree [L:K].
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="field"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="field"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_extension"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="relative_norm"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="extension_degree"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Compute the determinant of multiplication by x, which is a scalar matrix.
sketch_steps: translate: The norm is the determinant of multiplication by x on L as a K-vector space.
derive: In any K-basis this map has matrix x times the identity.
conclude: Its determinant is x to the power [L:K].

drafts.canonical_statement: An element x of the ring of integers of a number field K is a unit if and only if the absolute value of its norm to the rationals equals 1.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="number_field"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ring_of_integers"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="unit_element"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ring_of_integers"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="abs"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="relative_norm"></n1:OMS><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="Q"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Use multiplicativity for one direction and the product of the other conjugates as a cofactor for the other.
sketch_steps: derive: If xy = 1 with y integral then N(x)N(y) = 1 in the integers, so |N(x)| = 1.
setup: Conversely assume |N(x)| = 1.
construct: Put y = N(x)/x, the product of the remaining conjugates, which is an algebraic integer lying in K.
conclude: Since xy = ±1, the element x is a unit.

drafts.canonical_statement: Let p be an odd prime and ζ a primitive p-th root of unity in the p-th cyclotomic field K. The norm of ζ - 1 from the ring of integers of K to Z equals p.

drafts.proof_strategy: Evaluate the p-th cyclotomic polynomial at 1 and track the sign from the even degree.
sketch_steps: setup: The minimal polynomial of ζ over Q is Φ_p, of degree p - 1.
derive: The product of 1 - σζ over the conjugates equals Φ_p(1) = p.
derive: Since p - 1 is even, replacing 1 - ζ by ζ - 1 does not change the norm.
conclude: Hence the norm of ζ - 1 is p.

drafts.canonical_statement: Let K be the n-th cyclotomic field and ζ a primitive n-th root of unity in K. An element of K is an algebraic integer if and only if it lies in Z[ζ].

drafts.proof_strategy: Treat prime powers by a discriminant and Eisenstein argument, then reduce the general case to coprime composita.
sketch_steps: derive: Elements of Z[ζ] are algebraic integers because ζ is one.
apply_theorem: For n a prime power, the discriminant of Z[ζ] is a power of p.
derive: An Eisenstein argument at 1 - ζ shows the index of Z[ζ] is prime to p, so Z[ζ] is the full ring of integers.
translate: For general n, write K as a compositum of cyclotomic fields of coprime prime-power orders.
apply_theorem: Coprime discriminants make the ring of integers of the compositum the product of the two rings.
conclude: Induction on the number of prime factors gives the claim for all n.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a prime p and p-adic numbers x and y, the ultrametric inequality ‖x+y‖ ≤ max(‖x‖, ‖y‖) holds.

drafts.proof_strategy: Prove the valuation inequality on rationals and extend it by density and continuity.
sketch_steps: derive: For rationals, a power of p dividing both terms divides the sum.
translate: The valuation inequality becomes the ultrametric inequality for the norm.
conclude: Density of Q and continuity of the norm extend it to Q_p.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the ultrametric inequality in both directions, writing y as (x+y) - x.
sketch_steps: setup: Assume without loss of generality that ‖x‖ < ‖y‖.
derive: The ultrametric inequality gives ‖x+y‖ ≤ ‖y‖.
derive: Writing y = (x+y) - x gives ‖y‖ ≤ max(‖x+y‖, ‖x‖), which forces ‖y‖ ≤ ‖x+y‖.
conclude: Hence ‖x+y‖ = ‖y‖ = max(‖x‖, ‖y‖).

drafts.canonical_statement: A p-adic integer z is a unit of Z_p if and only if ‖z‖ = 1.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use multiplicativity of the norm and the description of Z_p as the closed unit ball.
sketch_steps: derive: If zw = 1 in Z_p then ‖z‖‖w‖ = 1 with both factors at most 1, so ‖z‖ = 1.
setup: Conversely suppose ‖z‖ = 1, so z has an inverse in Q_p.
conclude: The inverse has norm 1, hence lies in Z_p.

drafts.canonical_statement: The field Q_p of p-adic numbers is complete with respect to the p-adic metric.

drafts.proof_strategy: Approximate a Cauchy sequence in Q_p by rationals and take the class of the resulting rational Cauchy sequence.
sketch_steps: setup: Take a Cauchy sequence x_n in Q_p.
construct: Choose rationals q_n with ‖x_n - q_n‖ < 1/(n+1) by density.
derive: The sequence q_n is Cauchy in the p-adic norm on Q, so it defines an element q of Q_p.
conclude: The sequence x_n converges to q.

sketch_steps: setup: Define the Newton sequence starting at a.
induction: Taylor expansion shows ‖F'(z_n)‖ stays constant and ‖F(z_n)‖ decays doubly exponentially.
derive: The sequence is Cauchy, so it converges in Z_p by completeness.
derive: Continuity shows the limit z is a root with ‖z-a‖ < ‖F'(a)‖.
conclude: Taylor expansion at z shows any other root in that ball equals z.

drafts.proof_strategy: Isolate the residue class with Dirichlet characters and use nonvanishing of L(1, χ) to show the prime sum diverges.
sketch_steps: translate: Character orthogonality expresses the prime sum over the class as a combination of log L(s, χ).
derive: The principal character contributes a term diverging as s tends to 1 from above.
apply_theorem: For nonprincipal χ, L(1, χ) is nonzero, so its term stays bounded.
derive: Therefore the sum of 1/p over primes p ≡ a diverges.
conclude: A divergent sum has infinitely many terms, so there are infinitely many such primes.

sketch_steps: derive: Commutativity, the identity, and negatives follow from the explicit formulas.
construct: Assign to each point the class of an ideal in the coordinate ring.
derive: Ideal computations show this map sends the chord-tangent sum to the product of classes.
derive: A norm degree argument shows the map is injective.
conclude: Associativity in the class group transfers to the point addition.

drafts.canonical_statement: Compactness theorem. A first-order theory has a model if and only if each of its finite subsets has a model.

drafts.proof_strategy: Take an ultraproduct of models of the finite subsets along an ultrafilter that contains every tail, and apply Łoś's theorem.
sketch_steps: derive: A model of T is a model of every finite subset.
setup: For the converse, index by the finite subsets S of T and choose a model M_S of each.
construct: Extend the sets of finite subsets containing a given S to an ultrafilter.
apply_theorem: Łoś's theorem shows each sentence of T holds in the ultraproduct.
conclude: The ultraproduct is a model of T.

If M is nonempty and κ ≤ |M|, some structure of cardinality κ embeds elementarily into M. If M is infinite and |M| ≤ κ, then M embeds elementarily into some structure of cardinality κ.

sketch_steps: construct: For the downward direction, close a subset of size κ under Skolem functions.
apply_theorem: The Tarski–Vaught test shows the closure is an elementary substructure of size κ.
construct: For the upward direction, add κ new distinct constants to the elementary diagram of M.
apply_theorem: Compactness gives a model of size at least κ into which M embeds elementarily.
conclude: Apply the downward direction above the image of M to reach size exactly κ.

drafts.canonical_statement: Gödel's β-function lemma. For every finite list of natural numbers l_0, ..., l_{m-1}, there exist natural numbers a and b with a mod ((i+1)b+1) = l_i for all i < m.

drafts.proof_strategy: Choose b divisible by all small differences so the moduli are pairwise coprime, then apply the Chinese remainder theorem.
sketch_steps: construct: Let s bound m and every entry of the list and put b = s!.
derive: A prime dividing two moduli divides (j-i)b, hence divides b, hence divides 1, which is impossible.
derive: The moduli are therefore pairwise coprime, and each exceeds the corresponding entry.
apply_theorem: The Chinese remainder theorem yields a with a ≡ l_i for every i.
conclude: Since l_i is below the modulus, the remainder equals l_i exactly.

sketch_steps: setup: A chain map sends cycles to cycles and boundaries to boundaries, which defines the induced map.
derive: On a representative cycle, both sides of the composition formula give the class of ψ(φ(z)).
derive: The identity chain map sends each class to itself.
conclude: Uniqueness in the universal properties gives the same identities in the general setting.

sketch_steps: setup: The homotopy h satisfies f - g = dh + hd.
derive: On a cycle z the term hd z vanishes, so f(z) - g(z) = d h(z).
conclude: The two images differ by a boundary, so they define the same homology class.

sketch_steps: setup: Apply the opcycles functor in degree i and the cycles functor in degree j to the short exact sequence.
derive: The first row is right exact and the second row is left exact.
construct: The differential induces vertical maps whose kernels are H_i and whose cokernels are H_j.
apply_theorem: The snake lemma produces the connecting morphism δ and an exact sequence.
conclude: Reading off the sequence gives exactness at H_i(X₂), H_i(X₃), and H_j(X₁).

conclude: The resulting condition is the ε-δ condition.

drafts.canonical_statement: If f(x) tends to L and to M as x tends to a with x ≠ a, then L = M.

drafts.proof_strategy: Separate two distinct limits by disjoint neighborhoods and use that the punctured neighborhood is nonempty.
sketch_steps: contradiction: Suppose L ≠ M and put ε = |L-M|/2.
derive: Choose x ≠ a close to a so that f(x) is within ε of both L and M.
derive: The triangle inequality gives |L-M| < 2ε.
conclude: This contradicts the choice of ε.

drafts.canonical_statement: If f(x) ≤ g(x) for all x ≠ a, and f → L and g → M as x → a, then L ≤ M.

drafts.proof_strategy: Argue by contradiction with a band of half the gap.
sketch_steps: contradiction: Assume L > M and set ε = (L-M)/2.
derive: Near a, f(x) > L-ε and g(x) < M+ε.
conclude: Since L-ε = M+ε this gives g(x) < f(x), a contradiction.

drafts.canonical_statement: f(x) → L as x → a with x ≠ a if and only if f(x_n) → L for every real sequence (x_n) with x_n ≠ a for all n and x_n → a.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use first countability of the punctured neighborhood filter; shift indices to meet the everywhere-different condition.
sketch_steps: derive: The forward direction composes the limit with a sequence tending to a inside the punctured neighborhood.
contradiction: If the limit fails, some ε > 0 has witnesses in each shrinking punctured ball.
construct: The witnesses form a sequence x_n ≠ a with x_n → a.
conclude: Then f(x_n) stays ε away from L, contradicting the hypothesis.

drafts.canonical_statement: f is continuous at a if and only if for every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 such that |x-a| < δ implies |f(x)-f(a)| < ε.

sketch_steps: translate: Express continuity at a with balls around a and f(a).
conclude: Replacing dist by |x-a| gives the ε-δ condition.

drafts.canonical_statement: f is continuous at a if and only if both the left limit and the right limit of f at a exist and equal f(a).

drafts.proof_strategy: Split the neighborhood of a into the left part, the point a, and the right part.
sketch_steps: derive: Continuity restricts to each side, giving both one-sided limits.
setup: Conversely fix ε > 0 and take δ₁ on the left and δ₂ on the right.
derive: With δ = min(δ₁, δ₂) the bound holds on both sides and trivially at x = a.
conclude: Hence f is continuous at a.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show the infimum exists from the bound f(a), then use monotonicity on (a, y).
sketch_steps: derive: The set of values for x > a is bounded below by f(a), so its infimum m exists.
construct: For ε > 0 pick y > a with f(y) < m + ε.
derive: For a < x < y monotonicity gives m ≤ f(x) < m + ε.
conclude: Therefore the right limit is m.

drafts.canonical_statement: A nondecreasing function on the reals that is bounded above converges as x tends to +∞.

drafts.proof_strategy: Take the supremum of the range and use monotonicity past a near-supremum point.
sketch_steps: derive: The range is bounded above, so it has a supremum L.
construct: For ε > 0 pick y with f(y) > L - ε.

sketch_steps: setup: Reduce to f(a) ≤ u ≤ f(b) by replacing f with -f if needed.
construct: Let c be the supremum of {x in [a,b] : f(x) ≤ u}.
derive: Continuity gives f(c) ≤ u.
contradiction: If f(c) < u and c < b, points just right of c also lie in the set.
conclude: Thus f(c) = u.

sketch_steps: contradiction: An unbounded f gives points x_n with f(x_n) > n.

construct: Take a sequence with f(y_n) → sup f and a convergent subsequence with limit y.
conclude: Continuity gives f(y) = sup f; apply the same to -f for the minimum.

sketch_steps: construct: Define g(x) = f(x) - x, continuous on [0,1].
derive: g(0) ≥ 0 and g(1) ≤ 0 since f maps into [0,1].
apply_theorem: The intermediate value theorem yields c with g(c) = 0.
conclude: Then f(c) = c.

drafts.proof_strategy: The difference f(y) - f(x) is continuous and nonvanishing on the convex set of pairs x < y, so it has constant sign.

derive: g is continuous on T and has no zero because f is injective.
apply_theorem: The intermediate value theorem on segments in T shows that g has constant sign.
conclude: A positive sign means f is strictly increasing, a negative sign strictly decreasing.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the Carathéodory form of differentiability of g to avoid dividing by f(x)-f(a).
sketch_steps: construct: Write g(y)-g(f(a)) = (v+ε(y))(y-f(a)) with ε continuous at f(a) and ε(f(a)) = 0.
derive: Substitute y = f(x) and divide by x-a.
derive: Continuity of f at a gives ε(f(x)) → 0.
conclude: The quotient tends to v·u.

drafts.proof_strategy: Add and subtract f(a)g(x) in the difference quotient.
sketch_steps: derive: Decompose the increment as (f(x)-f(a))g(x) + f(a)(g(x)-g(a)).
apply_theorem: g is continuous at a because it is differentiable there.
conclude: Passing to the limit gives u·g(a) + f(a)·v.

drafts.proof_strategy: Put the difference of quotients over a common denominator and pass to the limit.
sketch_steps: derive: Near a, g(x) ≠ 0 by continuity.
derive: Combine f(x)/g(x) - f(a)/g(a) over the denominator g(x)g(a).
derive: Divide by x-a and split the numerator into the two difference quotients.
conclude: The limit is (u·g(a) - f(a)·v)/g(a)².

drafts.canonical_statement: For a natural number n, the derivative of x^(n+1) at x is (n+1)x^n.

drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on n with the product rule.
sketch_steps: induction: The base case is the derivative of y, which is 1.
apply_theorem: Write y^(n+2) = y^(n+1)·y and use the product rule.
conclude: The result simplifies to (n+2)x^(n+1).

drafts.canonical_statement: For x > 0 and real p, the function y^p has derivative p·x^(p-1) at x.

drafts.proof_strategy: Write y^p as exp(p log y) and use the chain rule.
sketch_steps: translate: For y > 0, y^p = exp(p log y).
apply_theorem: The chain rule gives exp(p log x)·p/x.
conclude: This equals p·x^(p-1).

drafts.canonical_statement: If f has derivative u at a, then exp(f(x)) has derivative exp(f(a))·u at a.

sketch_steps: apply_theorem: exp has derivative exp(f(a)) at f(a).

sketch_steps: apply_theorem: log has derivative 1/f(a) at f(a) > 0.

sketch_steps: apply_theorem: f attains its maximum and minimum on [a,b].
case_split: If they coincide, f is constant and the derivative vanishes everywhere.
derive: Otherwise f(a) = f(b) forces one extremum at an interior point c.
apply_theorem: The derivative at an interior extremum is zero.
conclude: Hence g(c) = 0.

sketch_steps: construct: Let h(x) = f(x) - (f(b)-f(a))(x-a)/(b-a).
derive: h(a) = h(b) and h is differentiable on (a,b).
apply_theorem: Rolle's theorem gives c with h'(c) = 0.
conclude: Rearranging gives f(b)-f(a) = g(c)(b-a).

sketch_steps: derive: On the left of a, f is nonincreasing, so f(x) ≥ f(a).
derive: On the right of a, f is nondecreasing, so f(x) ≥ f(a).
conclude: Both sides give f(x) ≥ f(a) near a, so a is a local minimum.

drafts.canonical_statement: Taylor's theorem with Lagrange remainder. If a ≠ x, f is C^n on the closed interval between a and x, and the n-th derivative within that interval is differentiable on the open interval, then for some c in the open interval, f(x) = sum_{k≤n} f^(k)(a)(x-a)^k/k! + f^(n+1)(c)(x-a)^(n+1)/(n+1)!, with derivatives taken within the closed interval.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply Cauchy's mean value theorem to the remainder as a function of the expansion point and to (x-t)^(n+1).
sketch_steps: construct: Let F(t) = f(x) - sum_{k≤n} f^(k)(t)(x-t)^k/k!.
derive: The derivative telescopes to F'(t) = -f^(n+1)(t)(x-t)^n/n!.
construct: Let G(t) = (x-t)^(n+1), so G(x) = 0 = F(x).
apply_theorem: Cauchy's mean value theorem gives c with F(a)/G(a) = F'(c)/G'(c).
derive: The quotient on the right equals f^(n+1)(c)/(n+1)!.
conclude: Rearranging gives the Lagrange form.

drafts.canonical_statement: If f is twice differentiable on the reals with first derivative f1 and second derivative f2, and a < b, then f(b) = f(a) + f1(a)(b-a) + f2(c)(b-a)²/2 for some c in (a,b).

drafts.proof_strategy: Choose the constant making the error vanish at b, then apply Rolle's theorem twice.
sketch_steps: construct: Choose K with f(b) = f(a) + f1(a)(b-a) + K(b-a)²/2.
construct: Define g(x) = f(x) - f(a) - f1(a)(x-a) - K(x-a)²/2, so g(a) = g(b) = 0.
apply_theorem: Rolle's theorem gives c1 in (a,b) with g'(c1) = 0.
derive: Also g'(a) = 0, so Rolle's theorem applied to g' gives c in (a,c1) with g''(c) = 0.
conclude: Since g''(c) = f2(c) - K, we get K = f2(c).

drafts.canonical_statement: For every real x, 1 + x ≤ e^x.

drafts.proof_strategy: Minimize e^x - 1 - x using the sign of its derivative.
sketch_steps: construct: Let g(x) = e^x - 1 - x.
derive: g'(x) = e^x - 1 is negative for x < 0 and positive for x > 0.
conclude: g attains its minimum g(0) = 0, so g ≥ 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: For every x > 0, log x ≤ x - 1.

drafts.proof_strategy: Substitute y = log x into 1 + y ≤ e^y.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Use 1 + y ≤ e^y for all real y.
derive: With y = log x this gives 1 + log x ≤ x.
conclude: Rearrange to log x ≤ x - 1.

drafts.canonical_statement: For every real x, |sin x| ≤ |x|.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the mean value theorem to sin on the interval between 0 and x.
sketch_steps: case_split: The case x = 0 is immediate.
apply_theorem: The mean value theorem gives sin x = x cos c.
conclude: Since |cos c| ≤ 1, |sin x| ≤ |x|.

drafts.canonical_statement: For every real x, 1 - x²/2 ≤ cos x.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the half-angle formula and |sin y| ≤ |y|.
sketch_steps: translate: Write cos x = 1 - 2 sin²(x/2).
apply_theorem: Bound |sin(x/2)| ≤ |x/2|.
conclude: Hence cos x ≥ 1 - x²/2.

drafts.canonical_statement: If x, y > 0, then log(xy) = log x + log y.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply exp to both sides and use the exponential law.
sketch_steps: derive: exp(log x + log y) = exp(log x)·exp(log y) = xy.
conclude: Taking log, the inverse of exp, gives the identity.

drafts.canonical_statement: For all real x, y, sin(x+y) = sin x cos y + cos x sin y and cos(x+y) = cos x cos y - sin x sin y.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show that the squared error of both formulas has zero derivative and vanishes at x = 0.
sketch_steps: setup: Define sin and cos by power series, so their derivatives are known without the addition formulas.
construct: Fix y and define the errors S(x) and C(x).
derive: S' = C and C' = -S, so S² + C² has zero derivative.
derive: S(0) = C(0) = 0, so S² + C² vanishes identically.
conclude: Hence S = C = 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: sin x / x tends to 1 as x tends to 0 with x ≠ 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Squeeze sin x / x between cos x and 1 by comparing areas on the unit circle.
sketch_steps: derive: For 0 < x < π/2, comparing areas on the unit circle gives sin x < x < tan x.
derive: Dividing by sin x and inverting gives cos x < sin x / x < 1.
derive: Both bounds are even in x, so they also hold for -π/2 < x < 0.
conclude: Since cos x → 1 as x → 0, the squeeze theorem gives the limit 1.

drafts.canonical_statement: For every real t, (1 + t/x)^x tends to e^t as x tends to +∞.

drafts.proof_strategy: Write the power as an exponential and reduce the exponent to the derivative of log at 1.
sketch_steps: translate: For large x, (1+t/x)^x = exp(x log(1+t/x)).
derive: With h = t/x, the exponent equals t·log(1+h)/h.
apply_theorem: log(1+h)/h → 1 as h → 0 because log has derivative 1 at 1.
conclude: Continuity of exp gives the limit e^t.

drafts.canonical_statement: x log x tends to 0 as x tends to 0 from the right.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_right_limit_at"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="fns1" name="lambda"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="transc1" name="ln"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Substitute y = -log x and use that the exponential dominates y.
sketch_steps: translate: With y = -log x, x log x = -y e^(-y) and y → +∞.
derive: e^y ≥ y²/2 for y ≥ 0, so 0 ≤ y e^(-y) ≤ 2/y.
conclude: The squeeze theorem gives the limit 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Express the difference quotient minus f(b) as an average of f(t) - f(b) and use continuity at b.
sketch_steps: derive: Additivity gives F(b+h)-F(b) = ∫_b^(b+h) f(t) dt.
derive: Subtracting f(b) writes the error as (1/h)∫_b^(b+h)(f(t)-f(b)) dt.
apply_theorem: Continuity at b bounds the integrand by ε for small h.
conclude: The difference quotient tends to f(b).

sketch_steps: construct: Let G(x) = ∫_a^x f(t) dt.

derive: F - G has zero derivative at interior points, hence is constant on the interval.
conclude: F(b) - F(a) = G(b) - G(a) = ∫_a^b f(x) dx.

sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The chain rule gives (log f)' = g/f on the interval.
derive: g/f is continuous because f is continuous and positive.
apply_theorem: The fundamental theorem of calculus applies.
conclude: The integral equals log f(b) - log f(a).

drafts.canonical_statement: e^(-x) is integrable on (0,∞), ∫_0^∞ e^(-x) dx = 1, and ∫_0^t e^(-x) dx tends to 1 as t tends to +∞.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compute the proper integral on [0,t] and let t tend to infinity.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The fundamental theorem gives ∫_0^t e^(-x) dx = 1 - e^(-t).
derive: e^(-t) → 0 as t → +∞.
derive: Positivity of the integrand turns convergence into integrability.
conclude: The improper integral equals 1.

drafts.canonical_statement: If p > 1, then x^(-p) is integrable on (1,∞) and ∫_1^∞ x^(-p) dx = 1/(p-1).

drafts.proof_strategy: Integrate on [1,t] with the power rule and let t tend to infinity.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The fundamental theorem gives ∫_1^t x^(-p) dx = (1 - t^(1-p))/(p-1).
derive: Since p > 1, t^(1-p) → 0.
derive: Positivity of the integrand gives integrability.
conclude: The value is 1/(p-1).

drafts.canonical_statement: If p < 1, then x^(-p) is integrable on (0,1] and ∫_0^1 x^(-p) dx = 1/(1-p).

drafts.proof_strategy: Integrate on [s,1] and let s tend to 0 from the right.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The fundamental theorem gives ∫_s^1 x^(-p) dx = (1 - s^(1-p))/(1-p).
derive: Since p < 1, s^(1-p) → 0 as s → 0+.
derive: Positivity of the integrand gives integrability.
conclude: The value is 1/(1-p).

drafts.canonical_statement: If p ≤ 1, then x^(-p) is not integrable on (1,∞).

sketch_steps: derive: For x ≥ 1 and p ≤ 1, x^(-p) ≥ x^(-1).
derive: Therefore ∫_1^t x^(-p) dx ≥ log t.
conclude: Since log t → +∞, the positive integrand is not integrable.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use uniform continuity to bound the error on each subinterval and sum the bounds.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: f is uniformly continuous on [a,b].
setup: Fix ε > 0, take the matching δ, and choose n with h = (b-a)/(n+1) < δ.
derive: Split the integral into n+1 subintervals by additivity.
derive: On each subinterval, |h f(x_k) - ∫ f| ≤ εh/(b-a+1).
conclude: Summing gives a total error below ε.

drafts.canonical_statement: For finite sets A and B, |A ∪ B| + |A ∩ B| = |A| + |B|.

drafts.proof_strategy: Partition the union into the parts lying only in A, only in B and in both, then compare counts.
sketch_steps: setup: Split A ∪ B into A only, B only and A ∩ B, with sizes a, b and c.
derive: Then |A| = a + c, |B| = b + c and |A ∪ B| = a + b + c.
conclude: Both sides of the identity equal a + b + 2c.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the two-set identity three times and use distributivity of intersection over union.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Apply the two-set identity to A ∪ B and C.
translate: Rewrite (A ∪ B) ∩ C as (A ∩ C) ∪ (B ∩ C).
apply_theorem: Apply the two-set identity to A and B and to A ∩ C and B ∩ C.
conclude: Add the three equalities and cancel the common terms.

drafts.canonical_statement: For finite sets A and B, the Cartesian product satisfies |A × B| = |A|·|B|.

drafts.proof_strategy: Group the pairs by first coordinate; every group has |B| elements.
sketch_steps: setup: For a in A, consider the fibre of pairs with first coordinate a.
derive: Each fibre is in bijection with B.
conclude: Summing over the |A| disjoint fibres gives |A|·|B|.

drafts.canonical_statement: The number of functions from a finite set A to a finite set B is |B|^|A|.

drafts.proof_strategy: A function is an independent choice of a value in B for each element of A.
sketch_steps: translate: Identify a function with the tuple of its values indexed by A.
apply_theorem: The product rule gives one factor |B| for each element of A.
conclude: The total is |B|^|A|.

drafts.canonical_statement: A finite set A has exactly 2^|A| subsets.

drafts.proof_strategy: Encode a subset by its membership choices and apply the product rule.
sketch_steps: translate: Identify a subset with its characteristic function A → {0,1}.
apply_theorem: Count these functions by the product rule.
conclude: There are 2^|A| of them.

drafts.canonical_statement: The number of bijections of a finite set A onto itself is |A|!.

drafts.proof_strategy: Choose images one at a time, excluding those already used.
sketch_steps: setup: Enumerate the n elements of A.
induction: The k-th element has n-k+1 possible images not yet used.
derive: An injective self-map of a finite set is automatically bijective.
conclude: Multiplying the numbers of choices gives n!.

drafts.canonical_statement: The number of k-element subsets of a finite set A is the binomial coefficient C(|A|, k).
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="size"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="size"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="k_subsets"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="binom"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="size"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on |A| by splitting subsets according to whether they contain a fixed element.
sketch_steps: induction: Induct on the size of A; the empty case is immediate.
case_split: Split k-subsets by whether they contain a fixed element a.
derive: The two classes correspond to (k-1)-subsets and k-subsets of A \ {a}.
apply_theorem: Pascal's identity adds the two counts.
conclude: The total is C(|A|, k).

sketch_steps: setup: Fix an element a of an (n+1)-element set.
case_split: Subsets containing a number C(n, k); those omitting a number C(n, k+1).
conclude: Adding the two classes gives C(n+1, k+1).

drafts.canonical_statement: If k ≤ n, then C(n, n-k) = C(n, k).

drafts.proof_strategy: Taking complements is a bijection between k-subsets and (n-k)-subsets.
sketch_steps: construct: Send each subset of an n-set to its complement.
derive: This involution exchanges size k with size n - k.
conclude: Hence the two binomial coefficients agree.

drafts.canonical_statement: If k ≤ n, then C(n, k) · k! · (n-k)! = n!.

drafts.proof_strategy: Count permutations by first choosing which elements occupy the first k positions.
sketch_steps: setup: Count the n! orderings of an n-element set.
construct: Choose the set in the first k positions in C(n, k) ways.
derive: Order that set in k! ways and the rest in (n-k)! ways.
conclude: Each ordering arises exactly once, giving the identity.

drafts.proof_strategy: Double count pairs consisting of a (k+1)-subset and a distinguished member.
sketch_steps: setup: Count pairs (S, x) with S a (k+1)-subset of an (n+1)-set and x in S.
derive: Choosing S first gives (k+1)·C(n+1, k+1).
derive: Choosing x first gives (n+1)·C(n, k).
conclude: The two counts are equal.

drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on n and collect coefficients with Pascal's identity.
sketch_steps: induction: The case n = 0 is immediate.
derive: Multiply the expansion for n by x + y.
derive: The coefficient of x^m y^(n+1-m) is C(n, m-1) + C(n, m).
apply_theorem: Pascal's identity turns it into C(n+1, m).

drafts.proof_strategy: Count all subsets of an n-set, grouped by size.
sketch_steps: setup: Classify subsets of an n-set by their size k.
derive: There are C(n, k) subsets of size k.
conclude: Summing over k gives the total number 2^n of subsets.

drafts.proof_strategy: Substitute x = -1 and y = 1 into the binomial theorem.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The binomial theorem gives Σ (-1)^k C(n, k) = (-1 + 1)^n.
derive: The base is 0 and the exponent n is positive.
conclude: The alternating sum vanishes.

drafts.proof_strategy: Classify (k+1)-subsets of {0, ..., n} by their largest element.
sketch_steps: setup: Consider (k+1)-subsets of {0, ..., n}.
case_split: Classify them by the largest element m, which ranges from k to n.
derive: Exactly C(m, k) subsets have largest element m.
conclude: Summing over m gives C(n+1, k+1).

drafts.proof_strategy: Remove the zero term, absorb the factor k, and use the sum of binomials.
sketch_steps: derive: The term k = 0 vanishes.
apply_theorem: The absorption identity gives k·C(n+1, k) = (n+1)·C(n, k-1) for k ≥ 1.
translate: Factor out n + 1 and reindex by j = k - 1.
conclude: Σ_j C(n, j) = 2^n yields the claim.

drafts.proof_strategy: Choose n people from two groups of size n and classify by the number taken from the first group.
sketch_steps: setup: Split a 2n-element set into two n-element parts.
case_split: Classify n-subsets by the number k of elements in the first part.
apply_theorem: Each class has C(n, k)·C(n, n-k) members.
derive: Symmetry gives C(n, n-k) = C(n, k).
conclude: Summing over k gives C(2n, n).

drafts.proof_strategy: Classify k-subsets of a disjoint union by how many elements come from each part.
sketch_steps: setup: Take a disjoint union of an m-element set and an n-element set.
case_split: Classify k-subsets by the pair (i, j) of counts in the two parts.
derive: The pair (i, j) with i + j = k accounts for C(m, i)·C(n, j) subsets.
conclude: Summing over all such pairs gives C(m+n, k).

induction: Induct on the finite set I; the empty case is trivial.
apply_theorem: Use a!·b! ∣ (a+b)! from integrality of binomial coefficients.
conclude: Combining with the induction hypothesis gives divisibility.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compute the contribution of each element to the right side using the alternating sum of binomials.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix an element x and let J be the set of indices i with x in S_i.
translate: x lies in the intersection over T exactly when T ⊆ J.
derive: The contribution of x is the sum of (-1)^(|T|+1) over nonempty T ⊆ J.
apply_theorem: The alternating binomial sum makes this 1 when J is nonempty.
conclude: The right side counts each element of the union exactly once.

derive: The permutations fixing k given elements number (n-k)!.

conclude: Simplify using C(n, k)·(n-k)! = n!/k!.

conclude: So two distinct elements of A share a value.

drafts.proof_strategy: Sum fibre sizes over B and compare with the bound |B|·n.
sketch_steps: contradiction: Suppose every fibre over B has at most n elements.
derive: A is the disjoint union of its fibres over B.
derive: Thus |A| ≤ |B|·n.
conclude: This contradicts |B|·n < |A|.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the pigeonhole principle to the remainder map modulo n.
sketch_steps: setup: Send x in S to its remainder modulo n.
derive: There are exactly n possible remainders.
apply_theorem: Since |S| > n, the pigeonhole principle gives distinct a and b with the same remainder.
conclude: Equal remainders mean n divides a - b.

sketch_steps: setup: Let E be the set of pairs (a, b) with r(a, b).
derive: Grouping E by a gives the left side.
derive: Grouping E by b gives the right side.
conclude: Both sides equal |E|.

drafts.proof_strategy: Verify that C(2n, n)/(n+1) satisfies the convolution recurrence, then use uniqueness.
sketch_steps: setup: Put D_n = C(2n, n)/(n+1).
derive: Show that D_0 = 1 and that D satisfies the convolution recurrence.
induction: Strong induction shows D_n = C_n.
conclude: Clearing the denominator gives the identity.

sketch_steps: induction: For n = 0 both sides equal 1.
derive: Adding F_n to the identity for n gives F_n + F_{n+1}.
conclude: The recurrence turns this into F_{n+2}.

drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on n, expressing the next terms in F_n and F_{n+1}.
sketch_steps: induction: Check the base case n = 0.
setup: Put a = F_n and b = F_{n+1}, so F_{n+2} = a + b and F_{n+3} = a + 2b.
derive: The expression at n + 1 equals minus the expression at n.
conclude: The induction hypothesis gives (-1)^(n+2).

drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on d, multiplying by 1 - X and using Pascal's identity on coefficients.
sketch_steps: induction: The case d = 0 is the geometric series identity.
derive: Multiply the series for d + 1 by 1 - X and compare coefficients.
apply_theorem: Pascal's identity gives the series for d.
conclude: The induction hypothesis finishes the proof.

drafts.canonical_statement: In a finite simple graph G, the sum of the degrees of all vertices equals twice the number of edges.

drafts.proof_strategy: Double count incident vertex–edge pairs.
sketch_steps: setup: Consider the pairs (v, e) with v an endpoint of the edge e.
derive: Grouping by v gives Σ deg(v).
derive: Grouping by e gives 2|E|, since a simple graph edge has two distinct endpoints.
conclude: The two counts agree.

sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The degree sum equals 2|E| and is therefore even.
derive: Removing the even-degree vertices leaves an even sum of odd numbers.
conclude: An even sum of odd numbers has an even number of terms.

drafts.proof_strategy: If all degrees differ, both 0 and n-1 occur, which is impossible.
sketch_steps: contradiction: Suppose all n degrees are distinct.
derive: Degrees lie in {0, ..., n-1}, so injectivity makes every value occur.
setup: Take u of degree 0 and w of degree n-1; they are distinct since n ≥ 2.
derive: The vertex w is adjacent to every other vertex, including u.
conclude: This contradicts deg(u) = 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: A finite tree has exactly one edge fewer than it has vertices.

drafts.proof_strategy: Remove a leaf and induct on the number of vertices.
sketch_steps: induction: A single-vertex tree has no edges.
construct: In a tree with at least two vertices, an endpoint of a longest path has degree one, since another neighbor would extend the path or close a cycle.
derive: Deleting that vertex and its edge leaves a tree.
conclude: Restoring one vertex and one edge preserves the identity.

drafts.proof_strategy: Turn two distinct paths into a cycle, and a cycle into two distinct paths.
sketch_steps: derive: In a tree, connectivity gives a path between any two vertices.
contradiction: Two distinct paths with the same endpoints would produce a cycle.
derive: Conversely, existence of paths gives connectivity.
contradiction: A cycle gives two distinct paths between adjacent vertices on it.
conclude: Therefore the two conditions are equivalent.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compare the degree sum 2n-2 with the lower bound from minimum degree two.
sketch_steps: derive: Connectivity and n ≥ 2 force every degree to be at least 1.
apply_theorem: The degree sum of a tree equals 2(n-1).
contradiction: If all degrees were at least 2, the sum would be at least 2n.
conclude: Hence some vertex has degree exactly 1.

drafts.proof_strategy: Delete cycle edges to reach a spanning tree and apply the tree edge count.
sketch_steps: derive: Removing an edge on a cycle keeps a graph connected.
construct: Repeating this produces a spanning tree of G.
apply_theorem: The spanning tree has |V| - 1 edges.
conclude: Since its edges are edges of G, |V| - 1 ≤ |E|.

drafts.canonical_statement: A simple graph is 2-colorable if and only if every closed walk has even length.

drafts.proof_strategy: Colors alternate along walks; conversely, color each vertex by the parity of a walk from a base point.
sketch_steps: derive: A proper 2-coloring changes color at each step, so closed walks are even.
setup: Conversely, choose a base point in each connected component.
construct: Color each vertex by the parity of a walk from the base point.
derive: Evenness of closed walks makes this parity independent of the walk.
conclude: Adjacent vertices get different colors, so the coloring is proper.

drafts.proof_strategy: Pair the edges at each vertex as consecutive entries and exits of the closed walk.
sketch_steps: setup: Follow the closed walk p and record the visits to x.
derive: Each visit uses one incoming and one outgoing edge at x.
derive: At the base point the first and last edges also pair up.
conclude: Since p uses each edge once, deg(x) is even.

sketch_steps: derive: Each interior passage through a vertex uses two of its edges.
derive: Vertices other than u and v therefore have even degree.
case_split: If u = v, the endpoint edges pair up and no vertex has odd degree.
case_split: If u ≠ v, exactly u and v have odd degree.
conclude: The number of odd-degree vertices is 0 or 2.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the pigeonhole principle to the neighbours of a fixed vertex and split on adjacency among three of them.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix a vertex v; at least five other vertices remain.
apply_theorem: The pigeonhole principle gives three neighbours or three non-neighbours of v.
case_split: For three neighbours, any edge among them forms a triangle with v.
derive: Otherwise those three are mutually non-adjacent.
conclude: The case of three non-neighbours is symmetric.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show that an edge-maximal clique-free graph is complete multipartite and balanced, then count its edges.
sketch_steps: setup: Take a graph with no (r+1)-clique and the maximum number of edges.
derive: Non-adjacency in such a graph is an equivalence relation.
derive: Moving a vertex between classes shows that class sizes differ by at most 1.
derive: Hence the graph is isomorphic to the Turán graph T(n, r).
conclude: Counting the edges of T(n, r) gives the stated bound.

case_split: If a proper subset S is tight, split into S and its complement.
derive: For infinite I, use compactness of the inverse system of finite matchings.

drafts.proof_strategy: Count orderings whose initial segment lies in F to get the LYM inequality, then bound by the middle binomial coefficient.
sketch_steps: setup: Consider all n! orderings of X.
derive: A set A of size k is an initial segment of k!(n-k)! orderings.
derive: The antichain condition allows at most one member of F per ordering.
derive: Therefore Σ_{A∈F} 1/C(n, |A|) ≤ 1.
apply_theorem: Each C(n, |A|) is at most C(n, ⌊n/2⌋).
conclude: Hence |F| ≤ C(n, ⌊n/2⌋).

sketch_steps: contradiction: Suppose x ≠ y both lie in C ∩ A.
derive: Since C is a chain, x and y are comparable.
derive: Since A is an antichain, x and y are incomparable.
conclude: This contradiction shows that C ∩ A has at most one element.

derive: The antichain condition forces them to be equal, so g is injective.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show that fractions with numerator in P form a proper ideal whose complement consists of units.
sketch_steps: setup: Let m be the set of fractions a/s with a in P and s outside P.
derive: m is an ideal of S, and it is proper because 1 = a/s would put a product ts outside P inside P.
derive: A fraction a/s with a outside P has inverse s/a.
conclude: The nonunits of S are exactly m, so S is local.

drafts.proof_strategy: Turn vanishing in the localization into honest vanishing after multiplying by an element of S, then use exactness upstairs.
sketch_steps: derive: The composite of the induced maps vanishes because h ∘ g = 0.
setup: Take m/s in the localized middle term killed by the induced h.
translate: Vanishing of h(m)/s means t h(m) = 0 for some t in S.
apply_theorem: Exactness gives x with g(x) = t m.
conclude: Then m/s is the image of x/(ts).

drafts.canonical_statement: If R is a local ring with maximal ideal m and M is a finitely generated R-module with mM = M, then M = 0.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="local_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="module_over"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finitely_generated_module"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ideal_smul_submodule"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="unique_maximal_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="whole_submodule"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="whole_submodule"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="zero_module_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Use a minimal generating set and the fact that 1 minus an element of m is a unit.
sketch_steps: setup: Suppose M is nonzero and take a generating set of minimal size.
translate: mM = M writes the last generator as a combination with coefficients in m.
derive: Moving the last term to the left gives (1 - a) x_n in the span of the others, and 1 - a is a unit.
contradiction: The last generator is redundant, against minimality.

drafts.canonical_statement: If R is local with maximal ideal m, M is a finitely generated R-module and N is a submodule with N + mM = M, then N = M.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="local_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="module_over"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finitely_generated_module"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="submodule_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="submodule_sum"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ideal_smul_submodule"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="unique_maximal_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="whole_submodule"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="whole_submodule"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="whole_submodule"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Apply Nakayama's lemma to the quotient M/N.
sketch_steps: setup: Consider the finitely generated module M/N.
translate: N + mM = M says m(M/N) = M/N.
apply_theorem: Nakayama's lemma gives M/N = 0.
conclude: Therefore N = M.

drafts.canonical_statement: If R is a Noetherian commutative ring, then the polynomial ring in n variables over R is Noetherian.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="noetherian_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="noetherian_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="mv_polynomial_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="variable_family"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on the number of variables using the one-variable basis theorem.
sketch_steps: induction: The case n = 0 is R itself.
translate: The ring in n + 1 variables is the one-variable polynomial ring over the ring in n variables.
apply_theorem: The one-variable Hilbert basis theorem applies to the Noetherian ring in n variables.
conclude: The ring in n + 1 variables is Noetherian.

drafts.canonical_statement: A commutative Artinian integral domain is a field.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="integral_domain"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="artinian_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="is_field"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Stabilize the descending chain of powers of a nonzero element and cancel.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix a nonzero element a of R.
derive: The chain of ideals generated by powers of a stabilizes, so a^n = b a^(n+1) for some n and b.
derive: Cancelling a^n in the domain gives 1 = b a.
conclude: Every nonzero element is a unit, so R is a field.

drafts.canonical_statement: A commutative ring is Artinian if and only if it is Noetherian and every prime ideal is maximal.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="artinian_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="noetherian_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="prime_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="maximal_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Write zero as a product of maximal ideals and compare chain conditions on the resulting filtration.
sketch_steps: derive: In either case primes are maximal, there are finitely many of them, and the nilradical is nilpotent.
construct: Hence some product of maximal ideals, with repetition, is zero.
derive: The successive quotients of the resulting filtration are vector spaces over residue fields.
apply_theorem: On a vector space the ascending and descending chain conditions coincide.
conclude: Thus R has one chain condition exactly when it has the other.

drafts.canonical_statement: For an ideal I of a commutative ring, an element x has a power in I if and only if x lies in every prime ideal containing I.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ideal_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="prime_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="subset"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: The forward direction uses primality; the converse uses a Zorn argument producing a prime avoiding the powers of x.
sketch_steps: derive: If x^n lies in I and P is a prime containing I, then x lies in P.
setup: Conversely, suppose no power of x lies in I.
construct: By Zorn's lemma take an ideal containing I maximal among those missing all powers of x.
derive: This maximal ideal is prime and does not contain x.
conclude: The two conditions are equivalent.

drafts.canonical_statement: The radical of a primary ideal of a commutative ring is a prime ideal.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="primary_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="prime_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ideal_radical"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the primary condition to the power x^n y^n lying in I.
sketch_steps: derive: rad(I) is proper because I is proper.
setup: Suppose x y lies in rad(I), so x^n y^n lies in I for some n.
apply_theorem: The primary condition gives x^n in I or a power of y^n in I.
conclude: Either x or y lies in rad(I), so rad(I) is prime.

drafts.canonical_statement: An ideal of a commutative ring whose radical is a maximal ideal is primary.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ideal_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="maximal_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ideal_radical"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="primary_ideal"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: In R/I every element is a unit or nilpotent, which is the primary condition.
sketch_steps: derive: The only prime of R/I is m/I, so R/I is local with nilpotent nonunits.
setup: Take x y in I.
case_split: If y is outside m, its image is a unit and x lies in I.
case_split: If y lies in m, a power of y lies in I.
conclude: I is primary.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every ideal of a Noetherian commutative ring is a finite intersection of primary ideals, the whole ring being the empty intersection (Lasker-Noether theorem).

drafts.proof_strategy: Decompose into irreducible ideals by Noetherian induction, then show irreducible ideals are primary.
sketch_steps: contradiction: A maximal counterexample to finite irreducible decomposition cannot exist.
derive: Such an ideal would be reducible, hence an intersection of two larger ideals that do decompose.
setup: Next pass to the quotient by an irreducible ideal and assume x y = 0.
derive: Stabilization of the annihilators of powers of y gives (x) ∩ (y^n) = 0 for large n.
apply_theorem: Irreducibility forces x = 0 or y^n = 0, which is the primary condition.
conclude: Every ideal is a finite intersection of primary ideals.

drafts.canonical_statement: A finitely generated module over a Noetherian commutative ring has only finitely many associated primes.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="comm_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="noetherian_ring"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="module_over"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finitely_generated_module"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="associated_primes"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Filter M with quotients R/P and use subadditivity of Ass along short exact sequences.
sketch_steps: construct: Take a finite filtration of M with successive quotients isomorphic to R/P_i.
apply_theorem: Ass(M) is contained in Ass(N) ∪ Ass(M/N) for a submodule N.
derive: Ass(R/P) = {P} for a prime P.
conclude: Ass(M) lies in the finite set {P_1, ..., P_n}.

drafts.proof_strategy: A maximal annihilator above Ann(x) is an associated prime containing r.
sketch_steps: derive: If r lies in the annihilator of a nonzero x, then r x = 0.
setup: Conversely take x nonzero with r x = 0.
construct: Choose y nonzero with Ann(y) maximal among annihilators containing Ann(x).
derive: Maximality shows Ann(y) is prime.
conclude: r lies in the associated prime Ann(y).

drafts.canonical_statement: If x and y in an R-algebra A are integral over R, then x + y and xy are integral over R.

drafts.proof_strategy: Place both elements in the finite R-module R[x,y] and apply the determinant trick.
sketch_steps: derive: R[x] is a finitely generated R-module, and R[x,y] is finitely generated over R[x].
derive: Hence R[x,y] is a finitely generated R-module.
apply_theorem: By Cayley-Hamilton, every element of a subalgebra that is a finite R-module is integral over R.
conclude: x + y and x y lie in R[x,y], so they are integral.

drafts.canonical_statement: An element of an R-algebra A that is integral over the integral closure C of R in A is integral over R, so C is integrally closed in A.
