sketch_steps: setup: Choose the preferred charts at x, f(x) and g(f(x)).
translate: Differentiability means the chart representations of f and g are differentiable.
derive: The representation of g∘f is the composite of the two representations.
apply_theorem: The chain rule in normed spaces gives differentiability and the composite derivative.
conclude: The tangent map is the derivative of the representation, so the formula follows.

drafts.canonical_statement: On charted spaces, where smoothness of the transition maps is not assumed, so the spaces need not be manifolds, the tangent map in the preferred charts of the identity at x is the identity of the tangent space at x, and the tangent map of a constant map is zero.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compute both tangent maps from their chart representations.
sketch_steps: translate: Write the maps in the preferred charts at x and at the value point.
derive: The identity map is represented near x by the identity, whose derivative is the identity.
derive: A constant map is represented by a constant, whose derivative is zero.
conclude: The tangent maps are as claimed.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a map f between real normed spaces viewed as manifolds over themselves, manifold differentiability at x is equivalent to Fréchet differentiability at x, and when f is Fréchet differentiable at x the tangent map equals the Fréchet derivative.

drafts.proof_strategy: The charts are identities, so the chart representation is f itself.
sketch_steps: setup: On a normed space viewed as a manifold over itself every preferred chart is the identity.
translate: The chart representation of f is f.
derive: Manifold differentiability reduces to continuity at x plus Fréchet differentiability.
derive: Fréchet differentiability already implies continuity.
conclude: The two notions and the two derivatives coincide.

drafts.proof_strategy: Build a radial cutoff from the function e^{-1/t} after passing to a Euclidean norm.
sketch_steps: setup: Transfer to a Euclidean norm using finite dimensionality and choose a closed ball in s.
construct: From e^{-1/t} build a smooth ρ that is 0 for t ≤ 0 and 1 for t ≥ 1.
construct: Define f(y) = ρ(2 - 2‖y-x‖/d).
derive: f equals 1 near x, vanishes outside the ball, and is smooth since the norm is smooth away from x.
conclude: Its support is a closed ball, which is compact in finite dimensions and lies in s.

drafts.canonical_statement: Let M be a Hausdorff σ-compact smooth manifold modelled on a finite-dimensional real space, s a closed subset and U a family of open sets covering s. Then there is a smooth partition of unity on s subordinate to U.

drafts.proof_strategy: Refine by locally finite smooth bump functions, then normalize by a telescoping product.
sketch_steps: setup: M is locally compact, σ-compact and Hausdorff, hence paracompact.
construct: Choose smooth bump functions near each point of s, supported inside some U_i.
derive: Extract a locally finite subfamily whose interiors of level sets cover s.
construct: Define f_j = g_j ∏_{k<j}(1 - g_k), which telescopes to a sum 1 on s.
derive: Local finiteness makes the sums and products smooth.
conclude: Group the functions by index i to get a partition subordinate to U.

drafts.canonical_statement: For points a, b, c of a real inner product (Euclidean affine) space, |ac|² = |ab|² + |cb|² - 2|ab||cb|cos∠abc.

drafts.proof_strategy: Expand the squared norm of a difference of vectors from b.
sketch_steps: setup: Put u = a - b and v = c - b, so a - c = u - v.
derive: Expanding gives |u-v|² = |u|² + |v|² - 2⟨u,v⟩.
apply_theorem: The definition of angle gives ⟨u,v⟩ = |u||v|cos∠abc.
conclude: Substituting yields the law of cosines.

drafts.canonical_statement: For vectors x, y in a real inner product space, ‖x+y‖² + ‖x-y‖² = 2(‖x‖² + ‖y‖²).

drafts.proof_strategy: Expand both squared norms by bilinearity and add them.
sketch_steps: derive: ‖x+y‖² = ‖x‖² + 2⟨x,y⟩ + ‖y‖².
derive: ‖x-y‖² = ‖x‖² - 2⟨x,y⟩ + ‖y‖².
conclude: Adding cancels the inner product terms.

drafts.canonical_statement: For points with a ≠ b and c ≠ b, |ac|² = |ab|² + |cb|² holds if and only if ∠abc = π/2.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the law of cosines and use that cosine vanishes on [0,π] only at π/2.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The law of cosines gives |ac|² = |ab|² + |cb|² - 2|ab||cb|cos∠abc.
derive: Since a ≠ b and c ≠ b, the product |ab||cb| is nonzero.
translate: The equation is therefore equivalent to cos∠abc = 0.
conclude: On [0,π] this is equivalent to ∠abc = π/2.

drafts.canonical_statement: For three distinct points a, b, c of a Euclidean affine space, ∠abc + ∠bca + ∠cab = π.

drafts.proof_strategy: Draw the parallel to bc through a and use alternate angles.
sketch_steps: case_split: In the collinear case one angle is π and the others are 0.
construct: Otherwise put d = a + (b-c) and e = a + (c-b) on the parallel to bc through a.
derive: Comparing inner products gives ∠dab = ∠abc and ∠eac = ∠bca.
derive: Rays ab and ac lie on the same side of the line, so ∠dab + ∠bac + ∠cae = π.
conclude: Substituting the alternate angles gives the sum π.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the power of the point and similar triangles to express everything through a, b, c, p, then close with Stewart's theorem.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The intersecting chords theorem gives |ap||cp| = |bp||dp|.
derive: Triangles apb and dpc are similar, so |cd| = (|cp|/|bp|)|ab|.
derive: Triangles bpc and apd are similar, so |da| = (|ap|/|bp|)|bc|.
translate: Substituting these and |dp| = |ap||cp|/|bp| reduces the claim to an identity in triangle abc.
apply_theorem: That identity is Stewart's theorem for the point p on side ac.
conclude: Ptolemy's equality follows.

drafts.canonical_statement: If points a, b, c, d lie on a common sphere and p lies in the affine span of {a,b} and in the affine span of {c,d} (a line when the two points differ, a single point otherwise), then |ap||bp| = |cp||dp|.

drafts.proof_strategy: Express each product as the absolute value of the power of p with respect to the sphere.
sketch_steps: setup: Let o and r be the center and radius of the sphere and m the midpoint of ab.
derive: Since om is orthogonal to ab, |op|² - r² = |mp|² - |ma|².
derive: For p on line ab, |ap||bp| = ||mp|² - |ma|²|.
derive: So |ap||bp| = ||op|² - r²|, and the same holds for c, d.
conclude: The two products are equal.

drafts.canonical_statement: For nonzero vectors x, y in a real inner product space, ⟨x,y⟩ = 0 if and only if the angle between x and y equals π/2.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="inner_product"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="vector_angle"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="divide"></n1:OMS><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="pi"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Use the defining formula of the angle and the injectivity of cosine on [0,π].
sketch_steps: setup: The angle θ in [0,π] satisfies ⟨x,y⟩ = ‖x‖‖y‖cos θ.
translate: Since x and y are nonzero, ⟨x,y⟩ = 0 is equivalent to cos θ = 0.
conclude: On [0,π], cos θ = 0 holds exactly at θ = π/2.

drafts.canonical_statement: A surjective isometry between real normed spaces is affine; it coincides with a bijective affine isometry.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="isometry"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="surjective"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="affine_isometry_equiv"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Show midpoints are preserved by a reflection argument, then upgrade midpoint preservation and continuity to affineness.
sketch_steps: setup: f is injective as an isometry, hence bijective, and f⁻¹ is an isometry.
derive: For bijective isometries g fixing x and y, g* = ρg⁻¹ρg also fixes them and moves z twice as far as g, where ρ is the reflection at the midpoint z.
derive: The supremum of ‖g(z) - z‖ is finite, so it is 0 and every such g fixes z.
apply_theorem: Applying this to ρf⁻¹ρ'f, with ρ' the reflection at the midpoint of f(x), f(y), shows f preserves midpoints.
derive: Then f - f(0) is additive, and continuity makes it real linear.
conclude: So f is a bijective affine isometry.

drafts.canonical_statement: An isometry f between Euclidean affine spaces preserves unoriented angles, that is, ∠f(a)f(b)f(c) = ∠abc for a ≠ b and c ≠ b.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="isometry"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="euclid_angle"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="euclid_angle"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Recover the angle from the three side lengths by the law of cosines.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The law of cosines expresses cos∠abc through |ab|, |cb| and |ac|.
derive: The denominator is nonzero because a ≠ b and c ≠ b.
derive: f preserves the three distances, so the cosines of the two angles agree.
conclude: Cosine is injective on [0,π], so the angles are equal.

drafts.canonical_statement: The interior and the closure of a convex subset of a real normed space are convex.

drafts.proof_strategy: Take limits of convex combinations for the closure and translate a common ball for the interior.
sketch_steps: derive: For closure points, approximate by sequences in S; convex combinations converge to the combination of limits.
setup: For interior points x and y choose r with balls of radius r around both inside S.
derive: For z = (1-t)x + ty and small w, z + w = (1-t)(x+w) + t(y+w) lies in S.
conclude: So z is interior, and both sets are convex.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compare partitions of [a,c] with pairs of partitions of [a,b] and [b,c].
sketch_steps: setup: L(a,c) is the supremum of polygonal sums over partitions of [a,c].
derive: Concatenating partitions of [a,b] and [b,c] gives L(a,b) + L(b,c) ≤ L(a,c).
derive: Inserting b in a partition does not decrease the sum by the triangle inequality, giving the reverse inequality.
conclude: The two-point partition gives d(f(a),f(c)) ≤ L(a,c).

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the fundamental theorem of calculus and the norm bound for integrals.
sketch_steps: setup: γ' is continuous, hence integrable on [a,b].
apply_theorem: The fundamental theorem of calculus gives γ(b) - γ(a) = ∫_a^b γ'(t) dt.
derive: The norm of an integral is at most the integral of the norm when a ≤ b.
conclude: This yields the claimed bound.

drafts.canonical_statement: If A ≠ C, B and D lie strictly on opposite sides of line AC, and line AB is parallel to line DC, then the alternate angles agree, ∠BAC = ∠DCA.

drafts.proof_strategy: Write DC as a positive multiple of AB, using the opposite-side hypothesis to fix the sign, then compare the two angles as angles between vectors.
sketch_steps: setup: Parallelism gives a real k with DC = k AB.
contradiction: k = 0 puts D on line AC, and k < 0 puts D on the same side as B.
translate: The angle DCA is the angle between -k AB and -AC.
conclude: Negating both vectors and dividing by k > 0 leaves the angle between AB and AC, which is ∠BAC.

drafts.canonical_statement: In a Euclidean plane, if A ≠ C, B and D lie strictly on opposite sides of line AC and ∠BAC = ∠DCA, then line AB is parallel to line DC.

drafts.proof_strategy: Upgrade the equality of unoriented angles to oriented angles using the opposite-side sign rule, then subtract to get a zero oriented angle between AB and DC.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix an orientation of the plane and note B ≠ A and D ≠ C.
derive: Opposite sides of AC give equal signs for the oriented angles BAC and DCA.
derive: Equal unoriented angles with equal signs give equal oriented angles.
translate: Negating both vectors rewrites the angle DCA as the angle from DC to AC.
conclude: The oriented angle from AB to DC is 0, so DC is a positive multiple of AB and the lines are parallel.

drafts.canonical_statement: If A lies strictly between E and C, B and D lie strictly on the same side of line AC, and line AB is parallel to line CD, then the corresponding angles agree, ∠EAB = ∠ACD.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show CD is a positive multiple of AB and CA is a positive multiple of AE, then use that positive scaling keeps angles.
sketch_steps: setup: Parallelism gives a real k with CD = k AB.
contradiction: k = 0 puts D on line AC, and k < 0 puts D on the opposite side from B.
derive: Since A is strictly between E and C, CA = r AE for some r > 0.
conclude: Hence ∠ACD is the angle between r AE and k AB, which equals ∠EAB.

drafts.canonical_statement: In a Euclidean plane, if A lies strictly between E and C, B and D lie strictly on the same side of line AC and ∠EAB = ∠ACD, then line AB is parallel to line CD.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the linear pair at A to turn the hypothesis into equal angles against AC, then use the same-side sign rule to upgrade to oriented angles.
sketch_steps: derive: The linear pair at A gives ∠EAB + ∠BAC = π.
derive: Hence AB and CD make the same angle with AC.
derive: The same-side hypothesis makes the two oriented angles against AC have equal sign.
derive: Equal angle and equal sign give equal oriented angles.
conclude: The oriented angle from AB to CD is 0, so the lines are parallel.

drafts.canonical_statement: In a Euclidean plane, if A ≠ B, C ≠ D, E ≠ F and lines AB and CD are both perpendicular to line EF, then line AB is parallel to line CD, coincidence allowed.

drafts.proof_strategy: The orthogonal complement of a nonzero vector in a plane is one-dimensional, so both direction vectors are multiples of each other.
sketch_steps: setup: The vector EF is nonzero and the plane has dimension 2.
derive: The orthogonal complement of EF has dimension 1 and contains AB and CD.
derive: Since AB ≠ 0, CD = c AB, and c ≠ 0 because CD ≠ 0.
conclude: The lines have the same direction, so they are parallel.

drafts.proof_strategy: Derive AD = BC from the defining vector equation, then read off lengths, midpoints and angles from vector identities.
sketch_steps: derive: AB = DC implies AD = BC as vectors.
derive: Equal vectors have equal lengths, so opposite sides agree.
derive: The vector equation is equivalent to A + C = B + D, so the midpoints coincide.
conclude: Opposite angles are angles between pairs of negated vectors, so they agree.

drafts.canonical_statement: If segments AC and BD have the same midpoint, then AB = DC as vectors.

drafts.proof_strategy: Write the midpoint equality with position vectors and rearrange.
sketch_steps: translate: Equal midpoints mean A + C = B + D in position vectors.
conclude: Rearranging gives B - A = C - D, that is AB = DC.

drafts.canonical_statement: If A, B, D are not collinear, line AB is parallel to line DC and line AD is parallel to line BC, then AB = DC as vectors.

drafts.proof_strategy: Express AC in two ways using the two parallel pairs and compare coefficients in the independent vectors AB and AD.
sketch_steps: setup: Non-collinearity makes u = AB and v = AD linearly independent.
translate: Parallelism gives DC = a u and BC = b v.
derive: AC = v + a u = u + b v, so (a-1)u + (1-b)v = 0.
conclude: Independence gives a = 1, so DC = AB.

drafts.canonical_statement: If B and D lie strictly on opposite sides of line AC, line AB is parallel to line DC and |AB| = |DC|, then AB = DC as vectors.

drafts.proof_strategy: Parallelism and equal lengths leave only k = 1 or k = -1, and k = -1 would make BD parallel to AC, which contradicts the opposite-side hypothesis.
sketch_steps: setup: Write DC = k AB; AB ≠ 0 since B is off line AC.
derive: Equal lengths force |k| = 1.
contradiction: If k = -1 then BD = AC, and a point of AC on segment BD forces B onto line AC.
conclude: Therefore k = 1 and AB = DC.

drafts.canonical_statement: If A ≠ C, B and D lie strictly on opposite sides of line AC, |AB| = |CD| and |BC| = |DA|, then AB = DC as vectors.

drafts.proof_strategy: Express AD in the independent vectors AB and AC, turn the two length equalities into polynomial equations, and use the sign from the opposite-side hypothesis to select the root.
sketch_steps: setup: Set u = AB, w = AC, v = AD and use the crossing point of BD with AC to write v = α u + β w with α < 0.
translate: The two length conditions become two equations in s = |u|², t = |w|², m = u·w.
derive: Their difference gives (α+1)m + (β-1)t = 0.
derive: Eliminating gives (α+1)(α-1)(st-m²) = 0.
derive: st - m² > 0 since u, w are independent, and α < 0, so α = -1 and then β = 1.
conclude: Hence v = w - u, that is DC = AB.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use vectors u = AB, v = AD with u·v = 0, expand the squared diagonals, and read the remaining angles from sign changes.
sketch_steps: setup: Put u = AB and v = AD, so u·v = 0, AC = u + v and BD = v - u.
derive: Both diagonals have squared length |u|² + |v|².
derive: The angles at B and D are π minus the angle between u and v.
conclude: The angle at C is the angle between -v and -u, so all four angles are right.

sketch_steps: setup: Put u = AB and v = AD, so the diagonals are u + v and v - u.
derive: Equal squared lengths give 4 u·v = 0.
conclude: Zero inner product means ∠DAB = π/2.

sketch_steps: derive: For any X, Y, Z, the midpoint of YZ minus the midpoint of XY is (Z - X)/2.
derive: Applying this to (A,B,C) and (C,D,A) gives PQ = SR = AC/2 as vectors.
conclude: Applying it to (B,C,D) and taking norms gives the lengths.

sketch_steps: derive: As vectors PQ = AC/2 and QR = BD/2.
derive: The inner product scales by 1/4, so the orthogonality conditions are equivalent.
conclude: The lengths scale by 1/2, so the equal-length conditions are equivalent.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the triangle angle sum to ABE, EBC and ABC, and eliminate using the straight angle at E.
sketch_steps: setup: Write the angle sums of triangles ABE, EBC and ABC.
derive: The straight angle at E gives ∠BEA + ∠CEB = π.
derive: E on segment AC gives ∠EAB = ∠CAB and ∠BCE = ∠BCA.
conclude: Eliminating gives ∠ABC = ∠ABE + ∠EBC.

drafts.proof_strategy: Split each vertex angle along the segment to E, then subtract the four angles at E from the total angle sum of the four triangles around E.
sketch_steps: derive: A point strictly inside a segment splits the opposite vertex angle into a sum.
derive: Each of the four angles splits along the segment to E.
derive: The four triangles around E have total angle sum 4π.
derive: The angles at E form two straight angles, totalling 2π.
conclude: The quadrilateral angle sum is 4π - 2π = 2π.

drafts.canonical_statement: In an oriented Euclidean plane, if p_0, ..., p_{n+2} are such that every triple with i < j < k has positive oriented angle sign, then the interior angles of the convex (n+3)-gon sum to (n+1)π.

drafts.proof_strategy: Induct by cutting off the triangle at the last vertex, using a lemma that adds angles at a vertex when all three oriented signs are positive.
sketch_steps: derive: Positive signs make each unoriented angle lie strictly between 0 and π, and cyclic rotation keeps the sign.
derive: If the three oriented angles at X are positive, the unoriented angles add, since their defect is a multiple of 2π in (-π, 2π).
induction: The base case n = 0 is the triangle angle sum.
derive: For the step, split the angles at p_{n+2} and p_0 along the diagonal p_0 p_{n+2}.
conclude: The sum separates into the smaller polygon and one triangle, adding π.

drafts.canonical_statement: In an oriented Euclidean plane, if p_0, ..., p_{n+2} are such that every triple with i < j < k has positive oriented angle sign, then the exterior angles, each π minus the interior angle, sum to 2π.

drafts.proof_strategy: Prove the interior sum (n+1)π by cutting off triangles, then subtract from (n+3)π.
sketch_steps: derive: Positive oriented signs let unoriented angles at a vertex add.
induction: The interior angle sum is (n+1)π, by cutting off the triangle at the last vertex.
conclude: The exterior sum is (n+3)π - (n+1)π = 2π.

drafts.canonical_statement: For points A, B, C of the Euclidean plane, the area of the convex hull of {A, B, C} equals (1/2)|AB||AC| sin ∠BAC.

drafts.proof_strategy: Realize the triangle as an affine image of the standard triangle, so its area is half the absolute determinant, and identify the determinant with |u||w| sin θ.
sketch_steps: derive: The standard triangle has area 1/2 by slicing.
construct: The linear map sending the unit vectors to AB and AC, followed by translation by A, carries it onto the convex hull.
apply_theorem: Linear maps scale area by the absolute determinant, and translations preserve it.
derive: The squared determinant is |u|²|w|² - (u·w)², so its absolute value is |u||w| sin θ.
conclude: The area is (1/2)|AB||AC| sin ∠BAC.

sketch_steps: construct: Map the standard triangle affinely onto the convex hull.
apply_theorem: Area scales by the absolute determinant, giving (1/2)bc sin θ.
apply_theorem: The cosine rule gives 2bc cos θ = b² + c² - a².
derive: The squared area factors as s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c).
conclude: Take the nonnegative square root.

drafts.proof_strategy: Express the area by the determinant of AB and AC, reduce it to det(HA, BC) using H on line BC, and evaluate it by orthogonality.
sketch_steps: derive: The area equals half the absolute determinant of AB and AC.
setup: Write H = B + t BC and set c = BC, h = HA.
derive: Bilinearity gives det(AB, AC) = -det(h, c).
conclude: Orthogonality gives |det(h, c)| = |h||c|, so the area is (1/2)|BC||AH|.

sketch_steps: derive: The area of a triangle equals half an absolute determinant.
setup: Write D = B + t BC and Δ = det(AB, AC).
derive: The two determinants are tΔ and (1-t)Δ.
derive: The lengths are |BD| = |t||BC| and |DC| = |1-t||BC|.

setup: Write AB' = r AB and AC' = t AC.
derive: Bilinearity gives S(AB'C') = |r||t| S(ABC).
conclude: Since |AB'| = |r||AB| and |AC'| = |t||AC|, both sides agree.

sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The area of a triangle is √(s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)) in terms of its sides.
derive: Scaling the sides by k scales each of the four factors by k.
conclude: The radicand scales by k⁴, so the area scales by k².

drafts.proof_strategy: Realize the convex hull as an affine image of the unit square and identify the determinant with |u||w| sin θ.
sketch_steps: setup: Put u = AB and w = AD, so C = A + u + w.
construct: The affine map (x, y) to A + xu + yw carries the unit square onto the hull, using bilinear convex weights.
apply_theorem: Area scales by the absolute determinant, and translation preserves it.
conclude: The absolute determinant equals |u||w| sin ∠BAD.

sketch_steps: setup: The side equalities are instances of the definition.
derive: Non-collinearity makes the vertices of each triple distinct.
apply_theorem: The law of cosines gives the same cosine for corresponding angles.
conclude: Injectivity of cosine on [0, π] gives equal angles.

drafts.proof_strategy: The Pythagorean theorem recovers the third side, then all pairwise distances agree.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The vanishing inner products give CA² = AB² + BC² and C'A'² = A'B'² + B'C'².
derive: Subtracting with the hypotheses gives BC² = B'C'².
derive: Nonnegativity gives BC = B'C'.
conclude: Three equal sides give congruence.

conclude: Injectivity of cosine on [0, π] gives equal angles.

drafts.proof_strategy: The product condition gives common ratio r on the two sides at A; the shared angle and the law of cosines give the third side.
sketch_steps: construct: Put r = AD/AC, so AD = r·AC and AE = r·AB.
derive: D and E lie on rays AB and AC, so ∠DAE = ∠CAB.
apply_theorem: The law of cosines at A gives DE² = r²CB².
conclude: All pairwise distances have ratio r.

drafts.canonical_statement: For non-collinear A, B, C, AB = AC if and only if ∠ABC = ∠ACB.

drafts.proof_strategy: Forward uses the cosine formula, converse uses the law of sines with positive sine.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: If AB = AC, the cosine formula gives equal cosines of the base angles.
derive: Injectivity of cosine on [0, π] gives equal base angles.
apply_theorem: Conversely the law of sines gives AB·sin∠ABC = AC·sin∠ACB.
conclude: Non-collinearity makes the sine positive, so AB = AC.

drafts.canonical_statement: For points A, B, C with M the midpoint of BC, AB = AC if and only if ⟨A-M, C-B⟩ = 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Write A-B and A-C through A-M and half of C-B and subtract the squared norms.
sketch_steps: setup: Put h = A-M and d = C-B, so A-B = h + d/2 and A-C = h - d/2.
derive: Expanding gives AB² - AC² = 2⟨h,d⟩.
conclude: AB = AC iff the squares agree iff ⟨h,d⟩ = 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: If A, B, C are not collinear and the median AM to BC bisects the angle at A, meaning ∠BAM = ∠MAC, then AB = AC.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the law of sines in the two triangles cut by the median, using supplementary angles at M.
sketch_steps: setup: M lies strictly between B and C and A is off line BC.
derive: The angles at M are supplementary, so they have equal sines.
apply_theorem: The law of sines gives BM·sin∠AMB = AB·sinθ and CM·sin∠AMC = AC·sinθ.
conclude: BM = CM and sinθ > 0 give AB = AC.

drafts.canonical_statement: If A, B, C are not collinear, AB = AC, D lies strictly between B and C, and ∠BAD = ∠DAC, then D is the midpoint of BC.

drafts.proof_strategy: The angle bisector theorem gives BD = DC, and a point of the segment at half distance is the midpoint.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The angle bisector theorem gives AB/AC = BD/DC.
derive: AB = AC forces BD = DC.
derive: BD + DC = BC gives BD = DC = BC/2.
conclude: D is the midpoint.

drafts.canonical_statement: If B ≠ C, AB = AC, H lies on line BC and ⟨A-H, C-B⟩ = 0, then H is the midpoint of BC.

drafts.proof_strategy: Parametrize H on line BC and compare AB² and AC² using orthogonality.
sketch_steps: setup: Write H - B = x·d with d = C - B and h = A - H orthogonal to d.
derive: AB² = ‖h‖² + x²‖d‖² and AC² = ‖h‖² + (x-1)²‖d‖².
derive: AB = AC and d ≠ 0 give x² = (x-1)².
conclude: x = 1/2, so H is the midpoint.

sketch_steps: apply_theorem: ∠ABC = ∠ACB gives AB = AC.

drafts.proof_strategy: The law of cosines with cos(π/3) = 1/2 gives BC = AB.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Write BC² by the law of cosines at A.
derive: Substituting AB = AC and cos(π/3) = 1/2 gives BC² = AB².
conclude: Nonnegativity gives BC = AB.

sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The exterior angle theorem gives ∠ACD = ∠ABC + ∠BAC.

sketch_steps: setup: Put β = ∠ABC and γ = ∠ACB.
apply_theorem: The law of cosines expresses both cosines through the sides.
derive: The difference of cosines has the sign of AC - AB, since (AB+AC)² - BC² > 0.
conclude: Cosine is strictly decreasing on [0, π], so the order of angles matches.

sketch_steps: derive: The angle range gives cos∠ABC ≤ 0.
apply_theorem: The law of cosines gives AC² ≥ AB² + CB².
derive: Positivity of AB and CB makes the inequalities strict.
conclude: Comparing squares of nonnegative lengths gives the result.

drafts.canonical_statement: If H lies on line BC with ⟨A-H, C-B⟩ = 0, then AH ≤ AX for every point X on line BC.

derive: A - H is orthogonal to H - X.
derive: AX² = AH² + HX² ≥ AH².
conclude: Compare the nonnegative lengths.

derive: Non-collinearity gives all three strict triangle inequalities.
conclude: Two of them combine into |AB - BC| < AC.

drafts.proof_strategy: Forward uses strict triangle inequalities; backward places B and C on an axis and solves for A, with non-collinearity from the strict inequalities.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Non-collinear points satisfy the three strict triangle inequalities.
derive: Conversely, adding two inequalities shows a, b, c > 0.
construct: Put x = (a²+c²-b²)/(2a) and y = √(c²-x²), which is defined by a factorization.
construct: Take B = (0,0), C = (a,0), A = (x,y).
derive: Direct computation gives BC = a, CA = b, AB = c.
contradiction: Collinearity would force one side to equal the sum of the other two.

conclude: Expanding AB·BC gives BD(AB + AC).

sketch_steps: setup: Write D = B + t(C-B) with t in [0,1], so the ratio gives c(1-t) = tb.
translate: Put u = B-A, w = C-A, v = (1-t)u + tw.
derive: b⟨u,v⟩ - c⟨v,w⟩ factors with the factor c(1-t) - tb = 0.
derive: The two cosines are equal.
conclude: Injectivity of cosine on [0, π] gives equal angles.

drafts.proof_strategy: In each right triangle the leg equals AX times the sine of an acute angle, and sine is injective on acute angles.
sketch_steps: derive: Orthogonality gives AX² = XH² + HA² and ⟨H-A,X-A⟩ = HA².
derive: Hence the angle at A is acute and XH = AX·sin∠HAX.
derive: The same holds for K.
conclude: Equal angles give equal legs; conversely injectivity of sine gives equal angles.

drafts.proof_strategy: The vector between the midpoints is half of B - C.
sketch_steps: derive: M - N = (1/2)(B - C).
derive: A nonzero scalar keeps the same direction space, so the lines are parallel.
conclude: Taking norms gives MN = BC/2.

drafts.canonical_statement: If A, B, C are not collinear, E lies on line AC, and the line through the midpoint of AB and E is parallel to line BC, then E is the midpoint of AC.

sketch_steps: setup: Put u = B-A, w = C-A, which are independent.
translate: E - A = tw and M - A = u/2.

derive: AB² = x‖d‖² and AC² = (1-x)‖d‖².

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the pigeonhole principle on powers of an element to produce a positive power equal to 1.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix a in S and note that every positive power of a lies in S.
derive: Finiteness of S gives i < j with a^i = a^j.
derive: Cancel to obtain a^(j-i) = 1, so 1 lies in S.
case_split: If j-i = 1 then a = 1; otherwise a⁻¹ = a^(j-i-1) is a positive power.
conclude: S contains the identity and inverses and is closed under products.

drafts.canonical_statement: For subgroups H and K of a group, the union H ∪ K is a subgroup if and only if H ⊆ K or K ⊆ H.

drafts.proof_strategy: Argue by contradiction with witnesses a in H outside K and b in K outside H, and locate ab.
sketch_steps: translate: If one subgroup contains the other, the union equals the larger subgroup.
setup: Assume the union L is a subgroup and neither inclusion holds.
construct: Choose a in H outside K and b in K outside H.
case_split: The product ab lies in H or in K.
contradiction: In the first case b lies in H; in the second case a lies in K.

drafts.canonical_statement: For subgroups H and K of a group, the product set HK is a subgroup if and only if HK = KH.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use inversion for the forward direction and swap the middle factors for the converse.
sketch_steps: setup: Let HK be the set of products hk and KH the set of products kh.
derive: If HK is a subgroup, then inverting x in HK writes x as an element of KH.
derive: If HK is a subgroup, it contains H and K and so contains every kh.
construct: If HK = KH, define the subgroup with carrier HK.
derive: Rewrite k₁h₂ as h₃k₃ to show closure under products.
derive: Inverses of hk lie in KH = HK.
conclude: Both implications hold.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a subgroup H of a group and elements a, b, the left cosets aH and bH are equal if and only if a⁻¹b ∈ H.

drafts.proof_strategy: Extract b as an element of aH for one direction and translate coset elements by a⁻¹b for the other.
sketch_steps: derive: If aH = bH, then b lies in aH, so a⁻¹b is in H.
setup: Conversely set c = a⁻¹b in H.
derive: Each ah equals b(c⁻¹h), which lies in bH.
derive: Each bh equals a(ch), which lies in aH.
conclude: The two cosets coincide.

drafts.canonical_statement: Two left cosets aH and bH of a subgroup H are either equal or disjoint.

drafts.proof_strategy: Case split on whether a⁻¹b lies in H.
sketch_steps: case_split: Either a⁻¹b lies in H or it does not.
derive: In the first case translating by a⁻¹b identifies the two cosets.
setup: In the second case suppose ac = bd with c, d in H.
contradiction: Then a⁻¹b = cd⁻¹ lies in H.
conclude: The cosets are equal or disjoint.

drafts.canonical_statement: Lagrange's theorem: for a subgroup H of a finite group G, [G:H]·|H| = |G|, and in particular |H| divides |G|.

drafts.proof_strategy: Partition G into left cosets of equal size.
sketch_steps: translate: The left cosets of H partition G.
derive: Every coset is in bijection with H.
derive: Count elements coset by coset to get |G| = [G:H]·|H|.
conclude: Divisibility of |G| by |H| follows.

drafts.canonical_statement: In a finite group G, the order of every element g divides |G|, and g^|G| = 1.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply Lagrange to the cyclic subgroup generated by g.
sketch_steps: translate: The order of g equals the order of the cyclic subgroup generated by g.
apply_theorem: Lagrange gives that this order divides |G|.
derive: Write |G| = mq with m the order of g.
conclude: Then g^|G| = (g^m)^q = 1.

drafts.proof_strategy: Lagrange restricts subgroup orders to 1 or p.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: By Lagrange a subgroup has order 1 or p.
derive: So every subgroup is trivial or all of G.
derive: For g ≠ 1 the subgroup generated by g is nontrivial, hence equals G.
conclude: A non-identity element exists since p ≥ 2, so G is cyclic.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply Lagrange three times and cancel |H|.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Write Lagrange for H in G, K in G and H in K.
derive: Substitute to get [G:H]|H| = [G:K][K:H]|H|.
conclude: Cancel the positive integer |H|.

drafts.proof_strategy: The order of the intersection is a common divisor of the two orders.
sketch_steps: translate: H ∩ K is a subgroup of both H and K.
apply_theorem: Lagrange shows its order divides |H| and |K|.
conclude: Coprimality forces the order to be 1.

sketch_steps: setup: Let m be the order of g and d = gcd(m, n).
translate: (g^n)^k = 1 holds exactly when m divides nk.
derive: This is equivalent to m/d dividing k(n/d).
derive: Since m/d and n/d are coprime, it is equivalent to m/d dividing k.
conclude: Therefore the order of g^n is m/d.

drafts.proof_strategy: Divide n by the order with remainder and use minimality.
sketch_steps: setup: Let m be the order of g and write n = mq + r with 0 ≤ r < m.
derive: Then g^n = g^r.
derive: Minimality of m forces r = 0 when g^n = 1.
derive: Conversely m | n gives g^n = (g^m)^q = 1.
case_split: In infinite order no positive power of g equals 1, so g^n = 1 exactly when n = 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show mn kills ab, then force any exponent killing ab to be divisible by m and n.
sketch_steps: setup: Let m and n be the orders of a and b.
derive: Commutativity gives (ab)^(mn) = 1.
setup: Suppose (ab)^k = 1.
derive: Raising a^k = b^(-k) to the n-th power gives a^(kn) = 1.
derive: Coprimality gives m | k, and symmetrically n | k.
conclude: Then mn | k, so the order of ab is mn.

drafts.canonical_statement: A group in which every element squares to the identity is abelian.

drafts.proof_strategy: Every element is its own inverse, so inverting a product swaps its factors.
sketch_steps: translate: g² = 1 means g⁻¹ = g for every g.
derive: ab = (ab)⁻¹ = b⁻¹a⁻¹ = ba.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use powers of a generator; for subgroups take the least positive exponent.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix a generator g of G.
derive: Powers of g commute, so G is abelian.
construct: For a nontrivial subgroup H take the least positive d with g^d in H.
derive: Division with remainder shows H is generated by g^d.
derive: The image of g generates the quotient G/N.

drafts.proof_strategy: Construct the subgroup from a power of a generator and identify any such subgroup with the solutions of x^d = 1.
sketch_steps: construct: Take a generator g and the subgroup generated by g^(n/d).
derive: Its order is d by the formula for the order of a power.
derive: The equation x^d = 1 has at most d solutions in a cyclic group.
derive: A subgroup of order d lies in the solution set by Lagrange.
conclude: By counting, the subgroup equals the solution set, so it is unique.

drafts.canonical_statement: If the quotient of a group by its center is cyclic, then the group is abelian.

drafts.proof_strategy: Write elements as a power of a coset representative times a central element.
sketch_steps: setup: Choose g whose image generates G/Z(G).
translate: Every element has the form g^m z with z central.
derive: Products of two such elements commute.
conclude: G is abelian.

drafts.canonical_statement: A subgroup H of a group G is normal if and only if gH = Hg for every g in G.

drafts.proof_strategy: Move g across elements of H using conjugation.
sketch_steps: derive: If H is normal, gh = (ghg⁻¹)g lies in Hg.
derive: If H is normal, hg = g(g⁻¹hg) lies in gH.
setup: Conversely assume gH = Hg and take n in H.
derive: Writing gn = hg gives gng⁻¹ = h in H.
conclude: The two conditions are equivalent.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every subgroup of index 2 in a group is normal.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="subgroup_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="subgroup_index"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normal_subgroup"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: The cosets of an index-two subgroup are forced to be H and its complement on both sides.
sketch_steps: translate: With index 2, the left cosets and the right cosets are both H and its complement.
case_split: Either g lies in H or it does not.
derive: In each case gH = Hg.
conclude: H is normal.

drafts.canonical_statement: The kernel of a group homomorphism f is a normal subgroup, and f is injective if and only if its kernel is trivial.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compute f on conjugates and on quotients x⁻¹y.
sketch_steps: derive: f(gng⁻¹) = f(g)f(n)f(g)⁻¹ = 1 for n in the kernel.
derive: If f is injective, f(x) = 1 = f(1) gives x = 1.
derive: If the kernel is trivial, f(x) = f(y) gives x⁻¹y = 1.
conclude: The kernel is normal and the equivalence holds.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a group homomorphism f from G to H, the preimage of a normal subgroup of H is normal in G, and if f is surjective the image of a normal subgroup of G is normal in H.

drafts.proof_strategy: Conjugate through f, using surjectivity to lift the conjugating element.
sketch_steps: derive: For x in the preimage, f(gxg⁻¹) = f(g)f(x)f(g)⁻¹ lies in N.
setup: Assume f is surjective and write h = f(g).
derive: Then h f(m) h⁻¹ = f(gmg⁻¹) lies in f(M).
conclude: Preimages and surjective images of normal subgroups are normal.

drafts.canonical_statement: If normal subgroups H and K of a group intersect trivially, then every element of H commutes with every element of K.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show the commutator lies in both normal subgroups.
sketch_steps: setup: Let c = hkh⁻¹k⁻¹.
derive: Normality of K puts c in K.
derive: Normality of H puts c in H.
conclude: Then c = 1, so hk = kh.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a normal subgroup N of a group G, the quotient G/N is abelian if and only if the commutator subgroup [G,G] is contained in N.

drafts.proof_strategy: Rewrite commutativity in the quotient as membership of commutators in N.
sketch_steps: translate: The images of a and b commute exactly when aba⁻¹b⁻¹ lies in N.
derive: If G/N is abelian, all commutators lie in N, so N contains the subgroup they generate.
derive: If N contains [G,G], then all images commute.
conclude: The two conditions are equivalent.

derive: Hence the commutator subgroup is contained in the kernel of f.
construct: Define φ on cosets of [G,G] by φ(x[G,G]) = f(x).
derive: Surjectivity of the projection gives uniqueness.

sketch_steps: translate: x ker f = y ker f is equivalent to f(x) = f(y).
construct: Define φ(x ker f) = f(x) on the quotient.
derive: The translation gives well-definedness and injectivity.
derive: φ is a homomorphism because f is.
conclude: φ maps onto the image of f, so it is an isomorphism.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the first isomorphism theorem to h ↦ hN.
sketch_steps: translate: Since N is normal, HN is a subgroup containing N as a normal subgroup.
construct: Define φ from H to HN/N by φ(h) = hN.
derive: φ is surjective because hnN = hN.
derive: The kernel of φ is H ∩ N.
apply_theorem: The first isomorphism theorem gives the result.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use image and preimage under the projection as inverse maps.
sketch_steps: construct: Send K to its preimage and L to its image.
derive: Surjectivity of π gives π(π⁻¹(K)) = K.
derive: N ≤ L makes L a union of cosets of N, so π⁻¹(π(L)) = L.
derive: Both maps preserve inclusion.
conclude: They give an order isomorphism.

drafts.canonical_statement: A group G is abelian if and only if Z(G) = G, and if and only if the commutator subgroup [G,G] is trivial.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="abelian_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group_center"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="abelian_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="commutator_subgroup"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="trivial_subgroup"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Unfold the definitions of center and commutator.
sketch_steps: translate: Membership of every element in Z(G) says that every two elements commute.
derive: If G is abelian, every commutator aba⁻¹b⁻¹ equals 1.
derive: If [G,G] is trivial, aba⁻¹b⁻¹ = 1 gives ab = ba.
conclude: The three conditions are equivalent.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a group action on a set, two orbits are either equal or disjoint.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group_action"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="or"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="action_orbit"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="action_orbit"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="intersect"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="action_orbit"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="action_orbit"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="emptyset"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: A common point lets one translate each orbit into the other.
sketch_steps: setup: Suppose z lies in both orbits and write z = gx = hy.
derive: Then x = g⁻¹hy, so the orbit of x lies in the orbit of y.
derive: The reverse inclusion follows by symmetry.
conclude: Orbits with a common point coincide.

drafts.canonical_statement: Orbit-stabilizer theorem: for an action of a finite group G and a point x, the size of the orbit of x times the size of the stabilizer of x equals |G|.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group_action"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="size"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="action_orbit"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="size"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="action_stabilizer"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="size"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Identify the orbit with the left cosets of the stabilizer and apply Lagrange.
sketch_steps: translate: gx = hx is equivalent to gG_x = hG_x.
construct: The map gG_x ↦ gx is a bijection onto the orbit.
derive: Hence the orbit size equals the index of the stabilizer.
apply_theorem: Lagrange gives the product formula.

drafts.canonical_statement: Burnside's lemma: for a finite group G acting on a finite set X, the sum over g in G of the number of points fixed by g equals the number of orbits times |G|.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group_action"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="size"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="sum"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="fns1" name="lambda"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="size"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="action_fixed_points"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="size"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="action_orbit_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="size"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Double count pairs (g, x) with gx = x and use orbit-stabilizer.
sketch_steps: setup: Consider the set of pairs (g, x) with gx = x.
derive: Counting by g gives the sum of |X^g|.
derive: Counting by x gives the sum of |G_x|.
apply_theorem: Orbit-stabilizer gives |G_x| = |G|/|Gx|.
derive: Each orbit contributes exactly |G| to the sum.
conclude: The sum equals |G| times the number of orbits.

drafts.canonical_statement: Cayley's theorem: every group G admits an injective homomorphism into the symmetric group on G.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group_hom"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="symmetric_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="injective_function"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Use the left regular action.
sketch_steps: construct: Send g to left multiplication L_g.
derive: L_g is a permutation with inverse L_{g⁻¹}.
derive: L_{gh} = L_g L_h, so the map is a homomorphism.
derive: Evaluating at 1 shows injectivity.

drafts.canonical_statement: Class equation: for a finite group G, |G| equals |Z(G)| plus the sum of the sizes of the conjugacy classes with more than one element.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="size"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="size"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group_center"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="sum"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="noncentral_conjugacy_classes"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="fns1" name="lambda"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="size"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Partition G into conjugacy classes and separate the singleton classes.
sketch_steps: translate: Conjugacy classes partition G.
derive: A class is a singleton exactly when its element is central.
derive: Singleton classes contribute |Z(G)| in total.
conclude: Add the remaining classes to obtain the equation.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a prime p and a positive integer n, the center of a group of order p^n is nontrivial.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="P"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="gt"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="size"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group_center"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="trivial_subgroup"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Reduce the class equation modulo p.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Write the class equation for G.
derive: Each non-singleton class has size a positive power of p.
derive: Therefore p divides |Z(G)|.
conclude: Since |Z(G)| ≥ 1, it is at least p.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a prime p, every group of order p² is abelian.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="P"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="size"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="abelian_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Combine the nontrivial center of a p-group with the cyclic quotient criterion.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The center of a p-group is nontrivial.
case_split: The center has order p or p².
derive: If it has order p, the quotient G/Z(G) is cyclic of order p.
contradiction: A cyclic quotient by the center forces G to be abelian, so Z(G) = G.
conclude: Therefore Z(G) = G.

drafts.canonical_statement: Cauchy's theorem: if a prime p divides the order of a finite group G, then G has an element of order p.

drafts.proof_strategy: Let Z/p act by cyclic shift on p-tuples with product 1 and count fixed points modulo p.
sketch_steps: setup: Let S be the set of p-tuples of elements of G with product 1.
derive: |S| = |G|^(p-1) is divisible by p.
construct: Cyclic shift gives an action of Z/p on S.
derive: Orbits have size 1 or p, so the number of fixed points is divisible by p.
derive: Fixed points are constant tuples (x, ..., x) with x^p = 1.
conclude: Since (1, ..., 1) is fixed, some x ≠ 1 satisfies x^p = 1, and it has order p.

drafts.canonical_statement: Sylow's first theorem: if p is prime and p^n divides the order of a finite group G, then G has a subgroup of order p^n.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="P"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="dvd"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="size"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="subgroup_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="size"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on the exponent, enlarging a p-subgroup inside its normalizer via Cauchy's theorem.
sketch_steps: induction: Start from the trivial subgroup and assume H has order p^k.
setup: Let H act on the left cosets of H.
derive: The fixed points correspond to N_G(H)/H and their number is congruent to [G:H] modulo p.
derive: Hence p divides the order of N_G(H)/H.
apply_theorem: Cauchy gives a subgroup of order p in N_G(H)/H.
construct: Its preimage in N_G(H) has order p^(k+1).

drafts.canonical_statement: Sylow's second theorem: any two Sylow p-subgroups of a finite group are conjugate.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="P"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="sylow_subgroup"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="sylow_subgroup"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="conjugate_subgroup"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Let one Sylow subgroup act on the cosets of the other and find a fixed point modulo p.
sketch_steps: setup: Let Q act on the left cosets of P by left multiplication.
derive: The number of fixed points is congruent to [G:P] modulo p, which is nonzero.
construct: Take a fixed coset gP.
derive: Then g⁻¹Qg is contained in P.
conclude: Equal orders give Q = gPg⁻¹.

drafts.proof_strategy: Count fixed points of P acting by conjugation, then use transitivity of G.
sketch_steps: setup: Let P act by conjugation on the set of Sylow p-subgroups.
derive: A fixed point Q has P in its normalizer, and then P = Q.
apply_theorem: The count is congruent modulo p to the number of fixed points, which is 1.
apply_theorem: The second theorem makes G act transitively, so n_p = [G:N_G(P)].
conclude: Since P ≤ N_G(P), n_p divides [G:P] = m.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a finite group has exactly one Sylow p-subgroup, then that subgroup is normal.

drafts.proof_strategy: Conjugates of a Sylow subgroup are Sylow subgroups.
sketch_steps: derive: Each conjugate gSg⁻¹ has the same order as S, so it is a Sylow p-subgroup.
derive: Uniqueness gives gSg⁻¹ = S.
conclude: S is normal.

drafts.canonical_statement: A group homomorphism from a simple group is either trivial or injective.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="simple_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group_hom"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="or"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group_kernel"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="injective_function"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Apply simplicity to the kernel.
sketch_steps: translate: The kernel of f is a normal subgroup of G.
case_split: Simplicity makes it trivial or all of G.
conclude: These cases give injective and trivial respectively.

drafts.canonical_statement: An abelian group is simple if and only if its order is prime.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="abelian_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="simple_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="size"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="P"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: In an abelian group every subgroup is normal, so simplicity means no proper nontrivial subgroups.
sketch_steps: translate: In an abelian group all subgroups are normal.
derive: A simple abelian group is generated by any non-identity element, so it is cyclic.
derive: The infinite cyclic group has the subgroup 2Z, so G is finite.
derive: A cyclic group of composite order has a proper nontrivial subgroup, so the order is prime.
derive: Conversely Lagrange shows a group of prime order has only trivial subgroups.

drafts.canonical_statement: The alternating group on a finite set with at least 5 elements is simple.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="geq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="size"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>5</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="simple_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="alternating_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Show that a nontrivial normal subgroup contains a 3-cycle, and that 3-cycles are conjugate and generate.
sketch_steps: translate: The alternating group is generated by 3-cycles.
derive: With at least 5 points all 3-cycles are conjugate in the alternating group.
setup: Let N be a nontrivial normal subgroup and take a non-identity element.
case_split: According to its cycle type, form commutators with suitable elements.
derive: These commutators lie in N and lead to a 3-cycle in N.
conclude: Then N contains all 3-cycles, so it is the whole group.

drafts.canonical_statement: The symmetric group on a finite set is generated by the transpositions.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="N"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="size"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="generated_subgroup"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="suchthat"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="symmetric_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="fns1" name="lambda"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="transposition"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="symmetric_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on the number of points moved, peeling off one transposition.
sketch_steps: induction: Induct on the number of points moved by σ.
setup: If σ(x) ≠ x, let τ swap x and σ(x).
derive: τσ fixes x and every point fixed by σ, so it moves fewer points.
conclude: Then σ = τ(τσ) is a product of transpositions.

drafts.proof_strategy: Realize the alternating group as the kernel of the surjective sign map.
sketch_steps: translate: The alternating group is the kernel of the sign homomorphism.
derive: A transposition exists, so the sign is surjective.
apply_theorem: The first isomorphism theorem gives index 2.
conclude: Lagrange and |Sym(X)| = n! give 2|A(X)| = n!.

drafts.canonical_statement: The alternating group on a finite set is generated by the 3-cycles.

drafts.proof_strategy: Pair up transpositions in an even permutation and rewrite each pair as 3-cycles.
sketch_steps: derive: A 3-cycle is a product of two transpositions, so it is even.
translate: An even permutation is a product of an even number of transpositions.
case_split: Two transpositions are equal, share one point, or are disjoint.
derive: In each case their product is a product of 3-cycles.
conclude: The 3-cycles generate the alternating group.

drafts.canonical_statement: If normal subgroups H and K of a group G satisfy H ∩ K = 1 and HK = G, then G is isomorphic to H × K.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use commuting of H and K to make multiplication a homomorphism and check bijectivity.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Normal subgroups with trivial intersection commute elementwise.
construct: Define φ(h, k) = hk.
derive: Commutativity makes φ a homomorphism.
derive: hk = 1 gives h = k⁻¹ in H ∩ K, so φ is injective.
derive: The subgroup generated by H and K equals HK, so φ is surjective.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a normal subgroup N and a subgroup H of G satisfy N ∩ H = 1 and NH = G, then G is isomorphic to the semidirect product of N by H for the conjugation action φ(h)(n) = hnh⁻¹.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show that (n, h) ↦ nh is a bijective homomorphism from the semidirect product.
sketch_steps: construct: Let φ(h) be conjugation by h on N and form the semidirect product.
derive: The map (n, h) ↦ nh is a homomorphism because nhn'h' = n(hn'h⁻¹)hh'.
derive: nh = 1 forces n = h⁻¹ in N ∩ H, so the map is injective.
derive: The subgroup generated by N and H is NH, so the map is surjective.

drafts.proof_strategy: Decompose into p-primary parts, then split off a cyclic subgroup of maximal order.
sketch_steps: translate: G is the direct sum of its p-primary components.
setup: Fix a finite abelian p-group A and choose x of maximal order.
derive: The cyclic subgroup generated by x is a direct summand of A.
induction: Apply induction to the complement.
conclude: G is a direct sum of cyclic groups of prime power order.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a normal subgroup N of a group G, G is solvable if and only if both N and G/N are solvable.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compare derived series of G, N and G/N.
sketch_steps: derive: The derived series of N is contained in that of G.
derive: The derived series of G/N is the image of that of G.
setup: Conversely assume the k-th derived subgroup of G/N and the l-th derived subgroup of N are trivial.
derive: Then G^(k) ≤ N, so G^(k+l) ≤ N^(l) = 1.
conclude: G is solvable exactly when both N and G/N are.

drafts.canonical_statement: The symmetric group S_n is not solvable for n ≥ 5.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show every derived subgroup contains all 3-cycles, using five distinct points.
sketch_steps: derive: With five points every 3-cycle is a commutator of two 3-cycles.
induction: Each term of the derived series contains all 3-cycles.
conclude: The derived series never becomes trivial, so S_n is not solvable.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every finite p-group is nilpotent.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="P"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="p_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="nilpotent_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on the order, dividing by the nontrivial center.
sketch_steps: induction: Induct on |G|, the trivial group being nilpotent.
apply_theorem: A nontrivial p-group has a nontrivial center.
derive: G/Z(G) is a smaller p-group, hence nilpotent.
conclude: A central extension of a nilpotent group is nilpotent.

drafts.canonical_statement: A nilpotent group is solvable, and a nontrivial nilpotent group has nontrivial center.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="nilpotent_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="solvable_group"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="trivial_subgroup"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="group_center"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="trivial_subgroup"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Use the upper central series, whose factors are abelian.
sketch_steps: setup: Take the upper central series ending at G.
derive: Its factors are central in the quotients, hence abelian.
conclude: This abelian series shows G is solvable.
contradiction: If Z(G) were trivial, every term of the series would be trivial, contradicting that the series reaches a nontrivial G.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every nontrivial finite group G has a normal subgroup N such that G/N is simple. This is the step used to build a composition series.

drafts.proof_strategy: Take a maximal proper normal subgroup and apply the correspondence theorem.
sketch_steps: construct: Finiteness gives a maximal element N among proper normal subgroups.
derive: G/N is nontrivial because N is proper.
setup: Let K be a normal subgroup of G/N with preimage L.
derive: L is a normal subgroup of G containing N.
case_split: If L = G then K = G/N; otherwise maximality gives L = N and K is trivial.
conclude: G/N is simple.

drafts.proof_strategy: Take a shortest nontrivial linear relation and eliminate one term using f minus a scalar.
sketch_steps: setup: Suppose a nontrivial linear relation among the eigenvectors exists and choose one with the fewest terms.
derive: Apply f and subtract μ_i times the relation to remove the i-th term.
derive: The surviving coefficients are multiplied by μ_j - μ_i, which are nonzero by distinctness.
contradiction: This is a shorter nontrivial relation, contradicting minimality.

sketch_steps: derive: Applying g gives x = g(f x) = μ g x by linearity.
contradiction: If μ = 0 then x = 0, contrary to the hypothesis.
conclude: Multiply by μ⁻¹ to obtain g x = μ⁻¹ x.

drafts.canonical_statement: A linear endomorphism f has eigenvalue 0 if and only if f is not injective.

drafts.proof_strategy: Identify the eigenspace for 0 with the kernel.
sketch_steps: translate: The eigenspace of f for 0 equals ker f.
apply_theorem: A linear map is injective exactly when its kernel is zero.
conclude: Hence eigenvalue 0 exists exactly when f is not injective.

sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Characteristic polynomials of XY and YX agree for square matrices.
derive: Take X = P A and Y = Q so that the polynomial of P A Q equals that of Q P A.
conclude: Since Q P = 1, this is the characteristic polynomial of A.

drafts.proof_strategy: Extract a basis from the spanning set of eigenvectors, and conversely span by the basis.
sketch_steps: setup: Let S be the set of vectors x with f x = a x for some scalar a.
translate: The sum of the eigenspaces is the span of S.
apply_theorem: A spanning set of a vector space contains a basis.
construct: Choose for each basis vector a scalar a with f b = a b.
derive: Conversely each basis vector lies in an eigenspace, so the sum contains the span of the basis.
conclude: The two conditions are equivalent.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a linear endomorphism satisfies f ∘ f = f, then the sum of its eigenspaces for 1 and 0 is the whole space.

drafts.proof_strategy: Decompose x as f x plus x - f x.
sketch_steps: setup: Write x = f x + (x - f x).
derive: f (f x) = f x shows that f x lies in the eigenspace for 1.
derive: f (x - f x) = 0 shows that x - f x lies in the eigenspace for 0.
conclude: The sum of the two eigenspaces is the whole space.

drafts.canonical_statement: Over an algebraically closed field, if the minimal polynomial of a linear endomorphism of a finite-dimensional space is squarefree, then its eigenspaces span the space.
