drafts.proof_strategy: Multiply the first-order expansions of f and g and collect the terms of order o(h).
sketch_steps: setup: Write the first-order expansions of f and g at a.
derive: Multiply them and isolate f(a)g(a) + f(a)M(h) + g(a)L(h).
derive: Bound every remaining term by a constant times the square of the norm of h or by a little-o term.
conclude: The linear part is f(a)M + g(a)L.

drafts.canonical_statement: If f has derivative L at a and g has derivative M at f(a), then the composite g∘f has derivative M∘L at a.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v6"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v7"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v8"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normed_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normed_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normed_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="has_fderiv_at"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v6"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v8"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="has_fderiv_at"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v7"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v8"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="has_fderiv_at"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="function_compose_map"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="operator_comp"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v7"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v6"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v8"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Substitute the expansion of f into the expansion of g and absorb the remainders using the Lipschitz bound on the increment of f.
sketch_steps: setup: Put k = f(a+h) - f(a) and expand it as L(h) plus a little-o term.
derive: Near 0 the norm of k is at most a constant times the norm of h.
apply_theorem: Expand g at f(a) and evaluate at k.
derive: Boundedness of M and the bound on k turn every remainder into o(h).
conclude: The linear part of the composite is M∘L.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a curve γ has velocity v at t and a real-valued function f has derivative L at γ(t), then s ↦ f(γ(s)) has derivative L(v) at t.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the chain rule, viewing the velocity as the linear map h ↦ hv.
sketch_steps: translate: View the velocity v as the derivative h ↦ hv of γ at t.
apply_theorem: Apply the chain rule to f∘γ.
conclude: The resulting linear map h ↦ hL(v) corresponds to the derivative L(v).

drafts.canonical_statement: A map f from a real normed space to R^m has derivative L at a if and only if for every i the component f_i has as derivative at a the i-th component of L.

sketch_steps: derive: On each coordinate axis f vanishes identically, so both partial derivatives are 0.
derive: For t different from 0, f(t,t) = 1/2.
contradiction: Continuity at the origin would force the limit along the diagonal to be f(0,0) = 0.
conclude: Hence f is not continuous at the origin.

sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The defining property of the gradient gives df(a)(e_i) as an inner product.
derive: The inner product with e_i is the i-th coordinate.
conclude: So the component of the gradient is the partial derivative.

conclude: This is the stated formula.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply Cauchy-Schwarz to the inner product representation and check equality at the normalized gradient.
sketch_steps: translate: Write df(a)(v) as the inner product of the gradient with v.
apply_theorem: Cauchy-Schwarz bounds it by the norm of the gradient for unit v.
construct: Assuming the gradient is nonzero, normalize it to get u.
derive: Compute the norm of u and the value df(a)(u).
conclude: The bound is attained in the gradient direction.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a real-valued function on a real Hilbert space is differentiable at a and has a local maximum or minimum at a, then its gradient at a is 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Restrict to lines through a, use the one-variable criterion, then test the gradient against itself.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix a vector v and define g(t) = f(a+tv).
apply_theorem: g has a local extremum at 0, so g'(0) = df(a)(v) = 0.
derive: Hence the inner product of the gradient with every v vanishes.
conclude: Taking v equal to the gradient shows that the gradient is 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: If f has a local extremum at a and the directional derivative p in direction v exists at a, then p = 0. In particular every existing partial derivative at a vanishes.

drafts.proof_strategy: Reduce to the one-variable extremum criterion along the line through a in direction v.
sketch_steps: construct: Define g(t) = f(a+tv).
derive: Continuity of the line implies that g has a local extremum at 0.
apply_theorem: The one-variable criterion gives g'(0) = 0.
conclude: Therefore p = 0.

sketch_steps: setup: The segment from x to y lies in s by convexity.
construct: Define g(t) = f(x + t(y-x)) on [0,1].
derive: The chain rule bounds the norm of g'(t) by C times the norm of y-x.
apply_theorem: The one-variable mean value inequality bounds g(1)-g(0).
conclude: Since g(1)-g(0) = f(y)-f(x), the inequality follows.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show that a level set of f is open and closed in s, using the mean value inequality on small balls.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix x_0 in s and define A as the set of points of s where f equals f(x_0).
derive: Continuity makes A closed in s.
apply_theorem: The mean value inequality with C = 0 makes f constant on balls in s, so A is open.
derive: A contains x_0, so it is nonempty.
conclude: Connectedness of s gives A = s.

drafts.canonical_statement: If the partial derivatives f_x and f_y of f from R^2 to R exist everywhere and are continuous, then f is differentiable at each point p with derivative (h,k) ↦ f_x(p)h + f_y(p)k.

drafts.proof_strategy: Change one variable at a time, apply the one-variable mean value theorem, and use continuity of the partial derivatives.
sketch_steps: setup: Split the increment of f into a change in x followed by a change in y.
apply_theorem: The one-variable mean value theorem expresses each piece through a partial derivative at an intermediate point.
derive: Continuity of the partial derivatives replaces the intermediate points by p up to o(h,k).
conclude: The sum is the claimed linear map plus a little-o remainder.

drafts.proof_strategy: Express the symmetric second difference through both mixed partials using the mean value theorem twice, then pass to the limit by continuity.
sketch_steps: construct: Define the second difference D(h,k) of f around (a,b).
apply_theorem: The mean value theorem in x, then in y, expresses D through one mixed partial.
apply_theorem: The same argument in the other order expresses D through the other mixed partial.
derive: Divide by hk and let h and k tend to 0.
conclude: Continuity of the second partial derivatives makes the two limits equal.

drafts.canonical_statement: If f from R^2 to R is of class C^2 with partial derivatives P = f_x and Q = f_y, then P_y = Q_x everywhere, so a gradient field is curl-free.

drafts.proof_strategy: Express P and Q through the first derivative of f and use symmetry of the second derivative.
sketch_steps: translate: Write P(q) = df(q)(1,0) and Q(q) = df(q)(0,1).
derive: Differentiating gives dP(p)(v) = d^2f(p)(v)(1,0) and dQ(p)(w) = d^2f(p)(w)(0,1).
apply_theorem: The second derivative of a C^2 function is symmetric.
conclude: Hence P_y = Q_x.

drafts.canonical_statement: If f : E -> R on a real normed space satisfies f(ty) = t^k f(y) for all t > 0 and y in E, with real k, and f has derivative L at x, then L(x) = k f(x) (Euler's homogeneous function theorem).

drafts.proof_strategy: Differentiate the identity f(tx) = t^k f(x) at t = 1 in two ways.
sketch_steps: construct: Define g(t) = f(tx) for real t.
apply_theorem: The chain rule along the ray gives g'(1) = L(x).
derive: Near t = 1 we have g(t) = t^k f(x), so g'(1) = k f(x).
conclude: Uniqueness of the derivative gives L(x) = k f(x).

drafts.canonical_statement: (Inverse function theorem) If a C^1 map f between Banach spaces has at a a derivative L with bounded inverse, then there is g with g(f(a)) = a that inverts f near a and near f(a), g is C^1 at f(a), and its derivative there is the inverse of L.

drafts.proof_strategy: Solve f(x) = y as a fixed point problem and apply the contraction mapping principle near a.
sketch_steps: translate: Rewrite f(x) = y as the fixed point equation x = x - L^{-1}(f(x) - y).
derive: Since f is C^1, this map is a contraction on a small closed ball around a.
apply_theorem: The contraction mapping principle gives a unique solution for each y near f(a).
construct: Let g(y) be this solution, a local inverse of f.
derive: Inverting the linear approximation of f gives the derivative of g.
conclude: The formula for the derivative shows that g is C^1 at f(a).

drafts.canonical_statement: If g is continuous at b, f(g(y)) = y for y near b, and f has at g(b) a derivative L that is a continuous linear isomorphism, then g is differentiable at b with derivative the inverse of L.

drafts.proof_strategy: Invert the first-order expansion of f at g(b) and use continuity of g to control the remainder.
sketch_steps: setup: Put k = y - b and h = g(y) - g(b).
derive: The expansion of f gives k = L(h) + o(h).
derive: Applying the inverse of L gives h = L^{-1}(k) + o(h).
derive: Continuity of g and boundedness of the inverse give a bound of h by a constant times k.
conclude: Therefore h = L^{-1}(k) + o(k), which is differentiability with the stated derivative.

drafts.canonical_statement: (Implicit function theorem) Let E_1, E_2, F be Banach spaces, f from E_1×E_2 to F be C^1 near u, and suppose the partial derivative M of the derivative L at u in the second variable has a bounded inverse. Then there is φ with φ(u_1) = u_2 such that, for v near u, f(v) = f(u) if and only if φ(v_1) = v_2. Moreover φ is differentiable at u_1 with derivative -M^{-1} composed with the partial derivative of L in the first variable.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the inverse function theorem to G(x,y) = (x, f(x,y)) and read off the implicit function from its local inverse.
sketch_steps: construct: Define G(x,y) = (x, f(x,y)).
derive: The invertibility of M makes the derivative of G at u invertible.
apply_theorem: The inverse function theorem gives a local inverse of G.
construct: Define φ from the second component of this local inverse at (x, f(u)).
derive: Near u the level set of f through u is the graph of φ.
conclude: Differentiating f(x, φ(x)) = f(u) by the chain rule gives the derivative of φ.

drafts.canonical_statement: (Lagrange multipliers) Let φ and g be real-valued functions on a Banach space, strictly differentiable at a with derivatives φ' and g', and suppose g' is nonzero. If φ restricted to the level set of g through a has a local extremum at a, then φ' = λ g' for some real λ.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show that the pair of derivatives is not surjective onto R^2, obtain a linear dependence, and exclude the vanishing coefficient of φ'.
sketch_steps: construct: Consider the map x ↦ (g(x), φ(x)) and its derivative at a.
contradiction: If the derivative were surjective, an open mapping argument would contradict the local extremum on the level set.
derive: Hence there is a nonzero pair (p,q) with p g' + q φ' = 0.
case_split: If q = 0 then p is nonzero and g' = 0, against the hypothesis.
conclude: So q is nonzero and φ' = (-p/q) g'.

drafts.canonical_statement: A function continuous on a closed box [a,b] in R^n is integrable on [a,b].

drafts.proof_strategy: Compactness gives boundedness, and a bounded measurable function on a set of finite measure is integrable.
sketch_steps: derive: The closed box is compact.
apply_theorem: A continuous function on a compact set is bounded.
derive: The box has finite volume, so the integral of the absolute value of f is finite.
conclude: Hence f is integrable on the box.

drafts.canonical_statement: If f from R^2 to R is continuous on the rectangle [a,b]×[c,d], then its double integral equals the iterated integral in either order.

sketch_steps: derive: The rectangle is compact, so continuous f is bounded and integrable on it.
apply_theorem: Fubini expresses the double integral as the iterated integral in x then y.
apply_theorem: Fubini also lets the order of the iterated integrals be exchanged.
conclude: All three integrals agree.

sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Fubini rewrites the double integral as an iterated integral.
derive: In the inner integral f(x) is constant.
derive: The integral of g is a constant in the outer integral.
conclude: The result is the product of the two single integrals.

drafts.proof_strategy: Approximate f locally by its derivative, deduce the measure formula, and extend from indicator functions to integrable functions.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: A linear map scales the volume of every set by the absolute value of its determinant.
setup: Partition s into small measurable pieces where f is close to its linearization.
derive: Summing gives the measure of f(A) as the integral of the absolute determinant over A.
derive: This is the integral formula for indicator functions.
conclude: Approximation by simple functions extends the formula to integrable g.

drafts.canonical_statement: The map Φ(r,θ) = (r cos θ, r sin θ) is differentiable at every point (r,θ), and the determinant of its derivative is r.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compute the Jacobian matrix of Φ and its determinant.
sketch_steps: derive: The partial derivatives of the components give the Jacobian matrix.
derive: Its determinant is r cos^2 θ + r sin^2 θ.
conclude: The identity cos^2 θ + sin^2 θ = 1 reduces the determinant to r.

drafts.canonical_statement: If f from R^2 to R is integrable, then its integral over the plane equals the integral over (0,∞)×(-π,π) of r f(r cos θ, r sin θ).

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the change of variables formula to polar coordinates and discard a null set.
sketch_steps: setup: Let Φ be the polar map on (0,∞)×(-π,π).
derive: Φ is injective there with Jacobian determinant r > 0.
derive: Its image is the plane minus a closed half-line, which has measure zero.
apply_theorem: The change of variables formula gives the integral of r f(Φ) over the domain.
conclude: This equals the integral of f over the plane.

drafts.canonical_statement: (Gaussian integral) For b > 0, the integral of exp(-b x^2) over the real line equals the square root of π/b.

drafts.proof_strategy: Square the integral, pass to polar coordinates, and take the positive root.
sketch_steps: setup: Let I be the integral, and note that I is positive.
apply_theorem: Fubini writes I^2 as a double integral over the plane.
apply_theorem: Polar coordinates turn it into an elementary integral of r exp(-b r^2).
derive: Evaluating gives I^2 = π/b.
conclude: Positivity of I gives the square root.

conclude: Since sx + ty is an integer, a divides bx + cy.

drafts.proof_strategy: Existence from the least nonnegative value of a - bk; uniqueness because a multiple of b smaller than |b| in absolute value vanishes.
sketch_steps: construct: Let r = a - bq be the least nonnegative element of {a - bk}.
contradiction: If r ≥ |b| then r - |b| is a smaller nonnegative element.
setup: Suppose a = bq' + r' is another such representation.
derive: Then b(q - q') = r' - r with |r' - r| < |b|.
conclude: Hence r' = r and, since b ≠ 0, q' = q.

drafts.canonical_statement: If integers satisfy a = bq + r, then gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, r).

drafts.proof_strategy: Show that the pairs (a, b) and (b, r) have the same common divisors.
sketch_steps: derive: A common divisor of a and b divides r = a - bq.
derive: A common divisor of b and r divides a = bq + r.
conclude: The sets of common divisors agree, so the greatest common divisors agree.

drafts.proof_strategy: Take the least positive value of ax + by and show it is the gcd.
sketch_steps: case_split: The case a = b = 0 is immediate with x = y = 0.
construct: Otherwise let d be the least positive integer of the form ax + by.
apply_theorem: Divide a and b by d; the remainders have the same form and are smaller than d.
derive: So the remainders vanish and d is a common divisor.
conclude: gcd(a, b) divides d, hence d = gcd(a, b).

drafts.proof_strategy: One direction is Bézout; the other uses that a common divisor divides the combination.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: If gcd(a, b) = 1, Bézout gives x and y with ax + by = 1.
derive: If ax + by = 1, every common divisor of a and b divides 1.
conclude: Hence gcd(a, b) = 1.

sketch_steps: derive: If ax + by = c, then gcd(a, b) divides c because it divides a and b.
setup: Conversely write c = gcd(a, b) k.
apply_theorem: Take s and t with as + bt = gcd(a, b) by Bézout.
conclude: Then x = sk, y = tk solves the equation.

conclude: a divides both summands, so a divides c.

drafts.proof_strategy: Factor out the gcd and identify the lcm using coprimality of the cofactors.
sketch_steps: case_split: If a or b is zero, both sides are zero.
setup: Otherwise write a = da' and b = db' with d = gcd(a, b) and a', b' coprime.
derive: Coprimality shows that the least common multiple is da'b'.
conclude: Multiplying by d gives ab.

sketch_steps: case_split: Assume p does not divide a.
derive: The only positive divisors of p are 1 and p, so gcd(p, a) = 1.
apply_theorem: Take x and y with px + ay = 1.
derive: Multiplying by b gives b = pbx + (ab)y.
conclude: p divides both terms, so p divides b.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every natural number n ≥ 2 has a prime divisor.

drafts.proof_strategy: The least divisor greater than 1 must be prime.
sketch_steps: construct: Let p be the least divisor of n greater than 1.
contradiction: A proper nontrivial divisor of p would be a smaller divisor of n.
conclude: So p is a prime divisor of n.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every composite number n ≥ 2 has a prime divisor p with p² ≤ n.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply minimality of the least prime factor to the cofactor.
sketch_steps: construct: Let p be the least divisor of n greater than 1; it is prime.
setup: Write n = pm.
derive: Since n is composite, m > 1, and so m ≥ p by minimality.
conclude: Therefore p² ≤ pm = n.

drafts.canonical_statement: For every natural number n there is a prime greater than n; that is, there are infinitely many primes.

drafts.proof_strategy: A prime factor of n! + 1 cannot be at most n.
sketch_steps: construct: Let p be a prime divisor of n! + 1.
contradiction: If p ≤ n then p divides n!, hence p divides 1.
conclude: So p > n.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every positive integer is a product of primes, and this factorization is unique up to the order of the factors.

drafts.proof_strategy: Existence by strong induction via a prime factor; uniqueness by induction using Euclid's lemma to cancel a common prime.
sketch_steps: induction: Prove existence by strong induction on n.
apply_theorem: For n ≥ 2 take a prime factor p and factor n/p.
setup: For uniqueness compare two factorizations of n.
apply_theorem: By Euclid's lemma p_1 divides some q_j, and then p_1 = q_j.
induction: Cancel p_1 and apply the induction hypothesis to n/p_1.
conclude: The two multisets of primes coincide.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a prime p and a natural number k with 0 < k < p, p divides the binomial coefficient C(p, k).

sketch_steps: setup: Write k!(p-k)! C(p, k) = p!.
derive: p divides the left side, while every factor of k! and (p-k)! is smaller than p.
apply_theorem: By Euclid's lemma p does not divide k!(p-k)!.
conclude: Hence p divides C(p, k).

sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Take u and v with mu + nv = 1.
construct: anv + bmu solves the system; add a multiple of mn to make it nonnegative.
translate: y solves the system exactly when m and n both divide y - x.
apply_theorem: For coprime m and n this is equivalent to mn dividing y - x.
conclude: Solutions form one residue class modulo mn.

drafts.proof_strategy: Multiplication by a permutes the nonzero residues; compare the products of all residues.
sketch_steps: setup: Consider the residues a, 2a, ..., (p-1)a modulo p.
derive: They are nonzero and pairwise incongruent, so they permute 1, ..., p-1.
derive: Taking products gives a^(p-1) (p-1)! ≡ (p-1)! modulo p.
apply_theorem: (p-1)! is coprime to p, so it can be cancelled.
conclude: Therefore a^(p-1) ≡ 1 modulo p.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a prime p and every integer a, a^p ≡ a modulo p.

sketch_steps: case_split: If p divides a, both sides are congruent to 0.
apply_theorem: Otherwise a^(p-1) ≡ 1 modulo p.
conclude: Multiply by a to get a^p ≡ a.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a prime p and integers a and b, (a + b)^p ≡ a^p + b^p modulo p.

drafts.proof_strategy: Expand with the binomial theorem and discard the middle terms, whose coefficients are multiples of p.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Expand (a + b)^p by the binomial theorem.
derive: For 0 < k < p the coefficient C(p, k) is divisible by p.
conclude: Only a^p and b^p survive modulo p.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a positive integer n and a natural number a coprime to n, a^φ(n) ≡ 1 modulo n, where φ is Euler's totient function.

drafts.proof_strategy: Multiplication by a permutes the reduced residues; compare the products.
sketch_steps: setup: List the reduced residues r_1, ..., r_φ(n) modulo n.
derive: Multiplication by a permutes them because gcd(a, n) = 1.
derive: Comparing products gives a^φ(n) R ≡ R modulo n, with R the product of the residues.
apply_theorem: R is coprime to n, so it can be cancelled.
conclude: Hence a^φ(n) ≡ 1 modulo n.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a prime p and a positive integer k, φ(p^k) = p^(k-1)(p-1).

drafts.proof_strategy: Count the multiples of p up to p^k.
sketch_steps: translate: An integer is not coprime to p^k exactly when p divides it.
derive: There are p^(k-1) multiples of p in 1, ..., p^k.
conclude: φ(p^k) = p^k - p^(k-1) = p^(k-1)(p - 1).

drafts.canonical_statement: For coprime positive integers m and n, φ(mn) = φ(m)φ(n).

drafts.proof_strategy: The Chinese remainder correspondence restricts to a bijection on reduced residues.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The Chinese remainder theorem pairs residues mod mn with residues mod m and mod n.
translate: x is coprime to mn exactly when it is coprime to both m and n.
derive: So the correspondence restricts to reduced residues.
conclude: Counting gives φ(mn) = φ(m)φ(n).

drafts.canonical_statement: For a positive integer n, the sum of φ(d) over the positive divisors d of n equals n.

drafts.proof_strategy: Partition 1, ..., n according to the gcd with n.
sketch_steps: setup: Classify k in 1, ..., n by the value of gcd(k, n).
translate: gcd(k, n) = n/d exactly when k = (n/d)j with 1 ≤ j ≤ d and gcd(j, d) = 1.
derive: Each such class has φ(d) elements.
conclude: Summing over the divisors d of n counts all n integers once.

drafts.proof_strategy: Factor x² - 1 and apply Euclid's lemma.
sketch_steps: translate: p divides x² - 1 = (x - 1)(x + 1).
apply_theorem: By Euclid's lemma p divides x - 1 or x + 1.
conclude: Hence x ≡ 1 or x ≡ -1 modulo p.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a natural number n ≥ 2, n is prime if and only if n divides (n-1)! + 1.

drafts.proof_strategy: Pair residues with their inverses for primes; a proper divisor rules out composites.
sketch_steps: setup: Let n be prime and pair each residue in 1, ..., n-1 with its inverse.
apply_theorem: Only 1 and n - 1 are self-inverse, because x² ≡ 1 forces x ≡ ±1.
derive: The pairs multiply to 1, so (n-1)! ≡ -1 modulo n.
case_split: Let n be composite with a divisor d, 1 < d < n.
contradiction: d divides (n-1)!, so if n divided (n-1)! + 1 then d would divide 1.
conclude: The divisibility holds exactly for primes.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a positive integer n, a natural number a coprime to n and a natural number k, the multiplicative order of a modulo n divides k if and only if a^k ≡ 1 modulo n.

drafts.proof_strategy: Divide k by the order and use minimality of the order on the remainder.
sketch_steps: setup: Let d be the order and write k = dq + r with 0 ≤ r < d.
derive: a^k ≡ a^r modulo n because a^d ≡ 1.
contradiction: If a^k ≡ 1 and r > 0, then r contradicts the minimality of d.
derive: If d divides k, then a^k = (a^d)^q ≡ 1.
conclude: The two conditions are equivalent.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a positive integer n and a natural number a coprime to n, the multiplicative order of a modulo n divides φ(n).

sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Euler's theorem gives a^φ(n) ≡ 1 modulo n.
conclude: The order divides every exponent with this property, so it divides φ(n).

drafts.proof_strategy: Count elements of each order, using that x^d = 1 has at most d roots modulo p and that φ sums to n over divisors.
sketch_steps: setup: Let ψ(d) be the number of residues of order d, for d dividing p - 1.
apply_theorem: x^d = 1 has at most d roots in the field Z/pZ.
derive: So ψ(d) is 0 or φ(d).
apply_theorem: The sum of φ(d) over the divisors of p - 1 is p - 1, as is the sum of ψ(d).
derive: Hence ψ(d) = φ(d) for every d.
conclude: In particular ψ(p - 1) = φ(p - 1) > 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: The forward direction is Fermat's little theorem; the converse writes a as a power of a primitive root and shows the exponent is even.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: If x² ≡ a, then a^((p-1)/2) ≡ x^(p-1) ≡ 1 by Fermat's little theorem.
construct: Conversely take a primitive root g and write a ≡ g^k.
derive: a^((p-1)/2) ≡ 1 means p - 1 divides k(p-1)/2.
derive: Hence k is even.
conclude: x = g^(k/2) satisfies x² ≡ a.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show that the power is ±1 by Fermat and identify the sign using Euler's criterion.
sketch_steps: case_split: If p divides a, both sides are congruent to 0.
apply_theorem: Otherwise b = a^((p-1)/2) satisfies b² ≡ 1, so b ≡ ±1.
apply_theorem: By Euler's criterion b ≡ 1 exactly when a is a quadratic residue.
conclude: Since 1 and -1 are incongruent, b agrees with the Legendre symbol.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the power formula modulo p and the fact that values in {0, 1, -1} are determined by their residues.
sketch_steps: case_split: The case p = 2 is checked directly.
apply_theorem: For odd p, (a/p) ≡ a^((p-1)/2) modulo p.
derive: Hence (ab/p) ≡ (a/p)(b/p) modulo p.
conclude: Both sides lie in {0, 1, -1}, which are distinct modulo p ≥ 3, so they are equal.

derive: Since 1 and -1 are incongruent modulo p, this says (p-1)/2 is even.
conclude: That is p ≡ 1 modulo 4.

drafts.proof_strategy: Express both symbols as signs of lattice point counts on either side of a diagonal in a rectangle (outline).
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Eisenstein's form of Gauss's lemma gives (q/p) = (-1)^S with S the sum of ⌊kq/p⌋.
apply_theorem: Likewise (p/q) = (-1)^T with T the sum of ⌊lp/q⌋.
translate: S and T count lattice points below and above the line y = qx/p in the rectangle.
derive: No lattice point of the rectangle lies on the line, because p and q are distinct primes.
derive: Therefore S + T = ((p-1)/2)((q-1)/2).
conclude: Multiplying the two symbols gives the sign.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use that -1 is a square modulo p to show p is reducible in the Gaussian integers, then take norms.
sketch_steps: case_split: p = 2 is 1² + 1².
apply_theorem: For p ≡ 1 mod 4 there is x with x² ≡ -1 modulo p.
derive: p divides (x + i)(x - i) but neither factor.
apply_theorem: Z[i] is a Euclidean domain, so p is reducible, p = αβ with non-units.
derive: N(α)N(β) = p² forces N(α) = p.
conclude: Writing α = a + bi gives p = a² + b².

drafts.proof_strategy: Descend by q² for primes q ≡ 3 mod 4; conversely combine prime representations with the two-squares identity (outline).
sketch_steps: setup: Suppose n = x² + y² and q ≡ 3 mod 4 divides n.
apply_theorem: -1 is not a square modulo q, so q divides both x and y.
induction: Dividing by q² repeatedly shows that q has even exponent.
setup: Conversely write n as a square times a product of 2 and primes ≡ 1 mod 4.
apply_theorem: Each such prime is a sum of two squares.
conclude: The two-squares identity shows the product is also a sum of two squares.

sketch_steps: derive: Squares are congruent to 0 or 1 modulo 4.
derive: Therefore x² + y² is congruent to 0, 1 or 2 modulo 4.
conclude: It cannot equal 4k + 3.

drafts.proof_strategy: Interchange the order of summation and apply the divisor sum of the Möbius function.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The sum of μ(d) over d | n is 1 for n = 1 and 0 otherwise.
setup: Assume g(n) is the divisor sum of f.
derive: Substituting and interchanging sums gives the sum over e | n of f(e) times the sum of μ(d) over d | n/e.
derive: Only e = n survives, which gives f(n).
conclude: The converse follows by the same interchange of sums.

sketch_steps: case_split: For n = 1 the sum is μ(1) = 1.
setup: For n ≥ 2 let p_1, ..., p_r be the distinct prime factors.
derive: Nonzero terms come from products of k of the primes and equal (-1)^k.
conclude: The sum equals (1 - 1)^r = 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Trivial for squares by factoring; for nonsquares use Dirichlet approximation and pigeonhole to divide two solutions of the same norm (outline).
sketch_steps: derive: If d = t², factoring (x - ty)(x + ty) = 1 forces y = 0.
apply_theorem: Otherwise Dirichlet's approximation gives infinitely many (x, y) with |x - y√d| < 1/y.
derive: For these pairs |x² - dy²| is bounded.
derive: By pigeonhole two distinct pairs have the same norm m and the same residues modulo |m|.
construct: Dividing one by the other in Z[√d] gives an integer solution of norm 1.
conclude: This solution has y ≠ 0 because the two pairs are distinct.

drafts.proof_strategy: Round the complex quotient to the nearest lattice point.
sketch_steps: construct: Round the real and imaginary parts of x/y to nearest integers to get q.
derive: Then |x/y - q|² ≤ 1/2.
setup: Put r = x - yq, a Gaussian integer.
conclude: N(r) = N(y)|x/y - q|² ≤ N(y)/2 < N(y).

drafts.canonical_statement: A prime number p is a prime element of the Gaussian integers if and only if p ≡ 3 modulo 4.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the two-squares theorem to factor p when p is not 3 mod 4; otherwise norms and residues modulo 4 show irreducibility.
sketch_steps: case_split: Suppose p is not congruent to 3 modulo 4.
apply_theorem: Then p = a² + b², so p = (a + bi)(a - bi) with non-units.
case_split: Suppose p ≡ 3 modulo 4 and p = αβ with non-units.
derive: Norms give N(α) = p, so p is a sum of two squares.
contradiction: Squares modulo 4 exclude this.
apply_theorem: Z[i] is a Euclidean domain, so the irreducible p is prime.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a predicate P on natural numbers has the property that P(n) implies P(m) for some m < n, then P(n) holds for no natural number n.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the well-ordering of the natural numbers to the set where P holds.
sketch_steps: contradiction: Assume P holds at some natural number.
construct: Take the least n_0 with P(n_0).
derive: The hypothesis yields m < n_0 with P(m).
conclude: This contradicts minimality, so P holds nowhere.

drafts.proof_strategy: Parametrize primitive Pythagorean triples twice and produce a smaller solution, contradicting minimality (outline).
sketch_steps: setup: Take a solution with least |c|; then a and b are coprime.
apply_theorem: (a², b², c) is a primitive Pythagorean triple, parametrized by m and n.
apply_theorem: (a, n, m) is also a primitive Pythagorean triple.
derive: Coprimality shows that the relevant factors are perfect squares.
construct: These squares form a new solution with smaller |c|.
contradiction: This contradicts the minimal choice, so no solution exists.

sketch_steps: derive: C(2n, n) ≥ 4^n/(2n).
contradiction: Assume there is no prime in (n, 2n].
apply_theorem: By Legendre's formula all prime factors are at most 2n/3 and prime powers are at most 2n.
apply_theorem: The bound on primorials gives the product of primes up to x at most 4^x.
derive: For large n the resulting upper bound is smaller than 4^n/(2n).
case_split: Small n are checked with an explicit list of primes.
conclude: A prime exists in (n, 2n] for every positive n.

sketch_steps: derive: The product rule gives (e^{P} y)' = e^{P} q on ℝ.
setup: P is differentiable hence continuous, so e^{P} q is continuous and interval integrable.
apply_theorem: The fundamental theorem of calculus gives e^{P(t)} y(t) - e^{P(a)} y(a) = ∫_a^t e^{P} q.
conclude: Rearrange and multiply by e^{-P(t)}.

drafts.proof_strategy: Differentiate H(y(t)) - G(t) by the chain rule and check that the derivative vanishes.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The chain rule gives (H∘y)'(t) = (1/h(y(t))) g(t) h(y(t)).
derive: Since h(y(t)) ≠ 0 this equals g(t), so (H∘y - G)' = 0.
apply_theorem: A function with zero derivative on ℝ is constant.
conclude: Hence H(y(t)) - G(t) = H(y(s)) - G(s).

drafts.proof_strategy: Differentiate the reciprocal of the denominator and compare with r y (1 - y) after clearing denominators.
sketch_steps: setup: Put D(s) = 1 + C e^{-rs}, so D'(t) = -r C e^{-rt} and D(t) ≠ 0.
apply_theorem: The quotient rule gives y'(t) = r C e^{-rt} / D(t)^2.
derive: Since D - 1 = C e^{-rt}, we have r y (1 - y) = r C e^{-rt} / D(t)^2.
conclude: The two expressions agree.

derive: On (s,t) we have g'(u) = (f'(u) - a f(u)) e^{-au} ≤ 0.
apply_theorem: A continuous function with nonpositive derivative on the interior is nonincreasing.
conclude: g(t) ≤ g(s), and multiplying by e^{at} > 0 gives the bound.

drafts.proof_strategy: Pass to the integral v(t) = c + K∫_a^t u, which satisfies a differential inequality, and apply the integrating factor e^{-K(t-a)}.
sketch_steps: setup: Extend u continuously from [a,b] to ℝ so that the integral is differentiable everywhere.
translate: Put v(t) = c + K ∫_a^t u, so u ≤ v and v' = K u on [a,b].
derive: Since K ≥ 0, v' = K u ≤ K v, so (v e^{-K(t-a)})' ≤ 0.
apply_theorem: A function with nonpositive derivative is nonincreasing, so v(t) e^{-K(t-a)} ≤ v(a) = c.
conclude: Therefore u(t) ≤ v(t) ≤ c e^{K(t-a)}.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compare the norm with the exact solution of φ' = Kφ + ε, φ(a) = δ, using a slope comparison on the right.
sketch_steps: translate: The upper right slope of ‖f‖ is at most ‖f'‖, hence at most K‖f‖ + ε.
construct: The bound φ(x) = δ e^{K(x-a)} + (ε/K)(e^{K(x-a)} - 1) satisfies φ' = Kφ + ε and φ(a) = δ.
contradiction: With ε slightly increased, ‖f‖ cannot cross φ, since at a first crossing the slopes would contradict.
conclude: Letting the increase tend to 0 gives the bound for ε.

sketch_steps: setup: Put h = f - g, so h(a) = 0.
derive: The Lipschitz condition gives ‖h'(t)‖ ≤ K‖h(t)‖ on [a,b).
apply_theorem: Grönwall's estimate with δ = 0 and ε = 0 gives ‖h(t)‖ ≤ 0.
conclude: Hence f = g on [a,b].

drafts.canonical_statement: (Picard–Lindelöf) Let E be a real Banach space, t₀ ∈ [tmin, tmax], and suppose that on the closed ball B(x₀, a) the field f(t, x) is K-Lipschitz in x, continuous in t and bounded in norm by L, with L·max(tmax - t₀, t₀ - tmin) ≤ a. Then x' = f(t, x), x(t₀) = x₀ has a solution on [tmin, tmax].

sketch_steps: translate: A solution is the same as a fixed point of Φ(α)(t) = x₀ + ∫_{t₀}^t f(s, α(s)) ds.
setup: Let X be the complete space of continuous curves with values in the closed ball B(x₀, a).
derive: The bound L and the time-width condition show that Φ maps X into X.
derive: The Lipschitz condition gives ‖Φ^n α - Φ^n β‖ ≤ (K T)^n / n! ‖α - β‖, so an iterate is a contraction.
apply_theorem: Banach's fixed point theorem gives a fixed point of Φ.
conclude: Differentiating the integral equation gives the solution.

derive: Applying it again gives y''.
conclude: Comparing coefficients of cos βt and sin βt gives y'' = 2α y' - (α² + β²) y.

conclude: Divide by r₁ - r₂ ≠ 0 to obtain c₁ and c₂.

conclude: Hence E(t) ≤ E(s) for s ≤ t.

drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="matrix_square"></n1:OMS><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="R"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="has_deriv_at"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="fns1" name="lambda"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="matrix_exp"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="matrix_scale"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="matrix_mul"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="matrix_exp"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="matrix_scale"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Differentiate the exponential power series term by term, using its infinite radius of convergence.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix a submultiplicative norm on the matrix algebra, which is finite-dimensional and complete.
apply_theorem: The exponential series has infinite radius of convergence, so it may be differentiated term by term.
derive: The termwise derivative is Σ t^{n-1} A^n / (n-1)!.
conclude: Factoring out A gives A exp(tA).

drafts.canonical_statement: For a real square matrix A and a vector x₀, the curve x(t) = exp(tA) x₀ solves the linear system x' = A x.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="matrix_square"></n1:OMS><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="R"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="has_deriv_at"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="fns1" name="lambda"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="matrix_vector_mul"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="matrix_exp"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="matrix_scale"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="matrix_vector_mul"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="matrix_vector_mul"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="matrix_exp"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="matrix_scale"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Compose the derivative of exp(tA) with the continuous linear evaluation map M ↦ M x₀.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The derivative of exp(tA) is A exp(tA).
construct: M ↦ M x₀ is a continuous linear map on matrices.
derive: The chain rule gives (exp(tA) x₀)' = (A exp(tA)) x₀.
conclude: Associativity rewrites this as A (exp(tA) x₀).

drafts.canonical_statement: If real square matrices A and B commute, then exp(A + B) = exp(A) exp(B).
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="matrix_square"></n1:OMS><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="R"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="matrix_square"></n1:OMS><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="R"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="commuting_matrices"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="matrix_exp"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="matrix_mul"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="matrix_exp"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="matrix_exp"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Expand with the binomial theorem, valid because A and B commute, and rearrange the absolutely convergent double series.
sketch_steps: derive: Commutativity gives (A+B)^n / n! = Σ_{k+l=n} A^k B^l / (k! l!).
apply_theorem: The exponential series converge absolutely, so their Cauchy product may be rearranged.
conclude: Grouping by k + l = n gives exp(A) exp(B) = exp(A+B).

drafts.canonical_statement: For a real square matrix A, exp(-A) is the inverse matrix of exp(A).
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="matrix_square"></n1:OMS><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="R"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="matrix_exp"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="unary_minus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="matrix_inverse"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="matrix_exp"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the exponential law to the commuting pair A, -A.
sketch_steps: translate: A and -A commute.
apply_theorem: The exponential law gives exp(A) exp(-A) = exp(0) = I.
conclude: Hence exp(-A) is the inverse of exp(A).

drafts.canonical_statement: For a probability measure P and a measurable event A, P(Aᶜ) = 1 - P(A).
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="probability_measure"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="measurable_event"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="prob"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="set_compl"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="minus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMI>1</n1:OMI><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="prob"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Split the whole space into A and its complement and use additivity.
sketch_steps: setup: Note that A and Aᶜ are disjoint with union Ω.
apply_theorem: Additivity gives P(A) + P(Aᶜ) = P(Ω) = 1.
conclude: Rearrange to obtain P(Aᶜ) = 1 - P(A).

drafts.canonical_statement: For measurable events A and B, P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A ∩ B).
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="probability_measure"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="measurable_event"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="measurable_event"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="prob"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="union"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="minus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="prob"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="prob"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="prob"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="intersect"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Use two disjoint decompositions sharing the piece B \ A.
sketch_steps: setup: Decompose A ∪ B = A ⊔ (B \ A) and B = (A ∩ B) ⊔ (B \ A).
apply_theorem: Apply additivity to both decompositions.
derive: Eliminate P(B \ A) between the two equations.
conclude: This yields P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A ∩ B).

drafts.canonical_statement: For a probability measure P and a finite family of arbitrary (not necessarily measurable) subsets A_i of the sample space, P(⋃_{i∈s} A_i) ≤ Σ_{i∈s} P(A_i), where P of a non-measurable set means its outer measure.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="probability_measure"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="finite_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="leq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="prob"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="union_over"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="sum"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="fns1" name="lambda"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="prob"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="seq_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on the finite index set using subadditivity for two sets.
sketch_steps: induction: Induct on the finite set s.
setup: The empty union has probability 0, which settles the base case.
apply_theorem: For the step, use P(B ∪ C) ≤ P(B) + P(C).
conclude: Combine with the induction hypothesis.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a probability measure P, a measurable event A with P(A) > 0 and an arbitrary set B, the conditional probability P(B|A) := P(A∩B)/P(A) satisfies P(B|A)·P(A) = P(A∩B) (P of a non-measurable set is its outer measure).

drafts.proof_strategy: Clear the denominator in the definition of conditional probability.
sketch_steps: translate: Write P(B|A) = P(A ∩ B) / P(A).
derive: Multiply by P(A), which is nonzero.
conclude: This gives P(B|A) P(A) = P(A ∩ B).

drafts.canonical_statement: If A and Aᶜ both have positive probability, then for an event B, P(B) = P(B|A) P(A) + P(B|Aᶜ) P(Aᶜ).

apply_theorem: Use additivity for the disjoint union.
derive: Rewrite each piece with the multiplication rule.
conclude: Sum the two terms.

drafts.proof_strategy: Intersect B with the partition, add up, and apply the multiplication rule termwise.
sketch_steps: setup: Write B as the union of the sets A_i ∩ B.
derive: These sets are measurable and pairwise disjoint because the A_i are.
apply_theorem: Finite additivity gives P(B) = Σ P(A_i ∩ B).
apply_theorem: The multiplication rule rewrites each term as P(B|A_i) P(A_i).
conclude: Summing the rewritten terms gives the formula.

drafts.proof_strategy: Express the same intersection in two ways by the multiplication rule.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Write P(A ∩ B) = P(B|A) P(A).
apply_theorem: Write P(B ∩ A) = P(A|B) P(B).
derive: Equate the right-hand sides since A ∩ B = B ∩ A.
conclude: Divide by P(A) > 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: Measurable events A and B are independent if and only if P(A ∩ B) = P(A) P(B).

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the pi-lambda theorem to pass between generators and generated sigma-algebras.
sketch_steps: translate: Interpret independence of events through the sigma-algebras they generate.
derive: The forward direction specializes to A and B.
apply_theorem: The backward direction uses that singletons are pi-systems and the pi-lambda theorem.
conclude: Hence the two conditions are equivalent.

drafts.canonical_statement: If the measurable events A and B are independent, then A and Bᶜ are independent.

drafts.proof_strategy: Subtract the independent intersection from P(A) and factor.
sketch_steps: setup: Decompose A into A ∩ B and A ∩ Bᶜ.
derive: Additivity gives P(A ∩ Bᶜ) = P(A) - P(A ∩ B).
apply_theorem: Independence turns this into P(A)(1 - P(B)).
conclude: Since 1 - P(B) = P(Bᶜ), the events A and Bᶜ are independent.

drafts.canonical_statement: If the measurable events A and B are independent and P(A) > 0, then P(B|A) = P(B).

drafts.proof_strategy: Substitute the product formula into the definition of conditional probability.
sketch_steps: translate: Write P(B|A) P(A) = P(A ∩ B).
apply_theorem: Independence gives P(A ∩ B) = P(B) P(A).
conclude: Cancel P(A) > 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: If random variables X and Y are independent and φ, ψ are measurable maps, then φ(X) and ψ(Y) are independent.

drafts.proof_strategy: Pull events back through the measurable maps and use independence of X and Y.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix measurable sets C and D in the target spaces.
translate: Rewrite the events through the preimages under φ and ψ.
apply_theorem: Apply independence of X and Y to those measurable preimages.
conclude: The product formula is exactly independence of φ(X) and ψ(Y).

drafts.canonical_statement: For integrable random variables X, Y and real numbers a, b, E[aX + bY] = a E[X] + b E[Y].

drafts.proof_strategy: Reduce to nonnegativity of the integral of Y - X.
sketch_steps: setup: Consider Y - X, which is integrable and almost surely nonnegative.
apply_theorem: The integral of an almost surely nonnegative function is nonnegative.
conclude: Linearity gives E[Y] - E[X] ≥ 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compute the integral of a two-valued simple function.
sketch_steps: translate: View the indicator as a simple function with values 1 and 0.
derive: Its integral is 1·P(A) + 0·P(Aᶜ).
conclude: This equals P(A).

derive: Extend to simple functions by bilinearity.

sketch_steps: setup: Put m = E[X].
derive: Expand (X - m)² = X² - 2mX + m².
apply_theorem: Take expectations with linearity.
conclude: Simplify to E[X²] - m².

drafts.proof_strategy: Expand the square of the centered sum; independence kills the cross terms.
sketch_steps: setup: Center each variable as U_i = X_i - E[X_i].
derive: Expand the square of the sum into diagonal and off-diagonal terms.
apply_theorem: Pairwise independence gives E[U_i U_j] = 0 for i ≠ j.
conclude: Only the diagonal terms remain, which are the variances.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a square-integrable random variable X has variance 0, then X = E[X] almost surely.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="probability_measure"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="square_integrable_rv"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="variance"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ae_eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="expectation"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: A nonnegative function with zero integral vanishes almost everywhere.
sketch_steps: translate: Write the hypothesis as E[(X - E[X])²] = 0.
apply_theorem: A nonnegative function with zero integral is zero almost everywhere.
conclude: Therefore X = E[X] almost surely.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a square-integrable random variable X and a real number a, E[(X - a)²] = Var(X) + (E[X] - a)².
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="probability_measure"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="square_integrable_rv"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="expectation"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="minus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="plus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="variance"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="minus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="expectation"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Insert the mean into the square and note that the cross term has zero expectation.
sketch_steps: setup: Put m = E[X] and write X - a = (X - m) + (m - a).
derive: Expand the square into three terms.
derive: The cross term has zero expectation because E[X - m] = 0.
conclude: The remaining terms are Var(X) and (m - a)².

drafts.canonical_statement: For square-integrable random variables X and Y, Cov(X, Y) = E[XY] - E[X] E[Y].
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="probability_measure"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="square_integrable_rv"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="square_integrable_rv"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="covariance"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="minus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="expectation"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="expectation"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="expectation"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Expand the product in the definition and apply linearity.
sketch_steps: setup: Expand the product of the two centered variables.
derive: Integrability of XY follows from square integrability.
apply_theorem: Take expectations by linearity.
conclude: Two of the product terms cancel.

drafts.canonical_statement: If square-integrable random variables X and Y are independent, then Cov(X, Y) = 0.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="probability_measure"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="square_integrable_rv"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="square_integrable_rv"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="indep_rv"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="covariance"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Combine the covariance formula with the product rule for independent variables.
sketch_steps: translate: Write Cov(X, Y) = E[XY] - E[X] E[Y].
apply_theorem: Independence gives E[XY] = E[X] E[Y].
conclude: The difference vanishes.

drafts.canonical_statement: For square-integrable random variables X and Y, Cov(X, Y)² ≤ Var(X) Var(Y).
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="probability_measure"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="square_integrable_rv"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="square_integrable_rv"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="leq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="covariance"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="times"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="variance"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="variance"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: A quadratic in t that is always nonnegative has nonpositive discriminant.
sketch_steps: construct: Consider the variance of tY + X as a function of t.
derive: Expand it to t² Var(Y) + 2t Cov(X, Y) + Var(X).
apply_theorem: Nonnegativity for all t forces the discriminant to be nonpositive.
conclude: Rearranging gives Cov(X, Y)² ≤ Var(X) Var(Y).

drafts.canonical_statement: For a square-integrable random variable X, E[X]² ≤ E[X²].
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="probability_measure"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="square_integrable_rv"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="leq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="expectation"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="expectation"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Rearrange nonnegativity of the variance.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The variance is the expectation of a square, so it is nonnegative.
translate: Use Var(X) = E[X²] - E[X]².
conclude: Rearrange the inequality.

drafts.canonical_statement: Markov's inequality: for an integrable, almost surely nonnegative random variable X and ε > 0, P(X ≥ ε) ≤ E[X] / ε.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="probability_measure"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="integrable_rv"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="ae_le"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="gt"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="leq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="prob"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="tail_event"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="divide"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="expectation"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Bound X from below by a multiple of the indicator of the tail event.
sketch_steps: setup: Let A = {X ≥ ε}.
derive: Almost surely ε 1_A ≤ X because X is nonnegative.
apply_theorem: Monotonicity of expectation gives ε P(A) ≤ E[X].
conclude: Divide by ε > 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: Chebyshev's inequality: for a square-integrable random variable X and c > 0, P(|X - E[X]| ≥ c) ≤ Var(X) / c².
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="probability_measure"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="square_integrable_rv"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="gt"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>0</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="leq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="prob"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="tail_event"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="abs"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="minus"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="expectation"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="divide"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="variance"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="arith1" name="power"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMI>2</n1:OMI></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Apply Markov's inequality to the squared deviation.
sketch_steps: setup: Put Y = (X - E[X])², which is nonnegative and integrable.
translate: The event |X - E[X]| ≥ c equals Y ≥ c².
apply_theorem: Markov's inequality bounds its probability by E[Y] / c².
conclude: E[Y] is the variance of X.

drafts.canonical_statement: Jensen's inequality: if g is convex and continuous on a closed convex set s, X is integrable with values almost surely in s, and g(X) is integrable, then g(E[X]) ≤ E[g(X)].

drafts.proof_strategy: The mean of a random point in a closed convex set stays in that set; apply this to the epigraph.
sketch_steps: construct: Form the epigraph of g over s.
derive: The epigraph is convex by convexity of g and closed by continuity and closedness of s.
translate: The pair (X, g(X)) lies almost surely in the epigraph.
apply_theorem: The mean of a probability measure on a closed convex set lies in that set.
conclude: Membership of (E[X], E[g(X)]) in the epigraph is the claim.

drafts.canonical_statement: Chernoff bound: if t ≥ 0 and exp(tX) is integrable, then P(X ≥ ε) ≤ exp(-tε) M_X(t) for every real ε, where M_X is the moment generating function.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply Markov's inequality to the exponential of tX.
sketch_steps: derive: If X ≥ ε then exp(tX) ≥ exp(tε), since t ≥ 0.
translate: Hence the tail event is contained in {exp(tX) ≥ exp(tε)}.
apply_theorem: Markov's inequality applies to the nonnegative variable exp(tX).
conclude: The bound is exp(-tε) M_X(t).

drafts.proof_strategy: Factor the exponential and use the product rule for independent variables.
sketch_steps: derive: Write exp(t(X + Y)) = exp(tX) exp(tY).
apply_theorem: Measurable functions of independent variables are independent.
apply_theorem: Expectation of a product of independent integrable variables factors.
conclude: The result is M_X(t) M_Y(t).

drafts.proof_strategy: Bound the probability of the complement with a product and 1 - x ≤ exp(-x).
sketch_steps: translate: Express the complement of limsup as a union of tail intersections of complements.
apply_theorem: Independence factors the probability of finite intersections of complements.
derive: Use 1 - x ≤ exp(-x) to bound the product by exp of minus the partial sum.
derive: Divergence of the series forces this bound to 0.
conclude: Countable subadditivity gives P((limsup A_n)ᶜ) = 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Truncate, control variances along a geometric subsequence, then interpolate by monotonicity.
sketch_steps: setup: Reduce to nonnegative variables by positive and negative parts.
construct: Truncate X_i at level i to obtain Y_i.
apply_theorem: The first Borel–Cantelli lemma shows X_i = Y_i for all but finitely many i.
apply_theorem: Chebyshev and Borel–Cantelli give convergence along a geometric subsequence.
derive: Monotonicity of partial sums fills the gaps between subsequence terms.
conclude: Hence the sample mean converges to E[X_0] almost surely.

sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The strong law for pairwise independent variables has exactly these hypotheses and gives almost sure convergence of the sample mean.
derive: Each sample mean is almost everywhere strongly measurable.
apply_theorem: On a finite measure space, almost sure convergence implies convergence in measure.
translate: Rewrite the distance as the absolute deviation.
conclude: The tail probabilities tend to 0 for every ε > 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compute the limit of characteristic functions and apply Lévy's continuity theorem.
sketch_steps: case_split: Treat the zero-variance case separately since all variables are almost surely constant.
setup: Standardize to mean 0 and variance 1.
apply_theorem: Independence turns the characteristic function of the normalized sum into a power.
derive: A second-order Taylor expansion gives the limit exp(-t²/2).
apply_theorem: Lévy's continuity theorem turns this into convergence in distribution.
conclude: Undo the standardization.

drafts.proof_strategy: Unfold the uniform measure as the counting measure conditioned on s.
sketch_steps: translate: Identify the uniform measure with the counting measure conditioned on s.
derive: Apply the conditional probability formula to t.
conclude: The counting measure turns the quotient into |s ∩ t| / |s|.

drafts.proof_strategy: Differentiate the binomial theorem in x and substitute y = 1 - x.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Start from the binomial theorem for (x + y)^n.
derive: Differentiate in x and multiply by x.
derive: Substitute x = p and y = 1 - p so that x + y = 1.
conclude: The left side becomes n p and the right side is the required sum.

drafts.proof_strategy: Express the second central moment through the factorial moments obtained from the binomial theorem.
sketch_steps: setup: Put b_k = C(n,k) p^k (1-p)^{n-k}.
apply_theorem: The binomial theorem gives Σ b_k = 1.
derive: Differentiating once and twice gives Σ k b_k = np and Σ k(k-1) b_k = n(n-1)p².
derive: Decompose (k - np)² = k(k-1) + (1 - 2np) k + (np)².
conclude: Substitute and simplify to n p (1 - p).

drafts.proof_strategy: Read the first two moments off the moment generating function.
sketch_steps: case_split: The case v = 0 is a point mass at m.
apply_theorem: For v > 0 the moment generating function is exp(mt + vt²/2).
derive: Differentiate at 0 to get the first moment m.
derive: Differentiate twice to get the second moment v + m².
conclude: The variance is therefore v.

sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Independence makes the moment generating function of X + Y a product.
derive: The product is exp((m₁+m₂)t + (v₁+v₂)t²/2).
apply_theorem: A moment generating function that is finite everywhere determines the law.
conclude: Hence X + Y is normal with the summed parameters.

drafts.proof_strategy: Factor the binomial probability into three pieces with explicit limits.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix k and write the binomial probability as a product of three factors.
derive: C(n,k)/n^k tends to 1/k!.
derive: (n p_n)^k tends to r^k.
derive: (1 - p_n)^{n-k} tends to exp(-r).
conclude: Multiply the limits to get the Poisson probability.

drafts.canonical_statement: For an integrable random variable X and a sub-sigma-algebra G, E[E[X|G]] = E[X].

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the defining property of conditional expectation to the whole space.
sketch_steps: translate: Recall the defining identity on every set in G.
derive: The whole space Ω belongs to G.
conclude: Taking A = Ω gives E[E[X|G]] = E[X].

drafts.canonical_statement: Tower law: for sub-sigma-algebras G ⊆ H and an integrable random variable X, E[E[X|H]|G] = E[X|G] almost surely.

drafts.proof_strategy: Check the defining integrals on sets of the smaller sigma-algebra and use uniqueness.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix a set A in G; it also lies in H.
derive: Chain the defining identities of the three conditional expectations on A.
apply_theorem: Conditional expectation is unique among G-measurable integrable functions.
conclude: The two sides agree almost surely.

drafts.canonical_statement: If X is G-measurable and Y and XY are integrable, then E[XY|G] = X E[Y|G] almost surely.

drafts.proof_strategy: Prove the identity for indicators and extend by approximation.
sketch_steps: setup: Treat X = 1_B with B in G using the defining identity on A ∩ B.
derive: Extend to simple functions by linearity.
apply_theorem: Approximate X by simple functions and pass to the limit by dominated convergence.
conclude: The identity holds almost surely for general X.

drafts.canonical_statement: If X is integrable and measurable with respect to a sigma-algebra H independent of G, then E[X|G] = E[X] almost surely.

drafts.proof_strategy: Verify that the constant E[X] satisfies the defining property, using independence of 1_A and X.
sketch_steps: setup: The constant E[X] is G-measurable and integrable.
derive: For A in G, independence gives E[1_A X] = P(A) E[X].
apply_theorem: Uniqueness of conditional expectation identifies E[X|G] with the constant.
conclude: Hence E[X|G] = E[X] almost surely.

drafts.canonical_statement: A martingale has constant expectation, that is, E[X_n] = E[X_0] for all n.

drafts.proof_strategy: Take expectations in the martingale identity and use the law of total expectation.
sketch_steps: translate: The martingale property gives E[X_n | F_0] = X_0.
apply_theorem: Taking expectations removes the conditioning.
conclude: Hence E[X_n] = E[X_0].

drafts.canonical_statement: For a submartingale X and i ≤ j, E[X_i] ≤ E[X_j].

drafts.proof_strategy: Take expectations in the submartingale inequality.
sketch_steps: translate: The submartingale property gives X_i ≤ E[X_j | F_i] almost surely.
apply_theorem: Monotonicity of expectation preserves the inequality.
apply_theorem: The law of total expectation simplifies the right side.
conclude: Hence E[X_i] ≤ E[X_j].

drafts.canonical_statement: For an integrable random variable Y and a filtration F_n, the process E[Y | F_n] is a martingale.

sketch_steps: setup: Let S be the sum of the X_i, and note that its mean is n m.
apply_theorem: Pairwise independence gives Var(S) = n σ².
derive: Pointwise, Σ(X_i - X̄)² = Σ(X_i - m)² - (S - nm)² / n.
derive: The first term has expectation n σ².
derive: The second term has expectation Var(S) / n = σ².
conclude: Dividing (n - 1) σ² by n - 1 gives σ².

sketch_steps: setup: Pick x₀ in S and an upper bound M, and start from [x₀ - 1, M], whose left end is not an upper bound.
construct: Bisect repeatedly, keeping the left end a non-upper-bound and the right end an upper bound.
derive: The ends form Cauchy sequences with a common limit c by completeness.
derive: Passing to the limit in x ≤ b_k shows c is an upper bound.
conclude: Any upper bound u exceeds each a_k, so c ≤ u and c is the supremum.

apply_theorem: Take b as the supremum of -S.
derive: The number -b is a lower bound of S, and each lower bound is at most -b.
conclude: Hence -b is the infimum of S.

drafts.canonical_statement: A real a is the supremum of S if and only if a is an upper bound of S and for every ε > 0 there is x in S with a - ε < x.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use that a - ε is not an upper bound, and conversely take ε equal to the gap with a smaller upper bound.
sketch_steps: derive: If a is the supremum, a - ε lies below a and so is not an upper bound.
construct: That produces x in S with a - ε < x.
contradiction: Conversely, an upper bound b < a contradicts the condition with ε = a - b.
conclude: Hence a is the least upper bound.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a is the supremum of a nonempty set S of reals, then there is a nondecreasing sequence in S converging to a.

drafts.proof_strategy: Choose points of S within 1/(n+1) of the supremum and take running maxima.
sketch_steps: construct: For each n pick x_n in S with a - 1/(n+1) < x_n ≤ a.
construct: Set u_n to the maximum of x_0, ..., x_n, which is monotone and lies in S.
derive: The bound a - 1/(n+1) < u_n ≤ a still holds.
conclude: The squeeze theorem gives u_n → a.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a is nondecreasing, b is nonincreasing and a_n ≤ b_n for all n, then some real lies in every closed interval [a_n, b_n].
