drafts.proof_strategy: Compare coefficients, simplify the discriminant to a²(q−p)², and take a square root using q ≥ p.
sketch_steps: derive: Comparing coefficients gives b = −a(p + q) and c = a p q.
derive: Hence b² − 4ac = a²(q − p)².
derive: Since |a|(q − p) ≥ 0, the square root equals |a|(q − p).
conclude: Divide by |a| ≠ 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Test x = 0 and ±t to get the sign of a, test the vertex for the discriminant, and use the square identity for the converse.
sketch_steps: derive: x = 0 gives c > 0.
contradiction: If a < 0, take t = √(c/(−a)); the values at ±t add up to 2(a t² + c) = 0, contradicting positivity.
derive: The value at x = −b/(2a) is (4ac − b²)/(4a) > 0, so b² − 4ac < 0.
derive: Conversely 4a f(x) = (2ax + b)² − (b² − 4ac) > 0.

sketch_steps: derive: Subtracting the equations at p and q gives a(p + q) + b = 0.
derive: Similarly a(p + r) + b = 0.
derive: The difference gives a(q − r) = 0, so a = 0.
conclude: Then b = 0 and c = 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Construct the coefficients by divided differences and show uniqueness by subtracting two solutions.
sketch_steps: construct: Put s1 = (v − u)/(q − p), s2 = (w − u)/(r − p), a = (s2 − s1)/(r − q), b = s1 − a(p + q), c = u − a p² − b p.
derive: The value at p is u by the definition of c.
derive: The values at q and r follow from a(p + q) + b = s1 and a(p + r) + b = s2.
setup: For uniqueness let A, B, C be the differences of two solutions.
derive: A x² + B x + C vanishes at p, q, r.
conclude: Subtracting and cancelling gives A = B = C = 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: If p < q and (a p² + b p + c)(a q² + b q + c) < 0, then a x² + b x + c = 0 has exactly one solution in the open interval (p, q).

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the intermediate value theorem for existence and factor through two hypothetical roots for uniqueness.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: f is continuous with values of opposite sign at p and q, so a root exists in (p, q).
setup: Suppose x ≠ y are two roots in (p, q).
derive: Then b = −a(x + y) and c = a x y, so f(t) = a(t − x)(t − y).
derive: This gives f(p) f(q) = a²(x − p)(y − p)(q − x)(q − y) ≥ 0.
contradiction: This contradicts f(p) f(q) < 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a > 0 and p < q: a (x − p)(x − q) < 0 if and only if p < x < q, and a (x − p)(x − q) > 0 if and only if x < p or q < x.

sketch_steps: translate: Since a > 0, the sign equals that of (x − p)(x − q).
case_split: The product is negative exactly when the factors have opposite signs, which with p < q means p < x < q.
case_split: The product is positive exactly when both factors have the same sign, that is x < p or q < x.

sketch_steps: setup: Put v = −b/(2a) and t = √(b²−4ac)/(2a) > 0, so α = v − t and β = v + t.
derive: Then b = −2av and c = a(v² − t²).
derive: Hence a x² + b x + c = a (x − α)(x − β).
case_split: Analyze the sign of the product using α < β.
conclude: This gives the two solution sets.

sketch_steps: setup: Put s = √k > 0, so s² = k.
translate: x² < k is equivalent to (x − s)(x + s) < 0.
conclude: Since x − s < x + s, this holds exactly when −s < x < s.

drafts.proof_strategy: Show the endpoints are roots by continuity, compare coefficients, and test the midpoint for the sign of a.
sketch_steps: derive: By continuity f ≤ 0 on the closure [p, q].
derive: The endpoints are not solutions, so f(p) ≥ 0 and f(q) ≥ 0; hence both vanish.
derive: Subtracting and cancelling p − q gives b = −a(p + q); then c = a p q.

contradiction: If v − t ≤ k then (k − v)² ≤ t², so f(k) ≤ 0, contrary to the hypothesis.

conclude: Hence k < v − t ≤ v + t < l.

drafts.proof_strategy: Eliminate r² and r from the two equations and combine the resulting relations.
sketch_steps: setup: Put P = ae − db, Q = af − dc and R = bf − ec.
derive: a times the second equation minus d times the first gives P r + Q = 0.
derive: e times the first equation minus b times the second gives P r² − R = 0.
conclude: Then Q² = P · P r² = P R.

drafts.proof_strategy: Expand the translated equation and substitute into the vertex formulas.
sketch_steps: translate: The translated graph is y = a (x − p)² + b (x − p) + c + q.
derive: Expanding gives the new coefficients.
derive: The vertex formula gives x-coordinate −b/(2a) + p.
conclude: The vertex formula gives y-coordinate (4ac − b²)/(4a) + q.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a ≠ 0: there exist real p, q with d x² + e x + f = a (x − p)² + b (x − p) + c + q for all x if and only if d = a.

sketch_steps: derive: Evaluate the identity at x = 1, −1 and 0.
derive: The second difference gives 2d = 2a.
construct: Conversely put p = (b − e)/(2a) and q = f − a p² + b p − c.
conclude: Expanding shows the identity holds.

sketch_steps: translate: The reflected graph is y = 2l − f(x).
derive: Its coefficients are −a, −b and 2l − c.
derive: The axis formula returns −b/(2a).
conclude: The vertex formula gives 2l − (4ac − b²)/(4a).

sketch_steps: derive: f(x) − f(−x) = 2 b x for every x.

sketch_steps: derive: A factorization gives b = −a(p+q) and c = apq.
derive: The conditions follow from a²(p−q)² ≥ 0, (p+q)/2 > k and a²(p−k)(q−k) > 0.
construct: For the converse write f(x) = a(x−(v−t))(x−(v+t)).
contradiction: If v−t ≤ k then (k−v)² ≤ t², contrary to a f(k) > 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Rewrite with the positive factor −a, solve the two sign cases and negate.
sketch_steps: derive: g(x) = (−a)(x−p)(q−x) with −a > 0.
derive: g > 0 iff p < x < q, and g ≥ 0 iff p ≤ x ≤ q.
conclude: The other two follow by negation.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a(x−p)²: if a > 0 it is nonnegative, never negative, positive iff x ≠ p and nonpositive iff x = p; if a < 0 it is nonpositive, never positive, negative iff x ≠ p and nonnegative iff x = p.

drafts.proof_strategy: Split on x = p; otherwise the square is positive and the sign of a decides.
sketch_steps: case: If x = p the value is 0.
case: If x ≠ p the square is positive, so the value has the sign of a.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a ≠ 0: ax²+bx+c < 0 for all x iff a < 0 and b²−4ac < 0; and ax²+bx+c ≤ 0 for all x iff a < 0 and b²−4ac ≤ 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use 4a f(x) = (2ax+b)² − D, a far point to rule out a > 0, and the vertex for D.
sketch_steps: derive: 4a f(x) = (2ax+b)² − D.
contradiction: If a > 0 a far point makes f positive.
derive: At the vertex 4a f = −D gives the discriminant condition.
conclude: Conversely a < 0 and the sign of D give the sign of f.

drafts.canonical_statement: For real a, b, c (a may be 0): ax²+bx+c > 0 for all x iff (a = b = 0 and c > 0) or (a > 0 and b²−4ac < 0).

derive: At the vertex 4a f = −D > 0.
conclude: The converse follows from the same identity.

drafts.canonical_statement: With L(x) = f(p) + (2ap+b)(x−p) the tangent line of f(x) = ax²+bx+c at p, f(x) − L(x) = a(x−p)²; for a ≠ 0, f(x) = L(x) iff x = p.

drafts.proof_strategy: Take the least m with N ≤ T_m for existence and use monotonicity of T for uniqueness.
sketch_steps: setup: Let T_m be the partial sums of the group sizes.
derive: T is strictly increasing, T_0 = 0 and T_m ≥ m.
construct: Take the least m with N ≤ T_m.
derive: Minimality gives T_{m-1} < N and m ≥ 1.
contradiction: Any other index y contradicts monotonicity.
conclude: Such m exists and is unique.

drafts.proof_strategy: Take the least m with 2N ≤ m(m+1) for existence and use monotonicity of y(y+1) for uniqueness.
sketch_steps: translate: The first m groups contain m(m+1)/2 terms.
construct: Take the least m with 2N ≤ m(m+1).
derive: Minimality gives m(m-1) < 2N and m ≥ 1.
contradiction: Any other index contradicts monotonicity of y(y+1).
conclude: Such m exists and is unique.

sketch_steps: translate: The first m - 1 groups contain m(m-1)/2 terms.
derive: Split the group sum into m copies of m(m-1)/2 and the sum of j.
apply_theorem: Use the formula for the sum of 1 through m.
conclude: Simplify to m(m^2+1)/2.

drafts.canonical_statement: For every real x, sin²x + cos²x = 1.

drafts.proof_strategy: Substitute the unit-circle coordinates of the angle into the circle equation.
sketch_steps: setup: Take the point of the unit circle at angle x, whose coordinates are (cos x, sin x).
conclude: Substituting the coordinates into u² + v² = 1 gives the identity.

drafts.canonical_statement: If x is real and cos x ≠ 0, then 1 + tan²x = 1/cos²x.

drafts.proof_strategy: Rewrite tan as sin over cos, put the sum over cos², and apply the Pythagorean identity.
sketch_steps: setup: Assume cos x ≠ 0 so that tan x = sin x / cos x.
derive: 1 + tan²x = (cos²x + sin²x) / cos²x.
conclude: The numerator equals 1.

drafts.canonical_statement: If x and t are real and sin x + cos x = t, then sin x cos x = (t² - 1)/2.

drafts.proof_strategy: Square the defining relation and eliminate sin²x + cos²x.
sketch_steps: setup: Assume sin x + cos x = t.
derive: Squaring gives sin²x + 2 sin x cos x + cos²x = t².
apply_theorem: Replace sin²x + cos²x by 1.
conclude: Solve for sin x cos x.

drafts.canonical_statement: For every real x, -1 ≤ sin x ≤ 1 and -1 ≤ cos x ≤ 1.

drafts.proof_strategy: Bound each square by the Pythagorean identity and take square roots.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Use sin²x + cos²x = 1.
derive: Since cos²x ≥ 0, sin²x ≤ 1, hence |sin x| ≤ 1.
conclude: The same argument with the roles exchanged bounds cos x.

drafts.canonical_statement: If 0 ≤ x ≤ π, then sin x = √(1 - cos²x). This form is restricted to that interval.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the Pythagorean identity and the nonnegativity of sine on [0, π] to remove the square root.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The Pythagorean identity gives 1 - cos²x = sin²x.
derive: On [0, π] we have sin x ≥ 0.
conclude: So the square root of sin²x equals sin x.

sketch_steps: setup: Compare the unit-circle points at angles x and -x.
derive: They are mirror images across the first axis, so cosine agrees and sine changes sign.
conclude: If cos x ≠ 0, the quotient changes sign.

drafts.canonical_statement: For every integer n, sin nπ = 0 and cos nπ = (-1)^n.

sketch_steps: setup: Start from sin 0 = 0 and cos 0 = 1.
induction: Each shift by ±π changes both signs.
conclude: After n shifts the values are 0 and (-1)^n.

drafts.canonical_statement: If T > 0 and sin(x + T) = sin x for every real x, then T ≥ 2π.

drafts.proof_strategy: Evaluate at x = π/2 to force cos T = 1, which is impossible on (0, 2π).
sketch_steps: contradiction: Assume 0 < T < 2π.
derive: Taking x = π/2 gives cos T = 1.
apply_theorem: cos T = 1 - 2 sin²(T/2) by the double-angle formula.
derive: 0 < T/2 < π gives sin(T/2) > 0, so cos T < 1.
conclude: This contradicts cos T = 1.

drafts.proof_strategy: Apply the sum formulas to x + (-y) and use the parity of sine and cosine.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Use the sum formulas with second angle -y.
derive: Substitute cos(-y) = cos y and sin(-y) = -sin y.
conclude: The difference formulas follow.

drafts.canonical_statement: If x, y are real with cos x ≠ 0, cos y ≠ 0 and cos(x+y) ≠ 0, then tan(x+y) = (tan x + tan y)/(1 - tan x tan y).

drafts.proof_strategy: Write tan(x+y) as a quotient via the addition formulas and divide by cos x cos y.
sketch_steps: setup: Assume cos x, cos y and cos(x+y) are nonzero.
apply_theorem: Expand the numerator and denominator by the addition formulas.
derive: Divide both by cos x cos y.
derive: The new denominator 1 - tan x tan y equals cos(x+y)/(cos x cos y), which is nonzero.
conclude: The quotient is the claimed formula.

drafts.canonical_statement: If x, y are real with cos x ≠ 0, cos y ≠ 0 and cos(x-y) ≠ 0, then tan(x-y) = (tan x - tan y)/(1 + tan x tan y).

drafts.proof_strategy: Write tan(x-y) as a quotient via the difference formulas and divide by cos x cos y.
sketch_steps: setup: Assume cos x, cos y and cos(x-y) are nonzero.
apply_theorem: Expand the numerator and denominator by the difference formulas.
derive: Divide both by cos x cos y.
conclude: The new denominator equals cos(x-y)/(cos x cos y), nonzero, so the formula holds.

drafts.canonical_statement: If x, y are real with cos x ≠ 0 and cos y ≠ 0, then tan x tan y = 1 if and only if cos(x+y) = 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Clear the denominator and recognize the addition formula for cosine.
sketch_steps: setup: Assume cos x and cos y are nonzero.
translate: tan x tan y = 1 is equivalent to sin x sin y = cos x cos y.
apply_theorem: cos x cos y - sin x sin y = cos(x+y).

drafts.proof_strategy: Normalize (a, b) to a point of the unit circle, name its angle, and recognize the addition formula.
sketch_steps: setup: Put r = √(a²+b²) > 0.
apply_theorem: (a/r, b/r) lies on the unit circle, so it equals (cos α, sin α) for some α.
derive: a sin x + b cos x = r(cos α sin x + sin α cos x).
conclude: The addition formula gives r sin(x+α).

drafts.canonical_statement: For all real a, b, x, |a sin x + b cos x| ≤ √(a²+b²).

sketch_steps: derive: (a sin x + b cos x)² + (a cos x - b sin x)² = a² + b².

sketch_steps: derive: A solution forces c² ≤ a² + b² by the sum-of-squares identity.
case_split: If a = b = 0 then c = 0 and every x solves the equation.
apply_theorem: Otherwise write a sin x + b cos x = r sin(x+α) with r > 0.
apply_theorem: Since |c/r| ≤ 1, the intermediate value theorem gives y with sin y = c/r.
conclude: x = y - α is a solution.

drafts.proof_strategy: Build the solution from a point of the unit circle and use strict monotonicity for uniqueness.
sketch_steps: construct: Take x in [0, π] with cos x = 1/√(1+a²).
derive: Then x < π/2 and sin x = |a|/√(1+a²).
case_split: Use x if a ≥ 0 and -x if a < 0 to get tan = a.
apply_theorem: tan y - tan x = sin(y-x)/(cos x cos y) > 0 for x < y in the interval.
conclude: The solution is unique.

case_split: If x ≥ y then tan x ≥ tan y by the same computation.
conclude: The two inequalities are equivalent.

case_split: Split according to x ≤ π/2 or x > π/2.
derive: For x ≤ π/2 the inequality means a ≤ x, and x ≤ π - a is automatic.
derive: For x > π/2 use sin x = sin(π - x), so the inequality means x ≤ π - a, and a ≤ x is automatic.

derive: Then f(sin x) = f(t) = y.
conclude: The same argument works for cosine with the values at 0 and π.

sketch_steps: setup: Assume the cosines are nonzero so all tangents are defined.
derive: sin C = sin(A+B) and cos C = sin A sin B - cos A cos B.
translate: Multiply the claim by cos A cos B cos C.
derive: The left side becomes sin C (cos C + cos A cos B).
conclude: That equals sin A sin B sin C.

sketch_steps: translate: Write |pa+qb|^2 as (pa+qb)·(pa+qb).

conclude: Replace a·a and b·b by |a|^2 and |b|^2.

sketch_steps: derive: Expand (a+b)·(a-b) = |a|^2 - |b|^2.
translate: The vanishing is equivalent to |a|^2 = |b|^2.
conclude: Norms are nonnegative, so this is equivalent to |a| = |b|.

sketch_steps: derive: Compute (a+t₀b)·b = a·b + t₀|b|^2 = 0.
setup: Put u = a+t₀b and write a+tb = u+(t-t₀)b.
derive: Since u·b = 0, |a+tb|^2 = |u|^2 + (t-t₀)^2|b|^2.
conclude: The extra term is nonnegative, so |u| ≤ |a+tb|.

sketch_steps: contradiction: If b = ka, then ka + (-1)b = 0 is a nontrivial relation.
setup: Conversely assume b is no multiple of a and take sa+tb = 0.
case_split: If t ≠ 0, solve b = -(s/t)a, a contradiction.
derive: So t = 0, then sa = 0 and a ≠ 0 give s = 0.
conclude: The pair is independent.

sketch_steps: setup: Put x, y, z for the vectors from P and D(u,v) = u₁v₂-u₂v₁.
derive: From βy = -αx-γz obtain βD(y,z) = αD(z,x).
derive: From γz = -αx-βy obtain γD(y,z) = αD(x,y).
conclude: Take absolute values using positivity of α, β, γ.

drafts.canonical_statement: Let a, b be linearly independent vectors of a real vector space and αβ ≠ 1. If real s, t satisfy (1-s)a + sβb = (1-t)b + tαa, then this common point equals (α(1-β)/(1-αβ))a + (β(1-α)/(1-αβ))b.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compare coefficients using independence, solve the linear system for s and substitute.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Independence gives 1-s = tα and sβ = 1-t.
derive: Eliminate t to get s(1-αβ) = 1-α.
derive: Since αβ ≠ 1, solve for s and compute 1-s and sβ.
conclude: Substitute these coefficients into the common point.

drafts.canonical_statement: For points a ≠ b and c of a real vector space, a, b, c are collinear if and only if c-a = t(b-a) for some real t.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use a common direction vector based at a; divide by the nonzero coefficient of b.
sketch_steps: translate: Collinearity means all points are a + r v for a fixed v.
derive: Write b-a = rv and c-a = r'v; a ≠ b forces r ≠ 0.
construct: Take t = r'/r.
conclude: Conversely v = b-a exhibits the three points with coefficients 0, 1, t.

drafts.canonical_statement: For linearly independent vectors a, b of a real vector space and real numbers x, y, the point xa+yb lies on the line through a and b if and only if x+y = 1.

drafts.proof_strategy: Parametrize the line and compare coefficients using independence.
sketch_steps: translate: Points of the line are (1-r)a+rb.
apply_theorem: Independence gives x = 1-r and y = r, so x+y = 1.
conclude: Conversely take r = y.

drafts.canonical_statement: For vectors a, b, p of a real vector space, p lies in the convex hull of 0, a, b if and only if p = sa+tb for some real s, t with s, t ≥ 0 and s+t ≤ 1.

drafts.proof_strategy: Describe the hull as the nonnegative combinations of 0, a, b with coefficient sum 1, and drop the coefficient of 0.
sketch_steps: translate: The hull is the set of combinations λ0+sa+tb with λ, s, t ≥ 0 and λ+s+t = 1.
derive: Such a combination equals sa+tb because the coefficient of 0 contributes nothing.
derive: Then s, t ≥ 0 and s+t = 1-λ ≤ 1.
construct: Conversely, given s, t ≥ 0 with s+t ≤ 1, put λ = 1-s-t ≥ 0.
conclude: Then p = λ0+sa+tb is a convex combination, so p lies in the hull.

drafts.canonical_statement: For linearly independent vectors a, b, c of a real vector space and real numbers x, y, z, the point xa+yb+zc lies in the affine span of a, b, c (the plane ABC) if and only if x+y+z = 1.

drafts.proof_strategy: Parametrize the plane from the base point a and compare coefficients.
sketch_steps: translate: Points of the plane are a + s(b-a) + t(c-a).
derive: Rewrite as (1-s-t)a + sb + tc.
apply_theorem: Independence of a, b, c gives x = 1-s-t, y = s, z = t.
conclude: Hence x+y+z = 1; conversely take s = y and t = z.

drafts.canonical_statement: If points a, b, c of a real vector space are not collinear, then a, b, c, p are coplanar if and only if p = a + s(b-a) + t(c-a) for some real s, t.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compare the direction space of the three points with that of the four points by dimension.
sketch_steps: setup: Let W and W' be the spans of differences from a for three and four points.
derive: Non-collinearity gives dim W = 2.
derive: Coplanarity gives dim W' ≤ 2, so W = W' and p-a lies in W.
translate: Membership in W is the required expression.
conclude: Conversely p-a in W gives W' = W, of dimension 2.

drafts.proof_strategy: Take the orthogonal projection of p onto the finite-dimensional span of a and b.
sketch_steps: setup: Let K be the span of a and b, a finite-dimensional subspace.
apply_theorem: Decompose p = q + r with q in K and r orthogonal to K.
derive: Write q = sa+tb.
conclude: r = p-(sa+tb) is orthogonal to a and b, which lie in K.

drafts.canonical_statement: For nonzero vectors a, b in a real inner product space with angle θ between them, a·b = |a||b| cos θ.

sketch_steps: translate: The angle is arccos of (a·b)/(|a||b|).
apply_theorem: Cauchy-Schwarz puts this quotient in [-1,1], so cos θ equals it.
conclude: Multiply by |a||b|.

sketch_steps: translate: Set x = (a·b)/(|a||b|), which has the sign of a·b.
apply_theorem: arccos is strictly decreasing with arccos 0 = π/2.
derive: x > 0 iff arccos x < π/2.
conclude: Negating x ≥ 0 iff arccos x ≤ π/2 gives the obtuse case.

sketch_steps: translate: cos θ = (a·b)/(|a||b|).
apply_theorem: The standard inner product is Σ a_i b_i and the norm is the root of Σ a_i².
conclude: Substitute.

drafts.proof_strategy: Rewrite the sine through the cosine using nonnegativity of sin on [0,π].
sketch_steps: derive: sin θ ≥ 0 on [0,π], so |a||b| sin θ = √(|a|²|b|² sin²θ).
derive: sin²θ = 1 - cos²θ and a·b = |a||b| cos θ.
conclude: The radicand equals |a|²|b|² - (a·b)².

drafts.canonical_statement: For a plane vector a = (a₁,a₂) ≠ 0 and b = (b₁,b₂), a₁b₂ - a₂b₁ = 0 if and only if b = ka for some real k.

drafts.proof_strategy: Divide by a nonzero component of a and solve for k.
sketch_steps: case_split: Either a₁ ≠ 0 or a₂ ≠ 0.
construct: Take k = b₁/a₁ or k = b₂/a₂ respectively.
derive: The determinant condition gives the other component.
conclude: Conversely substitute b = ka into the determinant.

drafts.canonical_statement: For vectors a, b, p in a real inner product space, (p-a)·(p-b) = 0 if and only if |p - (a+b)/2| = |a-b|/2.

drafts.proof_strategy: Substitute u = p-a, v = p-b and compare |u+v| with |u-v| through 4u·v.
sketch_steps: setup: Put u = p-a and v = p-b.
translate: The sphere condition becomes |u+v| = |u-v|.
derive: |u+v|² - |u-v|² = 4u·v.
conclude: The two conditions are equivalent.

sketch_steps: derive: Expand b·d and c·d by bilinearity.
derive: Each has the factor (|b||c| + b·c)/(|b|+|c|) times |b| or |c|.
derive: After dividing by |b||d| and |c||d| the quotients coincide.
conclude: The angles are arccos of equal numbers.

sketch_steps: derive: n·u = n·v = 0 by direct computation, so the parametric form satisfies the equation.
setup: For the converse put w = (x-x₀,y-y₀,z-z₀), N = |n|², A = (w×v)·n, B = (u×w)·n.
derive: Expanding components gives N w = A u + B v + (n·w) n.
construct: With n·w = 0 take s = A/N and t = B/N.
conclude: Then w = su + tv.

sketch_steps: setup: Put N = a²+b²+c² and k = ax₀+by₀+cz₀+d.
derive: On the plane k = a(x₀-x)+b(y₀-y)+c(z₀-z).
apply_theorem: Cauchy-Schwarz gives k² ≤ N times the squared distance.
construct: The foot is (x₀,y₀,z₀) - (k/N)(a,b,c).
derive: This point lies on the plane and has squared distance k²/N.
conclude: The minimum distance is |k|/√N.

drafts.proof_strategy: Take moduli to compare r and s, then compare real and imaginary parts and use periodicity.
sketch_steps: derive: Taking absolute values gives r = s.
derive: Cancel r and compare parts to get cos α = cos β and sin α = sin β.
apply_theorem: Equal cosine and sine mean the angles differ by 2kπ.
conclude: The converse is periodicity of cos and sin.

drafts.canonical_statement: For nonzero complex numbers z, w and the principal argument arg, arg(zw) = arg z + arg w + 2kπ for some integer k, and arg(z/w) = arg z - arg w + 2lπ for some integer l.

drafts.proof_strategy: Write both sides in polar form and apply equality of polar forms.
sketch_steps: setup: Write z and w in polar form with the principal arguments.
apply_theorem: The product and quotient formulas give polar forms with angles α+β and α-β.
apply_theorem: Equality of polar forms says angles agree up to 2π times an integer.
conclude: This yields the integers k and l.

drafts.canonical_statement: If z is a nonzero complex number with principal argument different from π, then arg(conj z) = -arg z and arg(z⁻¹) = -arg z.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compute polar forms of conj z and z⁻¹ with angle -θ, which stays in the principal range since θ ≠ π.
sketch_steps: setup: Put θ = arg z, so -π < θ < π.
derive: conj z and z⁻¹ have polar forms with angle -θ.
conclude: -θ is in (-π, π], so it is the principal argument.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a nonzero complex number z and a natural number n, arg(z^n) = n arg z + 2kπ for some integer k, where arg is the principal argument.

drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on n using additivity of the argument modulo 2π.
sketch_steps: induction: For n = 0 both sides vanish with k = 0.
apply_theorem: arg(z^(n+1)) = arg(z^n) + arg z + 2lπ.
conclude: Substitute the hypothesis to get the integer k+l.

drafts.proof_strategy: Split off r^n and apply de Moivre's formula.
sketch_steps: derive: (r w)^n = r^n w^n.
apply_theorem: De Moivre's formula gives w^n = cos nθ + i sin nθ for w = cos θ + i sin θ.
conclude: Combine the two equalities.

drafts.canonical_statement: De Moivre's formula for integer exponents. For real θ and an integer n, (cos θ + i sin θ)^n = cos nθ + i sin nθ.

drafts.proof_strategy: Rewrite through Euler's formula and use the exponential law for integer powers.
sketch_steps: translate: cos t + i sin t = exp(it) for real t.
apply_theorem: exp(iθ)^n = exp(inθ) for integer n.
conclude: Translate back with Euler's formula.

drafts.proof_strategy: Verify each candidate by de Moivre; conversely divide by one solution and use the classification of n-th roots of unity.
sketch_steps: derive: Each candidate satisfies the equation by de Moivre and periodicity.
setup: Let w₀ be the candidate with k = 0.
derive: Then (z/w₀)^n = 1.
apply_theorem: The n-th roots of unity are the powers ζ^k with k < n.
conclude: z = w₀ζ^k has the required polar form.

drafts.canonical_statement: If w = a + (z-a)(cos θ + i sin θ), then |w-a| = |z-a|; and if z ≠ a, then arg((w-a)/(z-a)) = θ + 2kπ for some integer k.

drafts.proof_strategy: Factor w-a = (z-a)u with |u| = 1 and read off the modulus and argument of u.
sketch_steps: setup: Put u = cos θ + i sin θ, so w-a = (z-a)u.
derive: |u| = 1 gives |w-a| = |z-a|.
conclude: The quotient is u, whose principal argument is θ up to 2kπ.

drafts.canonical_statement: For complex numbers a ≠ b and c, the real inner product Re(conj(b-a)(c-a)) of the plane vectors b-a and c-a vanishes if and only if Re((c-a)/(b-a)) = 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Express the inner product as |b-a|² Re u for the ratio u.
sketch_steps: setup: Put u = (c-a)/(b-a), so c-a = u(b-a).
translate: The inner product of x and y is Re(y conj x).
derive: The inner product equals |b-a|² Re u.
conclude: Since |b-a|² > 0, it vanishes iff Re u = 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: For complex numbers a ≠ b and c, the points a, b, c are collinear if and only if Im((c-a)/(b-a)) = 0.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use a common real direction based at a; the ratio of real multiples of v is real.
sketch_steps: translate: Collinear points are a + r v with real r.
derive: b-a = rv and c-a = r'v with r ≠ 0, so the ratio is r'/r.
conclude: Conversely if the ratio u is real, use v = b-a with coefficients 0, 1, u.

drafts.canonical_statement: For complex numbers a, b, c with a ≠ b and a ≠ c, the unoriented angle between b-a and c-a equals |arg((c-a)/(b-a))|, where arg is the principal argument.

drafts.proof_strategy: Compute the cosine of the angle from Re u/|u| and use injectivity of cos on [0,π].
sketch_steps: setup: Put u = (c-a)/(b-a) and φ = arg u.
derive: The cosine of the angle is Re u/|u| = cos φ = cos|φ|.
apply_theorem: |φ| lies in [0,π], where cos is injective.
conclude: The angle equals |φ|.

drafts.proof_strategy: Multiply by 1-k², set A = z-a and B = z-b, and compare squared norms through one identity.
sketch_steps: derive: Since k > 0 and k ≠ 1, 1-k² ≠ 0.
translate: With A = z-a and B = z-b, the circle condition is |A-k²B| = k|B-A|.
derive: |A-k²B|² - k²|B-A|² = (1-k²)(|A|² - k²|B|²).
conclude: Both conditions are equivalent to |A|² = k²|B|².

drafts.proof_strategy: Split according to whether ζ^k = 1, using the geometric sum identity otherwise.
sketch_steps: translate: For primitive ζ, ζ^k = 1 exactly when n divides k.
case_split: If n divides k, every term is 1 and the sum is n.
derive: Otherwise x = ζ^k ≠ 1 and (x-1)·sum = x^n - 1 = 0.
conclude: Dividing by x-1 gives 0.

drafts.canonical_statement: For an integer n ≥ 2, the sums of cos(2πk/n) and of sin(2πk/n) over 0 ≤ k < n are both 0.

sketch_steps: setup: Let ζ = cos(2π/n) + i sin(2π/n), a root of unity different from 1.
derive: The geometric sum of ζ^k vanishes.
apply_theorem: De Moivre gives ζ^k = cos(2πk/n) + i sin(2πk/n).
conclude: Take real and imaginary parts.

drafts.proof_strategy: Factor x^n - 1 over the roots of unity, cancel x-1 and evaluate at 1.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: x^n - 1 is the product of x - ζ^k for 0 ≤ k < n.
derive: Cancel x-1 to express the geometric sum as the remaining product.
derive: Evaluate at x = 1 to get the value n.
conclude: Taking absolute values gives the chord product.

sketch_steps: derive: The powers ζ^k for 0 ≤ k < n are distinct roots of x^n - 1.
apply_theorem: A monic polynomial of degree n with n distinct roots is the product of its linear factors.
conclude: Evaluate at z.

drafts.proof_strategy: Swap the order of summation and evaluate the inner geometric sum according to divisibility.
sketch_steps: derive: Swap sums and write (ζ^j)^k = (ζ^k)^j.
case_split: If n divides k, the inner sum is n.
derive: Otherwise ζ^k ≠ 1 is an n-th root of unity, so the inner sum is 0.
conclude: Only multiples of n remain.

drafts.proof_strategy: Induct on the finite index set using the binary intersection axiom.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix the finite index set s and the open sets U_i.
induction: The empty intersection is X, which is open.
derive: Adding one index intersects the previous open set with one more open set.
conclude: The binary intersection axiom keeps the result open.

drafts.canonical_statement: A subset S of a topological space is open if and only if every point of S lies in an open set contained in S.

drafts.proof_strategy: Write S as the union of the local open sets.
sketch_steps: case_split: Prove the two implications separately.
derive: If S is open, take U = S for each point.
construct: Otherwise pick U_x for each x in S and form their union.
conclude: The union equals S and is open.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the open complement in one direction and balls of radius 1/(n+1) in the other.
sketch_steps: case_split: Prove the two implications separately.
contradiction: A limit outside C would have an open neighborhood missing C.
construct: For a closure point a, choose a_n in C within distance 1/(n+1) of a.
derive: The sequence converges to a, so a lies in C.
conclude: The closure of C equals C, so C is closed.

drafts.canonical_statement: If a closed set C contains S, then C contains the closure of S.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the definition of closure as the intersection of closed supersets.
sketch_steps: translate: The closure of S is the intersection of all closed supersets of S.
derive: C is one member of this family.
conclude: The intersection is contained in C.

drafts.canonical_statement: A point x lies in the closure of S if and only if every open set containing x meets S.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="closure_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="open_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="intersect"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="emptyset"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Prove both contrapositives using the complement of a separating set.
sketch_steps: translate: Work with contrapositives of both implications.
derive: An open U missing S gives the closed superset U^c excluding x.
derive: A closed superset C excluding x gives the open set C^c missing S.
conclude: The two conditions are equivalent.

drafts.canonical_statement: The closure of a union of two subsets equals the union of their closures.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="closure_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="union"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="union"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="closure_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="closure_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Use monotonicity for one inclusion and minimality of the closure for the other.
sketch_steps: derive: Monotonicity gives cl(S) ∪ cl(T) ⊆ cl(S ∪ T).
derive: cl(S) ∪ cl(T) is a closed set containing S ∪ T.
apply_theorem: Minimality of the closure gives the reverse inclusion.
conclude: Both inclusions yield equality.

drafts.canonical_statement: The interior of the complement of S equals the complement of the closure of S.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="interior_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="setdiff"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="setdiff"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="closure_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Dualize the definitions of interior and closure through complements.
sketch_steps: translate: Open subsets of S^c correspond to closed supersets of S by complement.
derive: The complement of the union of the former is the intersection of the latter.
conclude: Hence int(S^c) is the complement of cl(S).

drafts.canonical_statement: A subset S is closed if and only if its closure equals S.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="closed_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="closure_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Combine minimality of the closure with the fact that closures are closed.
sketch_steps: derive: If S is closed, minimality gives cl(S) ⊆ S.
derive: S ⊆ cl(S) always holds, so they are equal.
conclude: Conversely S = cl(S) is closed because closures are closed.

drafts.canonical_statement: The boundary of S equals the intersection of the closure of S with the closure of its complement.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="frontier_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="intersect"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="closure_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="closure_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="setdiff"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Rewrite the complement of the interior as the closure of the complement.
sketch_steps: translate: The boundary is cl(S) minus int(S).
derive: The complement of int(S) equals cl(S^c).
conclude: Substituting gives cl(S) ∩ cl(S^c).

drafts.canonical_statement: A map f from X to Y is continuous if and only if the preimage of every closed subset of Y is closed in X.

drafts.proof_strategy: Translate between open and closed sets through complements of preimages.
sketch_steps: translate: Continuity means preimages of open sets are open.
derive: Preimages commute with complements.
conclude: The open-set and closed-set conditions are equivalent.

drafts.canonical_statement: A map f is continuous if and only if f(cl S) is contained in cl(f(S)) for every subset S.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="continuous_between"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="subset"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="image_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="closure_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="closure_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="image_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Use the closed preimage of cl(f(S)) forward, and test on S = f^{-1}(C) backward.
sketch_steps: case_split: Prove the two implications separately.
derive: If f is continuous, the preimage of cl(f(S)) is closed and contains S.
apply_theorem: Minimality of the closure gives f(cl S) ⊆ cl(f S).
construct: Conversely set S = f^{-1}(C) for a closed set C.
conclude: Then cl(S) ⊆ S, so preimages of closed sets are closed.

drafts.proof_strategy: Forward by neighborhoods; backward by choosing a witness sequence from the failure of epsilon-delta.
sketch_steps: case_split: Prove the two implications separately.
derive: Continuity pulls a neighborhood of f(a) back to a neighborhood of a.
contradiction: Assume f is discontinuous at a with witness ε.
construct: Choose a_n within 1/(n+1) of a with d(f(a_n), f(a)) ≥ ε.
conclude: The sequence converges to a but its image does not converge to f(a).

drafts.proof_strategy: Translate preimages of balls into balls contained in preimages.
sketch_steps: derive: The preimage of an ε-ball at f(b) is open and contains a δ-ball at b.
setup: Conversely fix an open set V and a point b of its preimage.
derive: Choose ε with the ε-ball inside V and take the matching δ.
conclude: The δ-ball lies in the preimage, so the preimage is open.

drafts.canonical_statement: Two continuous maps into a Hausdorff space that agree on a dense subset are equal.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="hausdorff_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="continuous_between"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="continuous_between"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="dense_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v6"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v6"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v6"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v6"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: The agreement set is closed and contains a dense set.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: The agreement set E of f and g is closed since Y is Hausdorff.
derive: E contains S, hence contains the closure of S.
conclude: The closure of S is X, so f = g.

drafts.canonical_statement: For a homeomorphism h, the image h(U) is open if and only if U is open.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="homeomorphism"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="open_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="image_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="open_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Express the image as a preimage under the inverse map.
sketch_steps: translate: The image h(U) is the preimage of U under the inverse of h.
derive: Continuity of the inverse gives one implication.
derive: U = h^{-1}(h(U)) and continuity of h give the other.
conclude: The two conditions are equivalent.

drafts.canonical_statement: A continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="compact_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="hausdorff_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="continuous_between"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="bijection_between"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="homeomorphism"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Show f is a closed map via closed subset, continuous image and compact-in-Hausdorff.
sketch_steps: translate: It suffices that f sends closed sets to closed sets.
derive: A closed subset C of the compact space X is compact.
derive: f(C) is compact as a continuous image.
apply_theorem: A compact subset of a Hausdorff space is closed.
conclude: f is a closed bijection, so its inverse is continuous.

drafts.canonical_statement: If B is a basis, a set S is open if and only if every point a of S lies in some member t of B with t contained in S.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="topological_basis"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="open_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="subset"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Use the description of open sets as unions of basis members.
sketch_steps: derive: An open S is a union of basis members, which gives t for each point.
derive: Conversely S is the union of the members t chosen for its points.
conclude: Unions of open sets are open.

drafts.canonical_statement: A second countable space has a countable dense subset.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="second_countable_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="countable_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="dense_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Choose one point from each nonempty member of a countable basis.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix a countable basis of X.
construct: Pick one point from each nonempty basis member to form D.
derive: Each nonempty open set contains a nonempty basis member, hence a point of D.
conclude: D is countable and dense.

drafts.canonical_statement: A separable metric space is second countable.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="metric_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="separable_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="second_countable_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Use rational balls centered on a countable dense subset.
sketch_steps: setup: Take a countable dense subset D of X.
construct: Let B be the balls with center in D and positive rational radius.
derive: B is countable.
derive: For x in open U choose rational r with B(x,2r) ⊆ U and c in D near x.
conclude: x ∈ B(c,r) ⊆ U, so B is a basis.

drafts.canonical_statement: In a second countable space, every family of open sets has a countable subfamily with the same union.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="second_countable_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="open_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="fn_value"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="subset"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="countable_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="family_union"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v5"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="family_union"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Index the subfamily by the countable basis members lying inside some U_i.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix a countable basis B.
construct: Let B' be the members of B contained in some U_i and pick one such i for each.
derive: The chosen index set T is countable.
derive: Each point of the union lies in a member of B' and so in some U_j with j in T.
conclude: The two unions agree.

drafts.canonical_statement: A subset V of a subspace A of X is open in A if and only if V is the trace on A of an open subset of X.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="subset"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="open_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="subspace_topology_on"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="exists"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="open_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="intersect"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Unfold the subspace topology as the topology induced by the inclusion.
sketch_steps: translate: The subspace topology is induced by the inclusion map.
derive: The preimage of U under the inclusion is U ∩ A.
conclude: Open sets of A are exactly the traces of open sets of X.

drafts.canonical_statement: A map into a product of two spaces is continuous if and only if both components are continuous.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="continuous_between"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="product_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="continuous_between"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="function_compose_map"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="projection_first"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="continuous_between"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="function_compose_map"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="projection_second"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Check continuity on the product basis.
sketch_steps: derive: Composing with continuous projections gives continuous components.
setup: Conversely consider a basic open set U × V.
derive: Its preimage is the intersection of the component preimages.
conclude: Preimages of basis members are open, so f is continuous.

drafts.canonical_statement: The closure of a product set equals the product of the closures.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="closure_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="product_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="product_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="product_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="closure_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="closure_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Test membership in the closure on basic neighborhoods U × V.
sketch_steps: translate: Use the characterization of closure by basic neighborhoods U × V.
derive: (U × V) ∩ (S × T) equals (U ∩ S) × (V ∩ T).
derive: This set is nonempty exactly when both factors are nonempty.
conclude: Hence (x,y) ∈ cl(S × T) iff x ∈ cl(S) and y ∈ cl(T).

drafts.canonical_statement: If q from X to Y is a quotient map, then g from Y to Z is continuous if and only if g composed with q is continuous.

drafts.proof_strategy: Use the defining property of quotient maps on preimages.
sketch_steps: derive: Composition with the continuous map q gives one direction.
setup: Conversely fix an open set V of Z.
derive: The preimage of g^{-1}(V) under q is the preimage of V under the composite.
conclude: By definition of the quotient topology g^{-1}(V) is open.

construct: Add the open set C^c to get an open cover of K.
apply_theorem: Extract a finite subcover of K.
conclude: Removing C^c leaves a finite subcover of C.

sketch_steps: setup: Fix an open cover of f(K).
derive: The preimages form an open cover of K.
apply_theorem: Compactness of K gives a finite subcover of preimages.
conclude: The corresponding open sets cover f(K).

sketch_steps: setup: Fix x outside K.
apply_theorem: For each y in K choose disjoint open U_y ∋ x and V_y ∋ y.
derive: Finitely many V_y cover K by compactness.
derive: The finite intersection of the corresponding U_y is an open neighborhood of x missing K.
conclude: The complement of K is open.

setup: Take an ultrafilter F on the product.
derive: Each projection of F is an ultrafilter on X_i and has a limit x_i.
construct: Choose the limits to form a point x of the product.
conclude: Componentwise convergence gives F converging to x.

conclude: A finite intersection with K is empty, contradicting the hypothesis.

drafts.canonical_statement: A compact subset of a metric space is closed and bounded.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="metric_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="compact_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="closed_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="bounded_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Hausdorffness gives closedness; a cover by balls gives boundedness.
sketch_steps: apply_theorem: Metric spaces are Hausdorff, so K is closed.
construct: Cover K by the balls B(a,n) centered at a point a.
derive: Finitely many balls suffice, so K lies in one ball.
conclude: K is bounded.

drafts.canonical_statement: A compact Hausdorff space is normal.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="compact_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="hausdorff_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normal_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Closed subsets are compact, then separate disjoint compact sets.
sketch_steps: setup: Take disjoint closed sets A and B.
derive: They are compact as closed subsets of a compact space.
apply_theorem: Disjoint compact sets in a Hausdorff space are separated by open sets.
conclude: X is normal.

drafts.canonical_statement: A continuous map from a compact metric space to a metric space is uniformly continuous.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="metric_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="compact_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="metric_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="continuous_between"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="uniformly_continuous_map"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Use a finite subcover to take a uniform δ.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix ε > 0 and pick δ_x from continuity at each point x.
apply_theorem: Compactness gives a finite subcover by the balls B(x, δ_x).
construct: Let δ be the minimum of the finitely many δ_{x_i}.
derive: Points within δ both lie within 2δ_{x_i} of a common center x_i.
conclude: The triangle inequality gives d(f(y), f(z)) < ε.

drafts.proof_strategy: Minimize the continuous positive function x ↦ d(x,C) on K.
sketch_steps: setup: Dispose of the trivial cases where K or C is empty.
derive: x ↦ d(x,C) is continuous and positive on K since C is closed and disjoint from K.
apply_theorem: The extreme value theorem gives a positive minimum r on K.
conclude: Hence d(x,y) ≥ d(x,C) ≥ r for x in K and y in C.

drafts.canonical_statement: A subset K of a metric space is compact if and only if every sequence in K has a subsequence converging to a point of K.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="metric_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="compact_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="sequentially_compact_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Compactness gives cluster points; conversely use total boundedness and a Lebesgue number (outline).
sketch_steps: contradiction: A sequence without convergent subsequence contradicts a finite cover by small balls.
derive: Sequential compactness implies total boundedness via ε-separated sequences.
derive: Sequential compactness gives a Lebesgue number for any open cover.
construct: Take a finite δ-net for the Lebesgue number δ.
conclude: Each ball of the net lies in a cover member, giving a finite subcover.

drafts.canonical_statement: A subset of Euclidean space ℝ^n is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded.

drafts.proof_strategy: Enclose K in a cube, which is a finite product of compact intervals.
sketch_steps: derive: Compact implies closed and bounded in any metric space.
setup: Conversely enclose a closed bounded K in a cube [-R,R]^n.
apply_theorem: Closed intervals are compact and finite products of compact sets are compact.
conclude: K is a closed subset of a compact set, so it is compact.

drafts.proof_strategy: Take a finite subcover by half-radius balls and the minimum radius.
sketch_steps: setup: For each x in K choose r_x with B(x,2r_x) inside a cover member.
apply_theorem: Finitely many balls B(x_j,r_j) cover K.
construct: Let δ be the minimum of the radii r_j.
derive: For x in B(x_j,r_j) the triangle inequality gives B(x,δ) ⊆ B(x_j,2r_j).
conclude: Hence B(x,δ) lies in a cover member.

drafts.canonical_statement: The image of a connected set under a continuous map is connected.

drafts.proof_strategy: Pull back a separation of the image.
sketch_steps: contradiction: Assume open U and V separate f(S).
derive: Their preimages are open by continuity and separate S.
conclude: This contradicts connectedness of S, so f(S) is connected.

drafts.canonical_statement: The union of a nonempty family of connected sets sharing a common point is connected.

drafts.proof_strategy: A separation of the union would separate the member containing a second point.
sketch_steps: contradiction: Assume open U and V separate the union, with x in U.
setup: Take a point y of the union in V and a member S_i containing it.
derive: S_i contains x and y, so U and V separate S_i.
conclude: This contradicts connectedness of S_i.

drafts.canonical_statement: If S is nonempty and connected and S ⊆ T ⊆ cl(S), then T is nonempty and connected; in particular closures of nonempty connected sets are connected.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="connected_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="subset"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="subset"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="closure_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="connected_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Each part of a separation of T must meet S because T lies in the closure of S.
sketch_steps: contradiction: Assume open U and V separate T.
derive: Points of T in U are closure points of S, so U meets S; likewise V.
conclude: U and V then separate S, a contradiction.

drafts.canonical_statement: The product of two nonempty connected sets is connected in the product space.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="connected_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="connected_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="connected_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="product_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="product_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Cover the product by connected crosses through a fixed point.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix (a,b) in S × T.
construct: For each (x,y) form the cross {x} × T ∪ S × {b}.
derive: Each cross is connected as a union of two connected sets sharing (x,b).
conclude: All crosses contain (a,b), so their union S × T is connected.

drafts.canonical_statement: A nonempty subset S of ℝ is connected if and only if it contains every point between any two of its points.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="subset"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="R"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="emptyset"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="connected_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMS cd="setname1" name="R"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="interval_like"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: A missing point separates; otherwise use a supremum argument.
sketch_steps: derive: A gap z gives the separation (-∞,z) and (z,∞).
contradiction: Otherwise assume open U and V separate S with x in U and y in V.
construct: Let z be the supremum of [x,y] ∩ U.
case_split: z lies in U or in V.
conclude: Either case contradicts the supremum since U and V are open.

drafts.canonical_statement: A path-connected set is connected.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="path_connected_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="connected_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Write S as a union of connected path images through a fixed point.
sketch_steps: setup: Fix a point a in S.
derive: Each path from a to x has connected image since [0,1] is connected.
conclude: The images share a and their union is S, so S is connected.

drafts.canonical_statement: The image of a path-connected set under a continuous map is path-connected.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="path_connected_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="continuous_between"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="path_connected_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="image_of"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v4"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v3"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Compose a path with f.
sketch_steps: setup: Take two image points f(a) and f(b) with a and b in S.
derive: A path in S from a to b exists.
conclude: Composing with f gives a path in f(S).

drafts.canonical_statement: A nonempty subset of a connected space that is both open and closed is the whole space.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="and"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="preconnected_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="open_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="closed_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="neq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="emptyset"></n1:OMS></n1:OMA></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="relation1" name="eq"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: S and its complement form an open partition of X.
sketch_steps: derive: S and S^c are disjoint open sets covering X.
apply_theorem: Connectedness forces one of them to be empty.
conclude: Since S is nonempty, S^c is empty and S = X.

drafts.canonical_statement: A sequence in a Hausdorff space has at most one limit.

drafts.proof_strategy: Separate the two limits and use eventual membership.
sketch_steps: contradiction: Assume L ≠ M.
apply_theorem: Hausdorffness gives disjoint open neighborhoods.
derive: For large n the term a_n lies in both.
conclude: This contradicts disjointness.

drafts.canonical_statement: A topological space is T1 if and only if every singleton is closed.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="equivalent"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="t1_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="set1" name="in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="closed_in"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="singleton_set"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v2"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Identify the complement of a singleton with the separating open sets.
sketch_steps: translate: T1 means each point y ≠ x has an open neighborhood excluding x.
derive: Then the complement of {x} is a union of open sets.
derive: Conversely the complement of {x} itself is such a neighborhood of y.
conclude: The two conditions are equivalent.

drafts.canonical_statement: Every metric space is normal.
drafts.openmath_xml: <n1:OMOBJ xmlns:n1="http://www.openmath.org/OpenMath" version="2.0"><n1:OMBIND><n1:OMS cd="quant1" name="forall"></n1:OMS><n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMBVAR><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="logic1" name="implies"></n1:OMS><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="metric_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA><n1:OMA><n1:OMS cd="pals2" cdbase="urn:pals:openmath:cd:v1" name="normal_space"></n1:OMS><n1:OMV name="v1"></n1:OMV></n1:OMA></n1:OMA></n1:OMBIND></n1:OMOBJ>
drafts.proof_strategy: Compare the distance functions to the two closed sets.
sketch_steps: setup: Take disjoint nonempty closed sets A and B.
construct: Let U and V be the sets where d(x,A) < d(x,B) and d(x,B) < d(x,A).
derive: Continuity of distance makes U and V open, and they are disjoint.
derive: Closedness gives A ⊆ U and B ⊆ V.
conclude: X is normal.

drafts.proof_strategy: Build a dyadic chain of open sets by normality and read f off the chain (outline).
sketch_steps: construct: Use normality to build open sets U_r indexed by dyadic rationals with cl(U_r) ⊆ U_s for r < s.
setup: Arrange A ⊆ U_r and U_r disjoint from B.
construct: Define f(x) as the infimum of r with x in U_r, or 1 if none.
derive: The nesting of U_r gives continuity of f.
conclude: f is 0 on A, 1 on B and takes values in [0,1].
